the fatimids faced trouble from europe as well.


christian crusaders took jerusalem from them in 1099.


over time, the fatimid caliphate got smaller.


it was cut down to egypt alone.


in the 1160s, the fatimids grew even weaker.


a power fight split them into two rival groups:


- one side asked christian crusaders for help

- his rival reached out to a sunni muslim army for aid instead


as a result of that first ask, egypt briefly became a crusader protectorate.


by 1169, that sunni army had pushed the crusaders out.


it was led by a kurdish general named saladin.


a few years later, saladin pledged loyalty to the abbassids.


this brought egypt back into the sunni-led islamic caliphate.

# The Black Death in China and the Middle East

## Arrival in China

We do not know the exact date the Black Death reached China. Chinese records first mention a deadly epidemic between 1331 and 1334.

The Chinese Imperial Maritime Customs Service compiled its accounts in the late nineteenth century. Those records say roughly thirteen million people died during this outbreak.

For people living in China, the devastation felt like a sign. It seemed to show that the Mandate of Heaven was being withdrawn from the Yuan dynasty rulers. In Chinese thought, epidemics and droughts were omens. They signaled divine displeasure. They meant a ruler had lost God's support.

## The Plague Moves West

After destroying China, the plague spread westward. It traveled along trade routes by land and sea. These same routes carried it into much of the Middle East.

The Il-Khanate depended heavily on Silk Road trade networks. This made it very vulnerable to the plague's disruption of trade communities.

At the time, the Il-Khanate was already in trouble. It was locked in a long conflict with the Golden Horde, a rival khanate to the north. The state was reeling from invasion shock and factional disputes. In 1335, their ruler Abu Sa'id Bahadur Khan died. He may have died of the plague.

The plague hit trade hard. It also killed many people. Both effects made Mongol rule in the Il-Khanate worse after Abu Sa'id's death.

## The Fall of Tabriz

Tabriz, in modern-day Iran, had long been a thriving trade center. By the 1340s, it was largely abandoned. Foreign merchants fled the city suddenly. Commerce collapsed.

To picture this: imagine New York, Tokyo, London, and Hong Kong all turning into deserted ghost towns overnight. That is what happened to Tabriz.

Contemporary observers were shocked by its decline. But few cities escaped the plague. Infected fleas rode on trade caravans. They moved easily across central Asia and into the Middle East.

## The Mamluk Empire

Mortality rates across the Middle East were high. Most of what we know about the plague's impact in the Muslim world comes from records of the Mamluk Empire (1250–1517). That empire lost roughly one-third of its population.

The Mamluk rulers were based in Cairo. The trade routes through the Nile delta were hit especially hard.

Just as in Yuan China, localized famines made things worse in Egypt. Famines disrupted agriculture. Many rural peasants left their farms. They moved to large cities like Cairo and Alexandria. They looked for work as unskilled wage laborers.

These cities were densely populated. That raised the risk of catching the plague.

The nomads of the region had a different strategy. For generations, they knew to avoid settled areas when strange diseases appeared. They retreated into the desert. In most cases, they outran the disease.

Some of Cairo's Mamluk elite fled north in 1347. But most chose to stay. They wanted to protect their citadel from rival attacks. Staying made them vulnerable to the plague. They suffered high mortality rates.

## How the Muslim World Responded

Islamic scholars wrote treatises about the plague in the 1340s. These texts served as chronicles of the disaster. They also gave medical guidance and advice on proper conduct during epidemics.

Doctors could not define the disease. They had no cure. So the plague texts turned to religion. They offered explanations drawn from the Quran and religious law.

These texts typically described the plague as noncontagious. They told readers not to flee. The epidemic was framed in two ways:

- A chance for martyrdom for faithful Muslims
- A warning sent directly by God to infidels

Other Arab writers took a different angle. They called the plague an apocalyptic catastrophe. They said it resulted from a breach in the gate that separated humanity from Gog and Magog. In tradition, these evil forces threatened to destroy the faithful.

Despite this apocalyptic tone, the Muslim response was notably different from what happened elsewhere. It lacked the doomsday predictions seen in Christian Europe. It also lacked the persecution of minorities.

Many people did flee the plague, despite what the treatises said. But Muslim writers stressed a collective and controlled response. They promoted resignation. They urged acceptance of God's will.

## Economic Aftermath in Mamluk Cities

Many formerly thriving industries in Mamluk cities fell into deep decline during the plague. But one sector boomed: construction. There was a sudden increase in building madrasas, mosques, and tombs. Survivors used these projects to express gratitude.

Urban artisans who worked on these buildings were paid very well for their skill.

Only one other group prospered after the plague: spice merchants. Egypt remained an important depot in the international spice trade. They kept doing business while everything else stalled.

As agriculture and other trades plummeted, the golden age of Mamluk rule ended abruptly in 1341. The Mamluks continued to govern until 1517. But fierce clashes and ethnic rivalries within their empire created deep political instability. That instability ultimately led to the empire's collapse.

# The End of the Indus Valley Civilization

## Trade Stops and Cities Empty

Around 1800 BCE, trade between the Indus Valley and Mesopotamia ended. Over the next four centuries, the cities slowly lost their people. The civilization declined. This likely happened in stages. We do not know why or how it happened.

## Climate Change as a Cause

One common view points to regional climate change. Around 2000 BCE, the floodplain of the Indus River shifted dramatically. Dry river beds appeared where cities had stood and water once flowed. Changes in seasonal wind and rainfall may have caused this. In South Asia, these patterns are called the **monsoon**.

Without a secure source of water for drinking and irrigation, the cities lost population.

## Other Environmental Theories

Another theory points to environmental degradation. Centuries of urbanization and large population growth made the land unsuitable for human life.

Still other views point to different causes:

- Tectonic activity that changed the course of rivers
- Epidemic disease that decimated the population

## The Aryan Invasion Theory

Before environmental factors were considered, many scholars held a different view. They believed the Indus Valley civilization was violently destroyed in a conquest. The conquerors were nomadic Indo-European speakers who called themselves **Aryans**. They were a Sanskrit-speaking group of nomadic pastoralists. They raised cattle and horses.

Some Aryans began migrating from the Eurasian Steppe around 3500 BCE. This area lies north of the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea. Over time, different groups spread into Europe, Anatolia, Iran, Pakistan, and India.

## The Rigveda and Its Claims

The Aryan invasion theory depends heavily on Indo-European religious literature. One key text is the *Rigveda*. It was produced between 1500 and 1000 BCE in northwestern India.

The *Rigveda* contains many hymns, rituals, and descriptions of deities. Much of it deals with religious topics. These include the origin of the universe and the nature of the divine. In parts, it also discusses the arrival of the Aryans. It describes them attacking walled cities and forts of the indigenous population.

Some of these descriptions were likely written centuries after the fall of the Indus Valley civilization. They may be unrelated to that event. Still, some scholars hold that these passages describe the conquest of Mohenjo-Daro. Archaeological evidence supports this in part. It shows that Mohenjo-Daro was attacked around 1500 BCE and mostly destroyed.

## Many Causes May Have Combined

We may never know what best explains the collapse. A few causes, or all of them, may have played a role.

Environmental degradation from years of resource exploitation and high population density certainly had an effect. These issues could have been compounded by climate change and disease. In a weakened state, the people of the region would have been far more vulnerable to attack. Raiding groups like the Aryans could then exploit that weakness.

## The Civilization Ends

However it happened, by around 1500 BCE, the social and political systems had broken down. The sophisticated culture of the Indus Valley civilization had collapsed.

The architectural styles that defined the cities at their height were abandoned. The writing system was abandoned. Sophisticated metalworking and other artisanal crafts were abandoned.

The Indus Valley civilization had come to an end.

---

## 1. Trade Stops and Cities Empty

Around **1800 BCE**, trade between the Indus Valley and Mesopotamia ended.

Over the next **four centuries**, the cities slowly lost their people.

The civilization declined in stages.

We do not know why or how it happened.

---

## 2. Climate Change as a Cause

One common view points to regional climate change.

Around **2000 BCE**, the floodplain of the Indus River shifted dramatically.

Dry river beds appeared where cities had stood. Water once flowed there. Now it did not.

Changes in seasonal wind and rainfall may have caused this shift. In South Asia, these patterns are called the **monsoon**.

Without a secure source of water for drinking and irrigation, the cities lost population.

---

## 3. Other Environmental Theories

Another theory points to environmental degradation.

Centuries of urbanization and large population growth made the land unsuitable for human life.

Still other views point to different causes:

- Tectonic activity that changed the course of rivers
- Epidemic disease that decimated the population

---

## 4. The Aryan Invasion Theory

Before environmental factors were considered, many scholars held a different view.

They believed the Indus Valley civilization was violently destroyed in a conquest.

The conquerors were nomadic Indo-European speakers who called themselves **Aryans**.

They were a Sanskrit-speaking group of nomadic pastoralists. They raised cattle and horses.

Some Aryans began migrating from the Eurasian steppe around **3500 BCE**. This area lies north of the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea.

Over time, different groups spread into Europe, Anatolia, Iran, Pakistan, and India.

---

## 5. The Rigveda and Its Claims

The Aryan invasion theory depends heavily on Indo-European religious literature.

One key text is the **Rigveda**. It was produced between **1500 and 1000 BCE** in northwestern India.

The Rigveda contains many hymns, rituals, and descriptions of deities. Much of it deals with religious topics. These include the origin of the universe and the nature of the divine.

In parts, it also discusses the arrival of the Aryans. It describes them attacking walled cities and forts of the indigenous population.

Some of these descriptions were likely written centuries after the fall of the Indus Valley civilization. They may be unrelated to that event.

Still, some scholars hold that these passages describe the conquest of **Mohenjo-daro**.

Archaeological evidence supports this in part. It shows that Mohenjo-daro was attacked around **1500 BCE** and mostly destroyed.

---

We may never know what best explains the collapse. A few causes, or all of them, may have played a role.

Environmental degradation from years of resource exploitation and high population density certainly had an effect. These issues could have been compounded by climate change and disease.

In a weakened state, the people of the region would have been far more vulnerable to attack. Raiding groups like the Aryans could then exploit that weakness.

---

However it happened, by around **1500 BCE**, the social and political systems had broken down.

The sophisticated culture of the Indus Valley civilization had collapsed.

What was abandoned:

- The architectural styles that defined the cities at their height
- The writing system
- Sophisticated metalworking and other artisanal crafts

# The Inner Asian Steppe

## Land and Climate

The eastern half of the Eurasian Steppe is called the **Inner Asian Steppe**. It holds vast grasslands, mountains, and deserts. These lands are not good for farming. Few people live there today.

Climate change shaped this region's history. Rainfall once fed herds of sheep, camels, goats, and horses across the Mongolian grasslands. But when the climate cooled, the grasslands shrank. Nomads had to roam in search of new pastures. Droughts could push them further. If nearby societies refused to trade, nomads often raided farms and cities just to survive.

Around 1500 BCE, the climate turned colder and drier. Many people here gave up farming. They switched to herding livestock instead. Grazing animals needed mobile groups of people. These groups had to find new pastures quickly. They also had to protect their herds from predators. Caring for livestock forced a cultural shift. People learned to ride horses.

## Food, Language, and Neighbors

As herders, steppe peoples ate a lot of meat and dairy. They made goods from animal flesh and furs. They traded these items in farming villages.

They spoke languages unrelated to Chinese. Turkic and Mongolic are examples. A few groups, such as the Jie, may have spoken Indo-European tongues.

A changing climate limited where herders could live. This kept them in constant contact with farming civilizations like China. The Chinese often saw nomads and their herds as a threat. They viewed them as a pestilence to their own livelihoods. For centuries, the Chinese and Koreans tried to build physical and cultural barriers against steppe groups. Yet the ethnic and ancestral lines between nomads and their neighbors stayed porous.

## Power, Raids, and Trade

Raids brought prizes back to the steppes. Silk, lacquerware, grain, and war captives were common spoils. Chieftains gave these prizes to loyal supporters. In return, supporters gave their leaders new titles. One title was *chanyu*, or **khan**. A khan held supreme power over both spiritual and military matters.

Khans commanded thousands of horses. In an age of cavalry warfare, this made them even more powerful. Tribal confederations on the steppes controlled the **Silk Roads**. These were trade routes that moved luxury goods between China, central Asia, India, and the Middle East.

For a mobile society, manufactured and luxury goods held great value. They mattered in material, social, and political ways. Silk was especially treasured. It was light, which made it ideal for hot summers. It was soft, which made it good for lining beds. Powerful generals and khans who gathered huge amounts of silk used it to show their power. The same was true of other luxury goods like wine.

## Daily Life and Social Structure

Most nomadic groups in Asia lived in small units. A unit was a family or a **clan**. A clan was a small group of several families. They shared an encampment. They herded or hunted together. Clans were united by loyalty to a chieftain. The chieftain was chosen for skill as a mounted warrior.

Steppe societies were more egalitarian than many other ancient cultures. Differences in role and status between men and women were smaller here. In cities and farming towns, those gaps were wider.

Recent digs have uncovered female skeletons from the Xiongnu, Xianbei, and Turkic peoples. These remains show that women rode horses. They also practiced combat skills like archery. This likely formed the basis for folktales about legendary female warriors. Stories such as Mulan began circulating in Chinese society in the sixth century.

A mobile lifestyle limited how much wealth people could gather. It also limited how they displayed it through buildings or clothing. This may explain why written scripts were less common on the steppes. On the other hand, steppe cultures readily absorbed new technologies, goods, and ideas from their neighbors.

## Horses, War, and Legacy

Steppe peoples pioneered the domestication of the horse. This gave them a major military edge over their neighbors. Riding and hunting served as training for war. People began both activities at an early age.

Hunting was central to nomadic culture. It formed the core of rituals that marked key life changes. A child became an adult through it. A low-ranking member could rise in status through it.

The steppes stretched across both Europe and Asia. They acted as a bridge. Developments like the chariot and cavalry warfare spread from here to the rest of Asia. Chariots and mounted warriors then sparked the growth of confederations. These confederations became a serious military threat.

Conquerors from the steppes led major campaigns. One was Modun, who rose to power in 209 BCE. His campaigns marked a turning point. They changed the relationship between the Inner Asian Steppe, the rest of China, and the growing Silk Roads as key routes of exchange across the ancient world.

# Conquest and the Roman Economy

Conquest helped the Roman economy in many ways. The Romans wanted to control natural resources. They also wanted wealth from the lands they conquered. This money fed the people. It also paid the troops.

## The Army Grew Over Time

In early Rome, the army was a volunteer force. Citizens joined only during times of war. By the time of the empire, this changed. The army became a standing, professional force. Soldiers served full-time.

The **legion** was the core unit of the Roman army. Its structure changed over the centuries. But it always held about five thousand soldiers. A **legate** commanded each legion. Legions also included craftspeople. They included workers who helped with building projects.

After Augustus reformed the military, twenty-eight legions were stationed across the empire. They guarded the provinces and the frontier. Each legion had a number. It also had a nickname. The nickname came from its place of origin or where it served. Legions could move around the empire. For example, the First German legion might be found in Spain.

Soldiers served for sixteen years. This term was later raised to twenty years. At the end of service, they received a set payment. During wartime, soldiers and military staff got a large share of the wealth captured. Some were also promised land taken from conquered peoples.

## Conquest Brought Resources

Many wars were fought to secure resources and capital. The conquest of Egypt in the first century BCE greatly expanded Rome's grain supply. Earlier, Rome had also conquered Sicily and Sardinia. These lands added more grain to the empire.

People captured during conquest were often sold at Roman slave markets. Enslaved people did much of the work in Roman industry. Their labor was the backbone of the economy. Freed people contributed as well.

## The Costs of Constant War

This system had trade-offs. The army grew larger over time. The frontier kept expanding. Conflict became more expensive. In early Rome, soldiers might campaign only part of the year. By the imperial period, fighting on the frontier was a regular thing. Campaigns could last for months. Some wars seemed to go on forever.

Distance added to the cost. Rome was far from many frontiers. Running campaigns in distant lands was very expensive. The army needed money to operate and pay its soldiers. This need pushed Rome toward more conquest. Over time, this cycle strained the military.

## Social Costs of Endless Conflict

Continuous war also hurt society. Romans were proud of their military strength. But the loss of life and property weighed heavily on many people. Wars abroad disrupted regional markets. Italy depended on those markets for goods. In 190 CE, a break in the grain supply caused famine in Rome. Riots followed.

The elites largely benefited from conquest. They gained wealth and status. The lower classes bore much of the burden. They felt the negative effects most directly.

At the end of service, they received a set payment. During wartime, soldiers and military staff got a large share of captured wealth. Some were also promised land taken from conquered peoples.


## Conquest Brought Resources

Many wars were fought to secure resources and capital.

The conquest of Egypt in the first century BCE greatly expanded Rome's grain supply. Earlier, Rome had also conquered Sicily and Sardinia. These lands added more grain to the Empire.

People captured during conquest were often sold at Roman slave markets. Enslaved people did much of the work in Roman industry. Their labor was the backbone of the economy.

Freed people contributed as well.


## The Costs of Constant War

This system had trade-offs.

The army grew larger over time. The frontier kept expanding. Conflict became more expensive.

In early Rome, soldiers might campaign only part of the year. By the imperial period, fighting on the frontier was a regular thing. Campaigns could last for months. Some wars seemed to go on forever.

Distance added to the cost. Rome was far from many frontiers. Running campaigns in distant lands was very expensive.

The army needed money to operate and pay its soldiers. This need pushed Rome toward more conquest. Over time, this cycle strained the military.


## Social Costs of Endless Conflict

Continuous war also hurt society.

# The Church and Secular Power After the Carolingian Collapse

The Carolingian Empire fell apart. This left a messy situation between secular rulers and the Christian Church.

Under German law, lords controlled everything on their land. That included churches and monasteries. Lords could appoint people to church offices like abbot or bishop. To keep loyal officials in place, lords filled these roles with family members. Sometimes they simply sold the position to the highest bidder.

The result was bad for the Church. People with no religious calling could become church leaders. Some had little knowledge of Christian doctrine. Even the office of pope (the bishop of Rome) could be put up for sale.

---

# The Cluniac Reform

Many people were disgusted by how religious offices were treated. A reform movement grew to remove secular lords from church management.

This movement is linked to the monastery of **Cluny** in France. Cluny won independence from its local aristocrat. Other monasteries across France wanted the same rights and privileges. They joined Cluny's network. This created a movement called the **Cluniac reform**.

The Cluniac movement also drew in other clergy. These clergy wanted the Church itself to control the election of bishops, free from secular influence. That desire for independence reached the very top: the office of the bishop of Rome (Figure 13.16).

---

# Reforms at the Top of the Church

The bishops of Rome were shaped by the Cluniac movement. They made several key changes:

- The sale of church offices was condemned as a sin called **simony**.
- Bishops must be elected by clergy, not appointed by a lord.
- Any clergy member who bought an office (or had it bought for them) could be removed.
- Priests were told to practice celibacy and forbidden to marry. This ended the practice of passing church positions down to an officeholder's children like a fief.

Celibacy was not new in the Catholic Church. But reforming monks and popes began enforcing it with real energy.

These changes caused bitter conflict with European rulers. The Church declared that any king who tried to appoint a bishop or demanded a bribe could be **excommunicated**. Excommunication meant being placed outside the church, its communion, and its sacraments. The goal was to reform the offender. In practice, excommunication threatened a king's rule and could spark rebellions.

---

# Christianizing Warfare: The Birth of Chivalry

The reformers also wanted a more thoroughly Christian society. One way they tried this was by drawing a line between legitimate and illegitimate warfare.

The Church argued that Christian soldiers (especially knights) should follow a code of conduct based on church values. For example, they should:

- Not loot monasteries
- Not hold clergy for ransom
- Protect the church, women, and the defenseless
- Observe publicly declared truces
- Not fight on religiously significant days like Easter

These principles fed into the ideals of **chivalry**. Chivalry was a code meant to Christianize knightly violence and behavior. It never fully curbed violence. But it was one strand in a broader, secular interest in a new chivalric culture of knighthood.

Images of Christian knights also helped popes justify their actions. Popes used these images to direct Europe's military classes against peoples seen as enemies of the Church and therefore of God.

---

# The East–West Divide

The reform movement gave the Church some moral prestige. But the growing power of the pope worsened relations between the eastern and western halves of Christianity.

By the Middle Ages, five ancient seats were recognized as the most prestigious:

1. Jerusalem
2. Antioch
3. Alexandria
4. Rome
5. Constantinople

Each was led by a bishop who held the honorary title **patriarch**. By the tenth century, only Rome and Constantinople sat in territory not controlled by Muslims.

The pope in Rome and the patriarch of Constantinople shared many beliefs. But linguistic and cultural differences drove a wedge between them:

| | West (Rome) | East (Constantinople) |
|---|---|---|
| Language | Latin | Greek |
| Clergy marriage | Celibate clergy required | Priests could marry; bishops should be unmarried |
| Authority | Pope is final authority for the whole Church | Other patriarchs are equally authoritative as the pope |

The reform movement made these divisions sharper, even if it did not create them.

---

# The Great Schism of 1054

In **1054**, the pope sent representatives to the patriarch of Constantinople. They were meant to discuss differences between the two halves of the Church.

The pope's chief representative felt the patriarch was not cooperating with the embassy. He did not even seem to recognize it. So he issued a letter excommunicating the patriarch and his followers.

Soon after, the patriarch sent back his own letter. It excommunicated the pope's representatives.

This event is called the **Great Schism of 1054**. After it:

- The eastern church became known as the **Eastern Orthodox Church**.
- The western half became the **Catholic Church**.

---

# After the Schism

The Great Schism was not the only cause of the split. Tensions and disagreements had been building for a long time. But the schism made clear that Christianity was being shaped by different forces in different parts of Europe.

From this point on, popes hoped to reunite the two halves under their authority. They wanted to impose their vision of a reformed church on the Orthodox Church.

Orthodox bishops might accept the pope as "first among equals." But the papacy insisted it was the supreme authority in the entire Church. That gap would not close easily.

# The Golden Horde and the Chagatai Khanate

## A Less Centralized Empire

The Golden Horde ruled northwest Asia and the lands of the Rus. These areas were less economically developed than other Mongol territories. People there lived many different kinds of lives. Authority was less centralized than under the Il-Khans. Because of this, the Horde avoided civil war for a long time. It took outside forces to break it apart. That happened more than a generation after the Il-Khanate fell.

## How the Golden Horde Ruled

Batu and Berke were the founding leaders of the Horde. They set up a capital city. Its main job was storing tribute, just as their grandfather had done. But they did not stay in one place. They mostly roamed with their armies. They raided neighbors or defended against attacks.

The people under Golden Horde rule were very different from one another. Some were Turkish peoples like the Kipchaks. Others were seminomads similar to the Mongols. Still others were settled Slavic peasants living in small towns.

The Mongols ruled the Turks indirectly. Local leaders enforced the *yassa*. They collected taxes. They conscripted labor and soldiers. Mongol officials stayed in the capital. They received tribute and distributed it. They also heard appeals against local decisions.

The Rus and other Slavic peoples faced more direct rule. The Mongols assigned an overseer to each local ruler. These overseers made sure taxes flowed in. They kept rebellion down.

## Islam in the Golden Horde

Berke was the first khan of the Golden Horde to embrace Islam. But not all his successors became Muslim. Still, Islam kept gaining followers among the Horde's Mongols. In 1313, Uzbeg made Islam the official religion of the Golden Horde. He did not remove the *yassa*'s tax exemption for other religions. Uzbeg's support for Islam strengthened the Islamic community across the Horde's lands.

## The Orthodox Church Grows Stronger

At the same time, the Horde's rule strengthened the Orthodox Christian church in its Slavic regions. The church came to represent Rus national identity. People turned to Christianity to set themselves apart from the Mongols. In some cases, they used it as a quiet form of resistance.

The *yassa* gave religious institutions tax and service exemptions. These exemptions were larger than what the church had received from Rus nobles before. Church-owned land expanded under the Horde. People donated land to help the church provide spiritual comfort and identity. But some donations were fraud. Elites would donate their land, then become the church officials in charge of it. This let them avoid Mongol taxation and obligation.

By the time Mongol rule collapsed in the late fifteenth century, the Russian Orthodox church owned about one-third of the arable land. This was in areas formerly ruled by Rus nobles.

## Trade and the Pax Mongolica

The Golden Horde benefited from the prosperity of the Pax Mongolica. It also helped create that prosperity. Direct European trade passed under their control. Goods heading east into the Mongol world almost always entered through the Golden Horde. This was true whether the goods were made by the Rus or brought in by Italian merchants. The Horde had the first chance to buy anything that came through.

# France: A Stronger Central Government

A stronger central government grew in France during the thirteenth century. This change came from a restructuring of local government. Royal bureaucrats replaced vassals and church officials. The monarchy had enough income to pay for their loyalty.

King Phillip II began this process in the late twelfth century. French monarchs seized land from their nobles. They used these opportunities to grow royal holdings.

The new lands were managed by salaried royal appointees. These were not vassals who could pass their holdings to heirs. By the early fourteenth century, much of France was under direct royal control. This greatly increased the resources French kings could use in conflicts with their vassals and the church.


# France: Conflict with the Church

By the reign of Phillip IV (which began in 1285), the French crown's relationship with the church had badly deteriorated. The crisis escalated until 1303. That year, Phillip sent soldiers to Rome to remove Pope Boniface.

This act deeply intimidated church officials. In 1305, it was time to select Boniface's successor. The cardinals chose a Frenchman allied with Phillip. He then moved the papacy from Rome to Avignon, France. It stayed there under the watchful eyes of French kings until 1376.


# England: A Different Path

England developed differently than other European states. From the thirteenth century onward, the monarch's power over vassals and the church was limited. The basic rights of commoners were also protected. "Commoners" generally meant adult males who were not bound as servants or apprentices.

King John was forced to become the pope's vassal and pay him tribute. His vassals saw his capitulation. They felt emboldened. In 1215, they compelled John to reaffirm those rights and expand them in **Magna Carta**. This document reiterated existing rights and relationships of vassals.

The document confirmed the papal position that the church was above the state. It stated the church "shall have its rights undiminished, and its liberties unimpaired . . . by our heirs in perpetuity."

Among the rights spelled out in Magna Carta, one stood out as perhaps the most important:

> "No free man shall be seized or imprisoned, or stripped of his rights or possessions, or outlawed or exiled, or deprived of his standing in any way, nor will we proceed with force against him, or send others to do so, except by the lawful judgment of his equals."

This requirement created a precedent for **trial by jury**. Trial by jury remains a staple of the judicial system in the West to this day.


# England: The Rise of Parliament

Another key development led toward centralized government with limited and specified powers. A new deliberative body was created. It included nobles, clergy, and commoners. This body replaced the Great Council of the king's vassals and high clergy.

This new body evolved into **Parliament**. It was designed to represent the interests of the people. Membership expanded over time:

- Representatives were elected by the vassals of the king's vassals.
- Starting in 1265, selected towns could send representatives to speak for merchants' interests.


# England: Parliament's Two Powers

Parliament had two primary powers.

**Power one:** Approve all tax increases.

**Power two:** Approve laws. Edward I asked Parliament to do this. His goal was uniform rule by the monarch. This replaced a decentralized set of laws from the nobility and a potentially conflicting set from the church.

Parliamentary approval made the laws England's laws, not just the king's laws. Even if the king had drafted them, the nobles, clergy, and wealthy commoners still had to agree.

Edward I called his first Parliament in 1275. During his thirty-five-year reign, the body met forty-six times.


# The Iberian Peninsula: Shared Struggles

In the thirteenth century, the Iberian Peninsula was split between Christian kingdoms and parts of the Islamic Almohad Caliphate. The Christian kingdoms held about three-fifths of the land. They were:

- Portugal
- Leon
- Navarre
- Castile
- Aragon

These kingdoms fought each other. They also fought their Islamic rivals. The same conflicts appeared between vassals and king, and between monarch and church, as in other Christian kingdoms.

The church and vassals joined together. They provided the king with revenue they deemed sufficient to keep the kingdom safe and orderly. Any further resources had to be agreed upon by a council called the **Cortes**. The Cortes included vassals, clergy, and merchant representatives.

As in England, the church and vassals were able to avoid being bypassed by kings. They asserted checks on royal finances and power.

2. France: Conflict with the Church
3. England: A Different Path
4. England: The Rise of Parliament
5. England: Parliament's Two Powers
6. The Iberian Peninsula: Shared Struggles

# France: A Stronger Central Government

In the 1300s, France built a stronger central government.

How? By changing how local areas were run.

The king replaced vassals and church officials with his own paid workers (bureaucrats).

The monarchy now had enough money to pay them for their loyalty.


**Who started this?**

King Phillip II began the process in the late 1200s.

French kings took land from their nobles.

They used that land to grow royal holdings.


**How was the new land managed?**

The king appointed paid officials to run it.

These were not vassals.

A vassal could pass his land to his heirs.

The king's appointees could not.


By the early 1300s, much of France sat under direct royal control.

This gave French kings far more resources.

They could now fight their vassals and the church with greater strength.


---

# France: Conflict with the Church

By the time Phillip IV took the throne in 1285, things between the crown and the church had gone badly wrong.

The crisis peaked in 1303.

That year, Phillip sent soldiers to Rome.

Their job: remove Pope Boniface from power.

This act deeply frightened church officials.


In 1305, it was time to pick a new pope.

The cardinals chose a Frenchman who was allied with Phillip.

He then moved the papacy from Rome to Avignon, France.

The papacy stayed in Avignon until 1376.

For over 70 years, French kings kept a close watch on it.


---

# England: A Different Path

England developed differently from other European states.

From the 1200s onward, the king's power was limited.

He could not do whatever he wanted to vassals or the church.

The basic rights of commoners were also protected.


**Who counted as a "commoner"?**

Generally: adult males who were not bound as servants or apprentices.


**What happened with King John?**

King John was forced to become the pope's vassal.

He had to pay tribute.

His own vassals watched this happen. They felt emboldened.

In 1215, they compelled John to reaffirm their rights and expand them in **Magna Carta**.

This document restated existing rights and relationships of vassals.


**What did Magna Carta say about the church?**

It confirmed that the church stood above the state.

It stated:

> "The church shall have its rights undiminished, and its liberties unimpaired . . . by our heirs in perpetuity."


**What was the most important right in Magna Carta?**

One clause stood out above all others:

> "No free man shall be seized or imprisoned, or stripped of his rights or possessions, or outlawed or exiled, or deprived of his standing in any way. Nor will we proceed with force against him, or send others to do so, except by the lawful judgment of his equals."

This created a precedent for **trial by jury**.

Trial by jury is still a core part of Western legal systems today.


---

# England: The Rise of Parliament

Another key development pushed England toward centralized government with limited, specified powers.

A new deliberative body was created.

It included nobles, clergy, and commoners.

This body replaced the old Great Council (made up only of the king's vassals and high clergy).


This new body evolved into **Parliament**.

Its purpose: represent the interests of the people.

Membership grew over time.

- Vassals of the king's vassals elected representatives.
- Starting in 1265, selected towns could send representatives to speak for merchants' interests.


---

# England: Parliament's Two Powers

Parliament held two primary powers.

**Power one:** Approve all tax increases.

**Power two:** Approve laws.


Edward I asked Parliament to approve laws.

His goal was uniform rule by the monarch.

This replaced a patchwork of local laws from the nobility and a potentially conflicting set from the church.

Parliamentary approval made the laws England's laws, not just the king's laws.

Even if the king had drafted them, the nobles, clergy, and wealthy commoners still had to agree.


Edward I called his first Parliament in 1275.

During his thirty-five-year reign, the body met forty-six times.


---

# The Iberian Peninsula: Shared Struggles

In the 1300s, the Iberian Peninsula was split between Christian kingdoms and parts of the Islamic Almohad Caliphate.

The Christian kingdoms held about three-fifths of the land.

They were:

- Portugal
- Leon
- Navarre
- Castile
- Aragon


These kingdoms fought each other.

They also fought their Islamic rivals.

The same conflicts appeared here as in other Christian kingdoms: vassals versus king, and monarch versus church.


**How did the church and vassals protect themselves?**

The church and vassals joined together.

They gave the king revenue they deemed sufficient to keep the kingdom safe and orderly.

Any resources beyond that had to be agreed upon by a council called the **Cortes**.

The Cortes included vassals, clergy, and merchant representatives.


As in England, the church and vassals avoided being bypassed by kings.

They asserted checks on royal finances and power.

# Life of Enslaved People in the Roman Empire

Enslaved people lived very different lives across the empire. Their daily life depended on their age. It also depended on their gender. Location mattered too. Rural life was not like urban life.

They held many kinds of jobs. Some were unskilled laborers. Others were artisans. Many assisted merchants and shopkeepers.

Some received training in skilled roles. They became teachers, doctors, musicians, or actors. Others built public works. This included bridges and roads. A few even served as imperial administrators.

In the city, life could be somewhat better. In a household especially, enslaved people had more advantages. They avoided the brutal physical labor found elsewhere. Mines, quarries, and *latifundia* across the empire demanded that harsh work.

On those large estates, more than one hundred enslaved persons might labor at once. Their lives were hard. They wore poor clothing. They faced cruel treatment. Many could not save enough money to buy their freedom.

---

## The Constant Threat of Punishment

No matter where they lived, enslaved people were always in danger. A slaveholder could punish them at any moment. Slaveholders feared conspiracy and rebellion. This fear shaped everything.

A culture of uncertainty grew from this constant threat. Coercion and submission became the norm. Enslaved people could be whipped. They could be beaten or tortured. Many suffered sexual abuse as well.

The writer Petronius captured part of this reality in his novel *Satyricon*. He wrote it in the first century CE. In it, a freed man named Trimalchio speaks about his past:

> "Still, I was my master's favorite for fourteen years. No disgrace in obeying your master's orders. Well, I used to amuse my mistress too. You know what I mean; I say no more, I am not a conceited man."

Enslaved people who ran away faced severe punishment if caught. Owners could brand them with a mark. Or they could force them to wear a collar. The collar carried the owner's name on it.

---

## Family and Work in the Household

The law denied enslaved people official marriage rights. Still, many formed families. They had children. This often happened in urban settings.

A slaveholder could manipulate these relationships for personal gain. There was no protection against this.

Enslaved children were put to work as well. Their duties might be simple tasks inside the house. Over time, an enslaved person might move into a different role within that same household. This was not a promotion in any free sense. It simply changed their daily tasks under the same owner's control.

# The Rise of Islam

## A New Religion in Western Arabia

At the start of the seventh century, the Byzantines and the Sasanians were at war. In western Arabia, something new was forming. A new world religion was taking shape. It drew deeply on the environment, people, and cultures of the late antique Middle East.

That religion was **Islam**. The word means "submission [to the one God]." Islam is a monotheistic faith. It shares many features with Judaism and Christianity. But it also has features that were uniquely Arabian. Over time, these features brought the culture and traditions of the Arabian Peninsula to greater prominence.

## Why Understanding the Origins Is Hard

Understanding Islam's origins and early decades can be challenging. Here is why:

- Much of what we know comes from sources *within* the Muslim community.
- These sources often assume the reader is already a believer.
- Because of this, they omit important details.
- Many people at this time were illiterate.
- They did not write their history as it happened.
- So we have less evidence outside religious scripture to help us reconstruct events.

The Arabs placed great emphasis on remembering the past. They remembered events and people from earlier times. But they passed this information down mainly through **memorization** and **oral recitation**. Memory aids, such as poetry, were vital tools. Material was passed down through generations this way. Written histories for future readers were seen as less important than the living "performance" of information through the oral tradition.

## Oral Tradition Was Not Unusual

Other contemporary societies had focused on writing for centuries before the seventh century. But the Arab commitment to oral transmission in this period was not unprecedented.

- The history of early Judaism was also transmitted orally before being written down much later.
- Historians face similar challenges reconstructing the origins of Christianity, because little contemporaneous writing survives.
- Memorializing and transmitting events through epic poetry has a long precedent. In the Mediterranean world, we see this in *The Iliad* and *The Odyssey*, attributed to the Greek poet Homer. In the ancient Indian world, we see it in the *Mahabharata*.

## The Center of Islam's Founding

Three things sit at the center of Islam's founding:

1. The city of **Mecca**
2. The worship of one God—**Allah**
3. The leadership of the **prophets**

Even to Muslims today, Allah is not a god separate from the God of Judaism and Christianity. "Allah" is simply the Arabic word meaning "the one God." In fact, Christians who live in the Middle East and speak Arabic refer to the God of the Christian Bible using the word "Allah" in their own worship.

Belief in the one God and the message of the Islamic prophet Muhammad is the first and most important of the **Five Pillars of Islam**. This pillar is called the **shahada**, or profession of faith. To embrace Islam, a person must recognize this creed:

> "There is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is the messenger of God."

Muhammad, as recognized by Muslims, was the final prophet in a long line. The one God had communicated with prophets throughout history. These included figures such as Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus. Muhammad was a divinely chosen man. He is not worshipped as a God. Nor has he ever been worshipped as a relative of God himself.

## The Other Pillars of Islam

Many of the other pillars share features with other world religions. These include ritual fasting, charity, and daily prayer. For Muslims, these acts are specified in particular ways:

- **Daily prayer** while facing the direction of the holy mosque in Mecca
- **Almsgiving**: donating money and goods to the community and people in need
- **Fasting** (if able) during **Ramadan**, the holy month when the Quran was first revealed to Muhammad
- Participating at least once (if able) in the pilgrimage to Mecca, called the **hajj**. During the hajj, pilgrims relive important moments from the life of Abraham and his family's arrival in Arabia. They also circle the house of God, the **Kaaba**, in prayer.

## Islam as a Continuation, Not a Break

Muslims have believed throughout their history that Islam is not a new faith created in the seventh century. Instead, they see it this way:

- The faith Muhammad brought to the Arabs in the early 600s was a **corrective** to earlier monotheistic religions.
- From the perspective of most Muslims, Islam is the same faith as Judaism and Christianity.
- Adherents of all three traditions worship the same God.
- All three recognize divine intercession in humanity through the leadership of prophets.

Muslims also recognize the holy scriptures of Judaism and Christianity. They believe these were given to humans by God but then corrupted over time. Islam thus sees itself as a purer form of these faiths, directly connected to both. The shared history and lineage of all three runs through the prophet **Abraham**, whom all list as an ancestor. Many modern scholars of religion refer to Judaism, Christianity, and Islam as the **Abrahamic faiths**.

## Uniquely Arabian Features

For all the influence that other monotheistic worship in the region may have had on Islam's formation, the faith has many features we might consider uniquely Arab or Arabian.

**The setting.** The land of modern Israel and Palestine played a central role in the narratives of Judaism and Christianity. But much of the story of Islam's formation as a distinct religion is found in western Arabia. This region of the peninsula is called the **Hijaz**. Its holiest sites lie here. The life of its founder was spent almost entirely there.

**The language.** The faith is firmly connected to Arabic, the indigenous language of the region. This connection is strongest in its holiest scriptures. It also shows up in cultural features, such as the survival of Arabic poetry as a means of recording the past.

**Tribal structure.** The tribal structure of pre-Islamic Arabian society defined the first several decades of the religion and the states it inspired. There was a social hierarchy that made conversion to Islam nearly impossible for most of the faith's first century—unless an individual was first embraced as a member of an Arab tribe. In this way, conversion was tied to the old ways of the Arabs. A convert did not need to be of a particular ethnicity or bloodline. But they did need to adopt the cultural traditions and markers of Arabian tribal society. For these earliest adherents, it seems likely that they felt the one God had chosen the western Arabian peoples and their traditions for special recognition. Embracing these features was a prerequisite for being among the "chosen" people.

**The prophet.** But perhaps nothing was more influential than the Muslims' belief in the leadership and message of the man whom God chose as his final prophet: an Arab from the early seventh century, from the Hijaz of western Arabia.

# Agriculture in Africa: Origins and Spread

## Three Regions of Farming

Scholars still debate how agriculture began in Africa. But most agree on one thing. Farming started in three separate regions:

- Along the Nile River in Egypt
- In the eastern Sahara of Sudan
- In the great bend of the Niger River in West Africa

The oldest evidence for farming in Africa is found along the Nile Valley in Egypt. After 7000 BCE, new agricultural knowledge arrived in this region. People brought techniques for growing wheat and barley. They also domesticated sheep, goats, and cattle. These methods likely came from southwest Asia. This change transformed the region. It put Egypt on a path to greatness. Over the next few thousand years, these farming practices spread west across North Africa. They reached Libya, Tunisia, Algeria, and Morocco.

## Farming in the Grasslands South of the Sahara

South of the Sahara, agriculture developed on its own. This process began as early as 9000 BCE. The Nilo-Saharan people of this region adopted grain-collecting and grinding techniques from their northern neighbors. They applied these methods to sorghum and pearl millet. These are tropical grasses native to the Nile region.

A long wet period made these changes possible. This wet phase began around 11,000 BCE and lasted for millennia. Monsoon-like weather rained heavily on the Sahara. Lakes formed. The landscape became lush with grasses and acacia forests. Countless varieties of wildlife lived there.

By around 8000 BCE, the Nilo-Saharans had domesticated wild cattle from the Red Sea hills. They also began making pottery. They used this pottery to store and cook their grains. By as early as 6000 BCE, gathering wild grains was turning into deliberate domestication. Over the next few thousand years, they domesticated many other plants. These included watermelons, cotton, and gourds.

## Farming in West Africa: The Niger River Bend

Far to the west of the Nilo-Saharans, agriculture also emerged on its own. This happened in the bend of the Niger River in West Africa. There, the Niger-Congo peoples began domesticating yams. This process developed slowly. It likely happened in a piecemeal fashion. It may have begun around the same time the Nilo-Saharans were adopting agriculture in the eastern Sahara.

By 3000 BCE, the Niger-Congo peoples were actively clearing land with stone tools. They planted crops such as yams, oil palm, peas, and groundnuts. Over the next couple of thousand years, they also domesticated a uniquely African variety of rice. They grew this rice in the wetlands of the Niger River region.

## Bronze Tools Boost Farming

Advances in metallurgy made farming even more productive. Bronze was introduced into Egypt from the Near East and Eastern Mediterranean just before 3000 BCE. From there, bronze technology spread west across North Africa. It also moved south up the Nile into sub-Saharan Africa.

Bronze is far harder than the materials these people had used before. This greatly increased agricultural output. Wooden plows could only scratch the surface of the soil. Bronze-bladed plows pulled by oxen could dig deep. They turned over large amounts of earth.

## Iron: A Harder Metal to Work

Iron tools were not unknown in Egypt during the Bronze Age. An iron dagger was placed in Pharaoh Tutankhamun's tomb in 1323 BCE. Archaeologists have also found several hundred iron objects in sites around the Near East and Eastern Mediterranean. These date to centuries before the Iron Age began. However, most of these early iron objects were ornamental. They included things like iron jewelry.

Iron is far more difficult to produce than bronze. The types of iron objects made earlier were weaker than bronze. That is why early iron items tended to be decorative rather than practical. Only after about 1000 BCE did the number of iron tools begin to overtake bronze tools across the Near East.

The Late Bronze Age Collapse (1200–1100 BCE) changed things. During this period, tin became hard to acquire. Tin is needed to make bronze. People began experimenting with iron more seriously. By about 900 BCE, many blacksmiths around the Near East had mastered ironworking. They could now create iron tools far stronger than bronze ones. Evidence of sophisticated ironworking in Egypt dates to the seventh century BCE. This technology was introduced from other parts of the Near East.

## Ironworking in Sub-Saharan Africa

For many years, historians assumed that ironworking spread to other parts of Africa from Egypt. The current consensus is different. Most modern scholars believe ironworking was developed independently in sub-Saharan Africa. They agree that iron smelting in sub-Saharan Africa likely predated its introduction into Egypt by a few centuries.

The earliest evidence dates to about 1000 BCE. It comes from Central Africa—modern Chad, the Central African Republic, and South Sudan. From there, the technology spread west to the Niger River area. By 500 BCE, it was being used by the Nok culture of West Africa.

## The Nok Culture and the Spread of Iron

The Nok people settled around the confluence of the Benue and Niger Rivers in present-day Nigeria. At first, they used iron to make jewelry. Eventually, they began using it for farming tools and weapons.

Iron had clear advantages. It made tougher, more durable tools. These tools could:

- Clear forests
- Aerate land
- Dig trench-based irrigation systems

Others saw the value of this new material. Over the next several centuries, ironworking technology spread around West Africa and later far beyond.

## The Bantu Migrations and Iron Age Farms

Migrating Bantus found iron technology indispensable. They used iron tools to clear surrounding trees. They extended prehistoric irrigation systems by digging deeper furrows. These furrows were shored up with embankments. Together, they created Iron Age farms. In this way, the Bantu spread ironworking technology throughout equatorial and subequatorial Africa.

# The Yuan Dynasty: A Different Kind of Rule

## How the Yuan Ruled Differently

The Yuan dynasty kept some Song policies. One example was rotating officeholders in their posts. But overall, it ruled very differently from earlier Chinese dynasties.

Kublai Khan made one major change. He replaced the old Confucian class system with a new one. The old system sorted people by economic role. The new system sorted them by ethnicity.

## The Four-Class System

The Yuan class structure had four levels:

- **Class 1:** Mongols
- **Class 2:** Non-Chinese peoples (Europeans, Jurchen, Tangut, Khitan)
- **Class 3:** Han Chinese who had lived under Jin rule in the north
- **Class 4:** Song Chinese who lived in the south

Mongols were not allowed to marry people from the bottom two classes.

Census records tracked each family's class. They also listed each head of household's occupation. Sometimes the government assigned an occupation if there was a shortage of certain workers.

## Separate Rules for Different Peoples

The Yuan borrowed an idea from the Khitan. That idea: rule different groups in different ways. So the dynasty set up separate administrations for its varied peoples.

More Mongols were becoming literate over time. Kublai himself could read. He was the first Mongol great khan to do so. Still, the old mandarin written exam system fell into disuse.

Mongols followed the *yassa* (Mongol law). The next two classes also followed it. Administrators governed these groups. Those administrators were appointed by either the chief local Mongol official or the emperor himself.

The Song Chinese sat at the bottom of the class system. Two administrators governed them:

- One was a Chinese person
- One was a Mongol or non-Chinese person

Both held their posts as imperial appointees. The Chinese administrator answered to his counterpart. He worked under that person's supervision.

All officials in these roles were rotated on a set schedule. This stopped anyone from building a local power base.

## Unwilling Bureaucrats

Some non-Chinese administrators did not want Yuan government jobs at all. They came seeking favors. Often they wanted the right to trade. In return, emperors required them to do administrative work.

One of these bureaucrats became world-famous: **Marco Polo**. He was a young merchant from Venice. He traveled with a Venetian trade caravan. He and several family members spent almost twenty-five years in Mongol lands. He later wrote a popular account of their experiences.

The Polos were the most famous "hostage bureaucrats." They served for about twenty years. But most of these officials were Muslim traders from other parts of the Mongol Empire.

No matter how well they worked, these outside bureaucrats rarely bonded with local populations. They did not build power bases that could challenge imperial authority.

## The Exam System Returns (1315)

Kublai died in 1294. After his death, flaws in his system became clear.

In 1315, his great-grandson **Buyantu** brought back the mandarin exam system. But it now reflected the dual nature of Yuan rule:

- Non-Chinese people took different exams than Chinese people
- The non-Chinese exams were shorter
- Between 25 and 50 percent of those who passed had to be non-Chinese

This quota had a big effect. Song Chinese made up more than 90 percent of the population, according to Yuan censuses. So the pool of Chinese candidates was huge. The smaller pool of non-Chinese candidates benefited from the quota. Between the easier exams and the set percentage, it was much simpler for Mongols and non-Chinese people to pass than for Chinese people.

## A Stagnant Economy

Travelers like Marco Polo wrote about Yuan China's impressive wealth. The North African Muslim traveler **Ibn Battuta** also noted its riches. But economic growth had at best stalled. Two main causes: inflation and heavy taxation. Together, they cut consumer purchasing power.

### Paper Money and Inflation

Paper currency was a major driver of inflation. On paper (pun intended), it could be exchanged for metal or silk. In practice, the Yuan government printed far more notes than it had metal or silk to back them up.

Kublai decreed that people must use this currency in transactions with the government. This guaranteed that paper money played a role in at least some economic activity. But it also trapped the population. They could not avoid inflation. Successive Yuan governments printed more paper money to pay their own bills. Then they forced the public to buy that same money to pay taxes.

More paper entered the system with no real value behind it. So people needed ever more of it to buy the same goods and labor.

### Where the Money Went

Rising taxes fed into narrow, unproductive sectors of the economy. This drained wealth from everything else. The Yuan spent lavishly on grand military campaigns that failed. These bankrupted the government. Most were Kublai's projects:

- Two invasions of what is now Vietnam
- Two sea invasions of Japan (even more costly)
- One sea invasion of Java

### Succession Chaos

The dynasty also faced periods of chaos from succession struggles. After Kublai's appointed successor and grandson died in 1307, **seven emperors** reigned over the next twenty-six years.

Resentment grew beneath the surface. It was strongest among the Song population. Government extraction of resources kept rising. Inflation kept eroding living standards.

## The Black Death and the End

In 1331, people outside the capital in the **Hebei** area began to sicken and die in large numbers. Within three years, **90 percent** of that region's population was dead from a strange new illness. It later became known as the **Black Death**.

The Mongol Yuan government, like much of its own people, did not survive long after this blow.

# Guns and the End of Nomadic Life

## How guns changed the world

Guns spread across Europe, Asia, and Africa. This change marked the beginning of the end for some nomadic cultures.

Before guns arrived, nomads shaped world history. They were key drivers of major historical change.

**The Indian subcontinent.** Around 1500 BCE, mounted Indo-Europeans arrived in India. Their arrival transformed life there. The Vedas are their sacred texts. Hinduism was built on those texts. The Indo-European social structure became the basis for the Hindu caste system. Sanskrit, their language, became the sacred tongue of both Hinduism and Buddhism.

**The Roman Empire.** Nomadic tribes in central Asia helped bring down Rome. In the fourth and fifth centuries CE, the Huns moved westward. They lived across central Asia, the Caucasus, and eastern Europe. The Huns attacked Germanic tribes on Rome's borders. Those tribes included the Goths and Visigoths. The Germans fled into Roman territory. This destabilized the empire.

**China.** Mounted nomads had a similar effect in East Asia. Over many centuries, groups like the Xiongnu and the Jurchen traded with Han Chinese settlements. They also attacked them. During the Qin dynasty (around 221 BCE), China began building a wall. The goal was to protect settled areas from roaming riders. The wall failed. It only covered parts of the border between Chinese lands and nomad territory. When the wall did not work, emperors paid tribute. They gave gifts and even Chinese princesses to aggressive tribes. This practice showed that women's status was seen as secondary to men's needs and power, even for high-ranking women.

## Why nomads settled down

In the early modern era, nomadic societies began to settle more often. Firearms played a role in this shift.

When guns and artillery became more accurate, they could fire farther and faster. Mounted archers could not compete with that firepower.

However, guns do not fully explain why nomadic life faded. Early firearms were heavy and awkward. They were hard to fire from horseback. Once guns got lighter, nomads *could* have adopted them. Some did. The Plains Indians of North America are one example.

## Not all nomads rode horses

Some nomads were mounted warriors. The Mongols, Arab Bedouins, Huns, and Xiongnu all fit this group.

But many nomadic groups never rode horses or formed armies. The Sami reindeer herders of Scandinavia and Russia are one example. The Gaddi shepherds of the Himalaya are another. Neither group was traditionally a warrior culture.

Settled societies also used mounted warriors. European knights in the Middle Ages are a clear case. Gunpowder and firearms ended the age of the knight. But it took several centuries for mounted warriors to fully leave armies. In World War I, European and U.S. forces still used cavalry.

So it is more accurate to say this: gunpowder made cavalry obsolete (except modern "cavalry," meaning tanks). It did not make nomads disappear. Today, mounted warriors are a thing of the past. But nomadic societies still exist around the world. Their numbers are much smaller now. Many modern Mongols and Arab Bedouin still live a nomadic life.

## Why states pushed nomads to settle

Firearms forced many nomads to adapt. Military, political, and social realities were changing. This push led many groups toward settled life (sedentarization).

But guns were only the *means*. They were not the *reason* nomadic groups declined. Modern states used guns to enforce their will on nomads. The reasons for that conflict varied.

**Fear.** Settled people often feared nomads. This was true especially when nomads waged war or competed for natural resources. In North America, settlers feared the mounted Plains Indians. They also wanted the land those tribes occupied. As long as Plains tribes claimed their hunting grounds, colonizing farmers, ranchers, and miners could not use the resources of the American West freely.

**Borders.** Modern nation-states have permanent borders. They did not want nomads crossing from one country to another at will. States saw nomads as a threat to national security and sovereignty. So they forced nomads to settle. Settled people were also easier to tax than people who were always on the move.

**Industrialization.** As nations industrialized, nomads lost access to what their herds needed. Private lands got fenced off. Water sources became polluted. Commercial livestock operations grazed the grasslands. Those operations produced meat for city dwellers. At the same time, industrialization made settled life more comfortable. Many nomads chose to leave their traditional way of life on their own.

## Climate change: a new threat

In the twentieth and twenty-first centuries, climate change has made nomadic life harder. Droughts are getting worse. Weather is becoming more severe. Both threaten grasslands and water sources for animals. A lack of grass is disastrous for nomadic pastoralists.

History shows how fragile this balance can be. At the Battle of Ain Jalut, soldiers of the Mamluk Sultanate used early cannons. But those cannons were not what won them the battle. The Mongol force they faced was much smaller than a typical Mongol army. The arid climate of the Levant could not supply enough grass for thousands of horses. Mongol warriors usually traveled with five or six horses each. Without enough grass, the Mongols had to field a smaller army.

Today, more nomad homelands face desertification and harsh winter temperatures. This may be the final blow for the world's few remaining nomadic societies.

# Guns and the End of Nomadic Life

## How Guns Changed the World

Guns spread across Europe, Asia, and Africa.

This change marked the beginning of the end for some nomadic cultures.

Before guns arrived, nomads shaped world history.

They were key drivers of major historical change.

---

### The Indian Subcontinent

Around 1500 BCE, mounted Indo-Europeans arrived in India.

Their arrival transformed life there.

The Vedas are their sacred texts.

Hinduism was built on those texts.

The Indo-European social structure became the basis for the Hindu caste system.

Sanskrit, their language, became the sacred tongue of both Hinduism and Buddhism.

---

### The Roman Empire

Nomadic tribes in Central Asia helped bring down Rome.

In the fourth and fifth centuries CE, the Huns moved westward.

They lived across Central Asia, the Caucasus, and eastern Europe.

The Huns attacked Germanic tribes on Rome's borders.

Those tribes included the Goths and Visigoths.

The Germans fled into Roman territory.

This destabilized the empire.

---

### China

Mounted nomads had a similar effect in East Asia.

Over many centuries, groups like the Xiongnu and the Jurchen traded with Han Chinese settlements.

They also attacked them.

During the Qin Dynasty (around 221 BCE), China began building a wall.

The goal was to protect settled areas from roaming riders.

The wall failed.

It only covered parts of the border between Chinese lands and nomad territory.

When the wall did not work, emperors paid tribute.

They gave gifts and even Chinese princesses to aggressive tribes.

This practice showed that women's status was seen as secondary to men's needs and power, even for high-ranking women.

---

## Why Nomads Settled Down

In the early modern era, nomadic societies began to settle more often.

Firearms played a role in this shift.

When guns and artillery became more accurate, they could fire farther and faster.

Mounted archers could not compete with that firepower.

However, guns do not fully explain why nomadic life faded.

Early firearms were heavy and awkward.

They were hard to fire from horseback.

Once guns got lighter, nomads could have adopted them.

Some did.

The Plains Indians of North America are one example.

---

## Not All Nomads Rode Horses

Some nomads were mounted warriors.

The Mongols, Arab Bedouins, Huns, and Xiongnu all fit this group.

But many nomadic groups never rode horses or formed armies.

The Sami reindeer herders of Scandinavia and Russia are one example.

The Gaddi shepherds of the Himalaya are another.

Neither group was traditionally a warrior culture.

---

Settled societies also used mounted warriors.

European knights in the Middle Ages are a clear case.

Gunpowder and firearms ended the age of the knight.

But it took several centuries for mounted warriors to fully leave armies.

In World War I, European and U.S. forces still used cavalry.

So it is more accurate to say this:

Gunpowder made cavalry obsolete (except modern "cavalry," meaning tanks).

It did not make nomads disappear.

Today, mounted warriors are a thing of the past.

But nomadic societies still exist around the world.

Their numbers are much smaller now.

Many modern Mongols and Arab Bedouin still live a nomadic life.

---

## Why States Pushed Nomads to Settle

Firearms forced many nomads to adapt.

Military, political, and social realities were changing.

This push led many groups toward settled life (sedentarization).

But guns were only the means.

They were not the reason nomadic groups declined.

Modern states used guns to enforce their will on nomads.

The reasons for that conflict varied.

---

### Fear

Settled people often feared nomads.

This was true especially when nomads waged war or competed for natural resources.

In North America, settlers feared the mounted Plains Indians.

They also wanted the land those tribes occupied.

As long as Plains tribes claimed their hunting grounds, colonizing farmers, ranchers, and miners could not use the resources of the American West freely.

---

### Borders

Modern nation-states have permanent borders.

They did not want nomads crossing from one country to another at will.

States saw nomads as a threat to national security and sovereignty.

So they forced nomads to settle.

Settled people were also easier to tax than people who were always on the move.

---

### Industrialization

As nations industrialized, nomads lost access to what their herds needed.

Private lands got fenced off.

Water sources became polluted.

Commercial livestock operations grazed the grasslands.

Those operations produced meat for city dwellers.

At the same time, industrialization made settled life more comfortable.

Many nomads chose to leave their traditional way of life on their own.

---

## Climate Change: A New Threat

In the twentieth and twenty-first centuries, climate change has made nomadic life harder.

Droughts are getting worse.

Weather is becoming more severe.

Both threaten grasslands and water sources for animals.

A lack of grass is disastrous for nomadic pastoralists.

History shows how fragile this balance can be.

At the Battle of Ain Jalut, soldiers of the Mamluk Sultanate used early cannons.

But those cannons were not what won them the battle.

The Mongol force they faced was much smaller than a typical Mongol army.

The arid climate of the Levant could not supply enough grass for thousands of horses.

Mongol warriors usually traveled with five or six horses each.

Without enough grass, the Mongols had to field a smaller army.

Today, more nomad homelands face desertification and harsh winter temperatures.

This may be the final blow for the world's few remaining nomadic societies.

# The Rise and Fall of the Songhai Empire

## A Golden Age Under Askia the Great

Under **Askia the Great**, the Songhai Empire flourished.

Religious scholars came to cities like **Timbuktu** and **Djenné**. Poets followed them. Islam became more widely practiced across the empire.

The state built new infrastructure. Workers dug canals to boost crop production. Trans-Saharan trade thrived.

## Power Shifts at Court

As Askia grew older, his personal grip on power weakened. He leaned heavily on palace officials to run the empire.

This upset his family. They resented **Ali Fulan**, Askia's head chamberlain. Ali Fulan held too much influence.

## Civil War and Collapse (1528–1531)

In **1528**, Askia's sons revolted. They deposed him. They declared one brother, **Musa**, the new king.

The transition was not peaceful. Civil war broke out.

As Musa fought his own kin to keep the throne, dozens of relatives were killed. In **1531**, Musa's brothers killed him. The crisis deepened.

One ruler after another tried to govern. Each failed. Political chaos spread through the ruling class and the military. Everyone vied for control.

Without strong leadership from the center, Songhai weakened. Outside groups began watching closely. They wanted a chance to seize the lucrative trans-Saharan trade in **salt** and **gold**. The **Saadi dynasty of Morocco** was especially interested.

## The Saadi Build Up (1578–1591)

In **1578**, the Saadi repelled a Portuguese invasion. But the cost was enormous. The imperial treasury was drained.

To avoid bankruptcy, Sultan **Ahmad I al-Mansur Saadi** searched for new sources of wealth.

Meanwhile, Songhai had found some stability. A calm period began under **Askia Ishaq II**, who took power in **1588**. But this revival would not last long.

## The Battle of Tondibi (1591)

In **1591**, the Saadi invaded Songhai.

The Saadi army was far smaller than the Songhai forces. Yet it held a huge advantage: guns, ammunition, and cannon. These weapons came from **Queen Elizabeth I of England**. She hoped to turn Morocco into an ally against Spain.

The Saadi army also included many Spanish Muslims. In **1502**, the Spanish monarchs had ordered all Muslims in Spain to convert to Christianity. Many fled the country. They joined forces like the Saadi's.

Outmatched, the larger Songhai army was defeated at the **Battle of Tondibi**. Askia Ishaq II was killed.

## Destruction and the End of an Empire

After winning on the battlefield, the Saadi commander moved on the empire's key cities. His name was **Judar Pasha**, an enslaved Spanish eunuch.

The Saadi sacked and pillaged **Djenné**, **Gao**, and **Timbuktu**. They burned these cities to the ground.

To seal their victory, the invaders filled in water wells. They destroyed fields of crops. They spared few people. Not even women and children were safe.

The looting and destruction broke Songhai's power. A decade later, the empire was shattered. Its provinces split into several smaller kingdoms and territories.

# The Sahara Trade Routes

Europeans had long known about three ancient trade routes through the Saharan Desert.

In the western Sahara, a route ran from Taghaza to Timbuktu. Farther east, a second route linked the oasis town of Ghadames with trade centers in Hausaland. A third route connected Tripoli, a major Mediterranean port city, with Bornu deep in the Central African interior.

Centuries of caravan travel had not made these routes safe. They remained dangerous. Travelers who knew the routes well understood where key cities and oases lay. They also understood the risks of Saharan weather patterns. These people were best positioned to control trans-Saharan trade and profit from it.

Muslim and Arab travelers and caravanners held this knowledge. It was in their interest to keep it secret. Sharing it would cut into their profits. So they monopolized the information.

As a result, European maps of the African interior stayed vague. Distances were only rough estimates. The locations of important cities like Timbuktu and Kano remained guesswork. Add the threat of raids. Add the risk of meeting hostile merchants. To Europeans, attempting a trans-Saharan journey on their own seemed likely to end in disaster.

# Pressure for New Wealth Sources

In the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, European powers faced growing pressure to boost national wealth. The discovery of the Americas made this urgency worse. Traveling to the Americas and setting up competing colonies there was expensive.

European states increasingly wanted to cut out the middlemen. These intermediaries controlled trade in exotic luxury goods and vital raw materials. Think Chinese silk. Indonesian spices. African gold.

Wresting control from these merchants was not easy. Their monopolies were often backed by kingdoms and states that benefited from them. The challenge hit poorer European states hardest. Portugal faced this problem especially badly.

# Portuguese Moves Along the West African Coast

When the Portuguese began sailing along the West African coast, their goal was not to find a new route to India. Their immediate aim was to secure West African gold.

Europeans had known about the region's goldfields since the fourteenth century. Sudanic gold had been imported as a raw material to mint European coins.

By the mid-fifteenth century, the Portuguese pushed along the Senegambian coast. They raided Amazigh settlements on the island of Arguin. Arguin was an extension of the trans-Saharan trade routes. The Portuguese took captives and enslaved them on Iberian plantations. They also explored the Senegal and Gambia Rivers in search of gold sources.

These ventures mark some of the earliest attempts at direct European involvement in trans-Saharan trade.

# Explorers, Forts, and Trade Posts

The Portuguese monarchy hired explorers to scout the region. One was Alvise Cadamosto, a Venetian slaver sent to survey Senegambia. These efforts gave the Portuguese a clearer picture of the scope of trans-Saharan trade. They also revealed interactions with the Wolof people, who sold enslaved people along interior trade routes in West Africa.
