Step by step, the Portuguese diverted trade traffic away from the old trans-Saharan routes. They redirected it along the West African coast.

# Sugar, Slavery, and São Tomé

In the 1470s, the Portuguese first saw São Tomé and Príncipe. These are a pair of islands in the Gulf of Guinea. By 1500, they had settled both islands. The location was strategically valuable, sitting off the West African coast. The tropical climate and volcanic soil were ideal for growing sugar.

Large-scale sugar plantations soon sprang up on the islands. The Portuguese entrenched themselves firmly in the Gulf of Guinea.

As the plantation economy on São Tomé expanded, its need for slave labor grew. By the early sixteenth century, the island was Europe's single largest sugar supplier. It was also home to a vast enslaved workforce. The settlers obtained these workers from Elmina.

# The Shift to Trans-Atlantic Slavery

Less than forty years passed between the Portuguese settlement of São Tomé and Príncipe and the first trans-Atlantic voyages carrying African captives sold into slavery in the Americas.

Chiefs on the African mainland saw a chance to profit. They raided their neighbors to capture people they could sell to Europeans. At first, these buyers were the Portuguese. Later, the Dutch, Spanish, French, and English joined in.

Competition among European powers grew as they raced to establish trading posts along the West African coast. Tensions flared among African polities. Some engaged in the growing trade in enslaved people. Others resisted it.

# The Fall of Songhai and a New Order

Songhai was the largest and most powerful Sudanic kingdom in the sixteenth century. In 1591, the Moroccan army shattered it at the Battle of Tondibi. This event permanently altered the situation in West Africa.

Without a strong central authority, many small states emerged. Their chiefs saw clear benefits in dealing directly with wealthy Europeans. They no longer needed to rely on the centuries-old system of caravan trade.

These changes caused a dramatic shift in the size and scope of the trade in enslaved Africans. In the sixteenth century, it involved a few thousand people. By the seventeenth century, it reached tens of thousands. For much of that next century, an average of about forty-five thousand people were traded per year.

# The Spread of Protestantism

## Luther's Legacy Spreads

Efforts to silence Martin Luther failed. A new form of Christianity emerged. It was called Protestantism. It spread across the German-speaking lands. By the end of the sixteenth century, it had taken root in western and central Europe as well.

Many rulers welcomed the new religion. They saw it as a reason to reject the pope's authority. Luther himself called on the German princes to do exactly that.

## The Peace of Augsburg (1555)

The Catholic Holy Roman emperor Charles V opposed Protestantism firmly. He was also known as Charles I of Spain.

However, the 1555 Peace of Augsburg changed things. It gave Lutheran rulers a right. They could make Lutheranism the official religion in their own lands. "Lutheran" was the name for Luther's followers. A prince's subjects had to support whichever church he chose.

The result was mixed:

- Many rulers in northern Germany became Lutheran.
- In Austria and Bavaria (the southern German-speaking lands), the Roman Catholic Church kept its power.
- No other religions were allowed.

## Zwingli in Zurich

In Switzerland, a man named Ulrich (Huldrych) Zwingli embraced Luther's reformation ideas. He worked in the city of Zurich. Zwingli had been a priest. He called for radical changes.

Zwingli rejected transubstantiation. This was a Catholic belief that Jesus was physically present in the communion wine and wafer at every Mass. Even Martin Luther had not gone this far.

Zwingli also:

- Preached against fasting before major religious holidays
- Called for religious imagery to be removed from churches
- Banned organs from churches
- Shut down monasteries and convents
- Had the Bible printed in German instead of Latin
- Called for an end to clerical celibacy
- Proclaimed that the Bible never referred to purgatory

Zwingli was killed in 1531. The killing happened during a conflict between Catholic and Protestant areas of Switzerland.

## Konrad Grebel and the Swiss Brethren

A Swiss merchant named Konrad Grebel was inspired by Zwingli's ideas. One claim moved him especially. Zwingli argued that baptism should be delayed until adulthood. At that point, a person could choose to renounce sin on their own.

Grebel found Zwingli too slow in reforming the Christian community in Zurich. So in 1524, Grebel started his own religious movement. He called it the Swiss Brethren.

## The Anabaptists

The Swiss Brethren was one of several Anabaptist churches. These were established in the sixteenth century. They appeared mainly in central Europe and the Low Countries.

Anabaptist churches rejected infant baptism. Instead, they practiced adult baptism. Here is why this mattered:

- Baptism was believed to remove the taint of original sin.
- Original sin came from Adam and Eve's transgression.
- Because of this belief, infant baptism was the norm among Catholics and most Protestants.
- Anabaptists disagreed. They believed only adults could meaningfully renounce sin. Only adults could make a real declaration of faith.
- So only adults could consciously decide to become Christians.
- But Catholic teaching held that a person could be baptized only once.
- Therefore, rebaptizing someone as an adult violated a core tenet of the Catholic faith.

Other Anabaptist movements included:

- The Hutterites
- The Mennonites
- The Amish (who broke from the larger Mennonite movement in the seventeenth century)

Beyond adult baptism, Anabaptist groups held other beliefs and practices:

- They advocated separation of church and state.
- They tended to be pacifists.
- They refused to hold public office.
- They refused to serve in the army.
- They rejected secular rulers' right to control religious affairs.

Because of these refusals, most European rulers widely feared Anabaptists. Anabaptists were often subject to violent attacks.

## John Calvin and Geneva

Another center of Protestant thought was the city of Geneva (in what is now Switzerland). Its religious leader was John Calvin.

Calvin had been raised a Catholic in France. He became a Protestant either before or shortly after fleeing to Switzerland. He fled to escape persecution for his beliefs.

His ideas were similar to Martin Luther's. But they differed in one crucial respect. Calvin espoused a doctrine called **predestination**. It held that God had already decided two things:

- Which souls would be granted salvation upon death
- Which souls were destined for hell

No person could ever know for certain whether they were saved or damned. There was nothing a person could do to ensure salvation.

Calvinists embraced this doctrine. Despite its denial of human agency, they strove to live a rigidly moral lifestyle. They focused on hard work and piety. In their ability to live like people destined for heaven, they sought reassurance that they had in fact been saved.

They rejected the following as ungodly:

- Dancing
- Public drunkenness
- Gambling
- Obscene speech

These acts were considered fit for punishment by a special tribunal called the **Consistory**.

Calvinism spread rapidly outside Geneva. It found adherents in:

- The Netherlands, where they established the Dutch Reformed Church
- Scotland, where the Presbyterian Church was formed
- France, where its followers were called Huguenots

## The English Reformation: A Different Story

Martin Luther, Ulrich Zwingli, John Calvin, and the Anabaptist leaders were true believers in the doctrines they espoused. The English Reformation was of a different character. In England, reform was imposed from the top down. It came not from a committed convert. It came from a king looking for an expedient way to exchange one queen for another.

## Henry VIII and Catherine of Aragon

Until he decided to remove himself from under the pope's authority, Henry VIII had a reputation as a devout Catholic. He was also a critic of Luther.

# Joint Stock Companies and the Funding of Colonies

After Roanoke Island, English colonial efforts needed new money. The English monarchy could not provide enough funding on its own.

Joint stock companies solved this problem. They worked much like modern corporations. A company sold shares to investors. Investors pooled their money together. The company then used that money to fund operations, including colonization in the Americas.

Shareholders had **limited liability**. This meant they were not legally responsible for the company's actions. They could never lose more than what they invested. But if the company succeeded, they could earn large profits.

This mix of limited risk and high reward attracted England's growing merchant class. Beginning in the early 1600s, these companies raised huge sums of money.

England promoted colonization for religious and political reasons. However, because it relied on private investors, the effort often shifted toward activities that would make a profit.

---

# The Virginia Company and Jamestown (1606–1607)

In 1606, the **Virginia Company** received its charter. It was named for Queen Elizabeth. She was called the "virgin queen" because she never married.

The company sent 144 men and boys to North America. In 1607, these colonists founded **Jamestown**. They chose a site on the banks of the Chesapeake Bay, in what is now Virginia. The settlement was named for the new English king, James I.

Who were these settlers? Many were younger sons of elite families. They would not inherit property because their older brothers claimed it first in England. Others were artisans, such as goldsmiths and jewelers. None of them were used to the hard physical labor needed to build a colony on a new continent.

---

# Mercantilism: The Economic Idea Behind the Colony

The settlers of Jamestown held economic ideas common among Europeans in the 1600s and 1700s. These ideas came from **mercantilism**.

Mercantilism was an economic theory. It assumed the world's wealth was finite. Wealth was measured in gold and silver. Under this view, if one nation gained wealth, another nation lost it.

Mercantilist nations expected their colonies to do two things:

- Export raw materials (especially precious metals like gold and silver) back to the home country
- Purchase finished goods from that same home country

The English government hoped the Virginia Company would find gold. Gold would improve England's trade balance and increase national wealth. Many in Jamestown also hoped to find gold. They wanted to get rich without hard work or hardship.

---

# Hardship at Jamestown

The settlers did not find gold. The region had little mineral wealth. But they did find suffering.

Problems included:

- Bad weather
- Starvation
- Disease
- Internal political disputes
- Military conflicts with the **Powhatan tribe** (named after its chief)

The Powhatans grew to hate the newcomers. The colonists brought disease and violence to their homeland.

Many colonists died during the winter of 1609–1610. This period became known as **"the starving time."** By May 1610, fewer than a hundred settlers remained. The colony had not produced a profit for the Virginia Company. It almost failed.

# The Road to Independence

Europeans sometimes became victims of their own success. Economic imperialism built strong new societies. These societies grew powerful enough to break free. They declared independence from the home country. In at least one case, thirteen former colonies formed a nation. That nation became wealthier and more powerful than the empire that came before it.


## The Colonies Grow

The British colonies in North America began as struggling trading outposts. This was in the early 1600s. By the middle of the 1700s, things had changed. More than two million people lived there. They largely governed themselves. Their commercial economy thrived.


## The Navigation Acts

British mercantilist policies threatened this growth. In the second half of the 1600s, England passed a series of laws called the Navigation Acts. These acts had three goals:

- Maximize profit from the colonies
- Deny colonial resources to other European powers
- Stop colonists from smuggling goods to avoid trade rules

The Navigation Act of 1660 listed specific goods. Colonies could sell these goods only in England or to English colonial possessions. English merchants set the price. They paid colonists what the merchants thought the goods were worth. Colonists could not sell to Dutch, French, Spanish, or other merchants. Those merchants might have paid more.


## What Could Only Be Sold to England

The list of restricted products was long. It included:

- Furs
- Tobacco
- Sugar

All of Europe wanted these goods. The list also included rice, ginger, cotton, and indigo. Indigo and other plants were used to make dye. English textile manufacturers needed the cotton and dyestuffs. To protect their interests further, the Exportation Act of 1660 banned the export of English wool.

Naval stores could only be sent to England as well. These were materials for building and maintaining ships. They included:

- Masts
- Hemp (used to make rope)
- Pine tree pitch (sealed ships and made them watertight)
- Pine tree sap (used to make turpentine)

Once these products arrived in England, they were heavily taxed. The tax revenue went to the English government. It did not go back to the colonies that had produced the goods.


## More Taxes on Imports

The Navigation Act of 1663 added another rule. All goods from outside the British Empire had to be shipped to England first. They had to be taxed there before they could continue to the colonies. This raised the price of non-English goods for colonists. Foreign shippers passed the cost of English taxes on to them.


## Limits on Colonial Manufacturing

At the end of the 1600s, Parliament added new restrictions. Colonists were banned from making certain goods. These were goods also produced in England. The goal was to stop colonists from underselling English merchants.

Colonists could not sell wool or iron goods. This applied to sales in England and to other English colonies. By the mid-1700s, they could not export beaver hats either. Beaver hats were a popular fashion in Europe. The English colonies took part in the fur trade. But Parliament only let colonists export unfinished furs. They could not sell finished hats. Finished hats would have fetched higher prices. This rule limited how much wealth colonial settlers could build.


## The French and Indian War Changes Everything

The French and Indian War ended, but tensions grew. British colonists in North America reacted with hostility to new actions by Parliament. They felt these actions unfairly restricted their economic opportunities.

Many colonists longed to move west of the Appalachian Mountains. They wanted farms on the rich lands of the Ohio Valley. In New England, families were large. With each generation, parents struggled to give enough land to their children. In the southern colonies, tobacco farming demanded new fertile land constantly.

Many colonies claimed territory west of the Appalachians. But the French had taken that land. Their numerous Native American allies lived there. After the British victory over the French and their Indigenous allies, colonists expected to finally claim it.

The British government said no. It wanted to avoid angering the tribes of the Ohio Valley. It also wanted to avoid costly new wars. So it promptly banned settlement west of the Appalachians. Many colonists were dismayed and angry. They had fought alongside British troops in the war that had just ended.


## Troops, Taxes, and Courts

Britain kept troops in North America after the war. These troops policed the frontier. They regulated colonial trade. They collected taxes. Britain also wanted to repay its war debts. The cost of maintaining the army led to new attempts to tax colonists. Or to enforce collection of existing taxes more strictly.

Colonists had long tried to evade trade rules by smuggling. Parliament countered this with new laws. Smugglers would now be tried in admiralty courts. These courts did not use a jury. Many colonists felt this violated protections guaranteed by the English Bill of Rights.


## The Quebec Decision and the Final Break

In 1774, Parliament made another set of decisions. It granted control of the Ohio Valley to Quebec. Quebec was a newly acquired French province. Parliament allowed Quebec to keep its French civil law. It also extended religious toleration to the province's Roman Catholics. Most British colonists were Protestant. They were outraged by this ruling.

At the same time, these actions interfered with a long tradition of colonial self-government. That tradition had lasted over a century and a half. Many colonists began to see Britain as hostile to their interests. Growing resentment of British rule erupted in bloodshed in 1775. A declaration of independence followed in 1776.

---

## The Road to Independence

Europeans sometimes became **victims of their own success**.

Economic imperialism built strong new societies.

Those societies grew powerful.

They grew powerful enough to **break free**.

They declared independence from the home country.

In at least one case, thirteen former colonies formed a nation.

That nation became **wealthier and more powerful** than the empire that came before it.

---

## The Colonies Grow

The British colonies in North America began as **struggling trading outposts**.

This was in the early 1600s.

By the middle of the 1700s, things had changed:

- More than **two million people** lived there.
- They largely **governed themselves**.
- Their commercial economy **thrived**.

---

## The Navigation Acts

British mercantilist policies threatened this growth.

In the second half of the 1600s, England passed a series of laws.

These laws were called the **Navigation Acts**.

The acts had three goals:

- **Maximize profit** from the colonies.
- **Deny colonial resources** to other European powers.
- **Stop colonists** from smuggling goods to avoid trade rules.

The Navigation Act of 1660 listed specific goods.

Colonies could sell these goods **only in England**.

Or to English colonial possessions.

English merchants set the price.

They paid colonists what the merchants thought the goods were worth.

Colonists could not sell to Dutch, French, Spanish, or other merchants.

Those merchants might have paid more.

---

## What Could Only Be Sold to England

The list of restricted products was long:

- **Furs**
- **Tobacco**
- **Sugar**

All of Europe wanted these goods.

The list also included rice, ginger, cotton, and indigo.

Indigo and other plants were used to make **dye**.

English textile manufacturers needed the cotton and dyestuffs.

To protect their interests further, the Exportation Act of 1660 banned the export of **English wool**.

**Naval stores** could only be sent to England as well.

These were materials for building and maintaining ships:

- **Masts**
- **Hemp** (used to make rope)
- **Pine tree pitch** (sealed ships; made them watertight)
- **Pine tree sap** (used to make turpentine)

Once these products arrived in England, they were **heavily taxed**.

The tax revenue went to the English government.

It did not go back to the colonies that had produced the goods.

---

## More Taxes on Imports

The Navigation Act of 1663 added another rule:

All goods from outside the British Empire had to be **shipped to England first**.

They had to be taxed there.

Then they could continue to the colonies.

This raised the price of non-English goods for colonists.

Foreign shippers passed the cost of English taxes on to them.

---

## Limits on Colonial Manufacturing

At the end of the 1600s, Parliament added new restrictions.

Colonists were **banned from making certain goods**.

These were goods also produced in England.

The goal: stop colonists from underselling English merchants.

- Colonists could not sell **wool or iron goods** (in England or to other English colonies).
- By the mid-1700s, they could not export **beaver hats** either.

Beaver hats were a popular fashion in Europe.

The English colonies took part in the fur trade.

But Parliament only let colonists export **unfinished furs**.

They could not sell finished hats.

Finished hats would have fetched higher prices.

This rule limited how much wealth colonial settlers could build.

---

## The French and Indian War Changes Everything

The French and Indian War ended, but **tensions grew**.

British colonists in North America reacted with hostility to new actions by Parliament.

They felt these actions unfairly restricted their economic opportunities.

Many colonists longed to move **west of the Appalachian Mountains**.

They wanted farms on the rich lands of the Ohio Valley.

- In **New England**, families were large. With each generation, parents struggled to give enough land to their children.
- In the **Southern colonies**, tobacco farming demanded new fertile land constantly.

Many colonies claimed territory west of the Appalachians.

But the French had taken that land.

Their numerous Native American allies lived there.

After the British victory over the French and their indigenous allies, colonists expected to finally claim it.

**The British government said no.**

It wanted to avoid angering the tribes of the Ohio Valley.

It also wanted to avoid costly new wars.

So it promptly **banned settlement west of the Appalachians**.

Many colonists were dismayed and angry.

They had fought alongside British troops in the war that had just ended.

---

## Troops, Taxes, and Courts

Britain kept troops in North America after the war.

These troops:

- Policed the frontier.
- Regulated colonial trade.
- Collected taxes.

Britain also wanted to **repay its war debts**.

The cost of maintaining the army led to new attempts to tax colonists.

Or to enforce collection of existing taxes more strictly.

Colonists had long tried to evade trade rules by smuggling.

Parliament countered this with new laws:

Smugglers would now be tried in **admiralty courts**.

These courts did not use a jury.

Many colonists felt this violated protections guaranteed by the **English Bill of Rights**.

---

## The Quebec Decision and the Final Break

In 1774, Parliament made another set of decisions:

- It granted control of the Ohio Valley to **Quebec** (a newly acquired French province).
- It allowed Quebec to keep its **French civil law**.
- It extended religious toleration to the province's **Roman Catholics**.

Most British colonists were Protestant.

They were **outraged** by this ruling.

At the same time, these actions interfered with a long tradition of **colonial self-government**.

That tradition had lasted over a century and a half.

Many colonists began to see Britain as hostile to their interests.

Growing resentment of British rule erupted in **bloodshed in 1775**.

A declaration of independence followed in **1776**.

# Print Culture and the Enlightenment

## A Growing Reading Public

The Enlightenment era saw a boom in print culture. People talked and debated ideas in public spaces. This was tied directly to the growth of books and newspapers.

Literacy rates rose sharply in French cities:

- **Late 1600s:** About 30% of men could read. About 14% of women could read.
- **Mid-1700s:** About 48% of men could read. About 27% of women could read.

More readers meant more printed material. Books, pamphlets, newspapers, and political cartoons appeared in large numbers.

Print also changed how knowledge worked. It standardized spelling. It organized systems of knowledge. News, opinions, poetry, political philosophy, scientific texts, and all kinds of information reached far more people than speech alone could carry.

## The Republic of Letters

The "Republic of Letters" was a community of writers. They lived across Europe and the Atlantic world. In the 1600s and 1700s, they wrote to each other by hand. They also shared published materials of every kind. This created a vital international exchange of ideas.

This was not a political republic. Its "citizens" did not live in one place. Instead, they were united by ideas spread through print. Any literate person could belong. It did not matter where they lived. Members treated each other as intellectual equals. They exchanged ideas freely. This mirrored the ideal of a political republic, where citizens are free and equal.

Famous members included Voltaire, Benjamin Franklin, and Catherine the Great.

## A Language Barrier

Participants came from many countries. They spoke many languages. So much writing was done in Latin. In that era, Latin was the universal language of scholarship across Europe. Other writing needed skilled translators to be understood.

This barrier made it hard for most people to take part directly in Enlightenment print culture.

## Who Could Actually Read?

Print culture had a wide influence. But its direct reach into everyday life was limited. Literacy among artisans, peasants, and tradespeople stayed low.

Rates were climbing fast among the urban elite. Wealthy merchants and aristocrats led this growth. At the bottom of the social ladder, literacy stayed below 20%. This was especially true in rural areas.

In theory, the Enlightenment supported democratic sharing of knowledge. In practice, only people with enough money and free time could take part. Books cost too much for all but the very wealthy. Even cheap pamphlets were a real expense for most laborers and peasants.

## New Ways to Share Books

By the second half of the 1700s, lending libraries appeared. They aimed to widen access to printed material. But only select academics and government officials could borrow books.

By the end of the century, reading clubs grew in number. Members paid an annual fee. In return, they got access to books and periodicals. These clubs expanded the reading public. They also raised literacy levels among the middle class.

# The Haitian Revolution and Its Impact on the Americas

## What the Early Declarations Really Meant

In 1776, the U.S. Declaration of Independence was written. In 1789, France wrote its Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen. Both documents said that all men were created equal.

But they did not mean everyone. They mainly applied to White men of European descent. Women were left out. Enslaved people were left out. This was true in both Europe and the United States.

The rights listed in these documents served free White men. These included property rights, freedom of expression, and the right to take part in government.

Only a small group of radical thinkers read these documents differently. They argued that women should have the same rights as men. They also argued that people of different races deserved equal rights and social status. Most people did not agree with them.

Still, these documents had a real effect. They partly inspired a slave revolt in Saint-Domingue. This revolt became one of the most important results of the French Revolution in the Americas.


## Saint-Domingue: A Colony Built on Enslaved Labor

Saint-Domingue was a French colony. It sat on the western side of the Caribbean island of Hispaniola. France founded it in the mid-1600s.

Soon, it became the most profitable colony in the Americas. This profit came mostly from enslaved African labor. Enslaved people were brought to the island by force. They worked on sugar plantations, coffee plantations, and indigo plantations.


## The Revolt Begins (1791)

In 1791, freed and enslaved Africans rose up. Other islanders of African descent joined them. Two leaders stood out: Toussaint Louverture and Jean-Jacques Dessalines. Both had been born enslaved on local plantations.

The revolt grew into a full revolution. It led to the colony's independence. In 1804, Haiti declared itself a free republic.


## What Made Haiti Unique

The Haitian Revolution was unlike any other in the Americas. In the British colonies of North America, White colonists fought for political representation and greater economic freedom. They were already near the top of the social order.

In Saint-Domingue, it was different. The fight for independence was led by people at the very bottom of the social hierarchy. Enslaved and formerly enslaved people drove the revolution forward.


## Two Goals, Two Kinds of Freedom

The rebellion in Haiti had two goals. It sought two forms of liberation.

For free Black people and mixed-race elites, freedom meant an end to colonialism. They wanted independence from French rule.

For enslaved Black people, liberation was more basic. It meant freedom from abuse on the plantation. It meant an end to slavery itself.


## Victory in 1804

By January 1804, Black revolutionaries had won. They used successful guerrilla tactics. The French army was already weakened by an outbreak of yellow fever. The revolutionaries decimated it.

Haiti became a nation. It was the second liberated territory in the Western hemisphere to have a republican system.


## Fear Spreads Across the Americas

# The Great Divergence

The United States and European nations built factories. They became industrialized.

African, Latin American, and Asian nations did not. Japan was the one exception.

This gap left a lasting disadvantage. These nations fell behind in three key areas:

- Economy
- Technology
- Military power

They could not compete with the industrialized world.

## Why Did This Happen?

Historians disagree on the cause. They call this gap the **Great Divergence**. No single answer exists.

**One view:** These nations lacked key natural resources. European nations had abundant coal. Many other regions did not. Coal powered factories and industry. Without it, industrialization was harder to start.

**Another view:** Colonies played a major role. Britain and France built colonies in the Americas and Asia. Those colonies provided three things:

- Capital (money)
- Raw resources
- New markets for goods

This helped fuel their own industrial growth.

At the same time, European powers forced unequal treaties on Africa, Asia, and Latin America. They used deadlier weapons to do so. These treaties locked those regions into a weaker position.

## A Different Argument

Some scholars offer a contrasting view. Countries like Egypt and many Latin American nations made a deliberate choice. They saw their real strength in producing raw materials.

They supplied the industrializing nations with what they needed.

Several factors shaped this path:

- History
- Geography
- Climate
- The nature of local labor forces

These factors made agriculture and raw material production a better fit. Widespread factory-based industry was not.

## No Single Story

No one cause explains everything. In each nation, a unique mix of circumstances shaped the road it took. The Great Divergence was not one event. It was many different stories unfolding at once.

# The Great Divergence


The United States and European nations built factories.

They became industrialized.



African, Latin American, and Asian nations did not.

Japan was the one exception.



This gap left a lasting disadvantage.

These nations fell behind in three key areas:

- Economy
- Technology
- Military power



They could not compete with the industrialized world.



## Why Did This Happen?


Historians disagree on the cause.

They call this gap **the Great Divergence**.

No single answer exists.



### One View


These nations lacked key natural resources.

European nations had abundant coal.

Many other regions did not.

Coal powered factories and industry.

Without it, industrialization was harder to start.



### Another View


Colonies played a major role.

Britain and France built colonies in the Americas and Asia.

Those colonies provided three things:

- Capital (money)
- Raw resources
- New markets for goods



This helped fuel their own industrial growth.



At the same time, European powers forced unequal treaties.

They did this to Africa, Asia, and Latin America.

They used deadlier weapons to do so.

These treaties locked those regions into a weaker position.



## A Different Argument


Some scholars offer a contrasting view.

Countries like Egypt and many Latin American nations chose this path.

They saw their real strength in producing raw materials.

They supplied the industrializing nations with what they needed.



Several factors shaped this path:

- History
- Geography
- Climate
- The nature of local labor forces



These factors made agriculture and raw material production a better fit.

Widespread factory-based industry was not.



## No Single Story


No one cause explains everything.

In each nation, a unique mix of circumstances shaped the road it took.

The Great Divergence was not one event.

It was many different stories unfolding at once.

# Latin America's Struggle to Industrialize

## Becoming Export Economies

The nations of Latin America became export economies. They had just been freed from Spanish and Portuguese control. They wanted to industrialize. But they faced many obstacles.

In the early 1800s, some countries made progress:

- **Brazil** imported steam engines. It built facilities for sugar refining, coffee processing, and textile production.
- **Paraguay** built an iron foundry. It also started a steamship line.
- **Chile** opened coal mines. It built sawmills and flour mills.
- Many countries built rail lines.

But they did not become heavily industrialized. Their development took another path.

## Independence Made Things Harder

Ironically, independence was part of the problem.

When Spain and Portugal controlled their economies, Latin American merchants resented the rules. But those rules had a hidden benefit. They taxed foreign-made goods heavily. This protected local handicraft industries.

After independence, merchants could trade with any country they chose. Goods made in Europe and the United States flooded in.

Latin America faced the same problem as India and Egypt. Local manufacturers could not make or sell goods as cheaply as imports. They also could not produce enough to meet internal demand.

Brazilians and Chileans watched their silver flow overseas. It was no longer spent at home.

## Sticking with What Worked

Latin Americans made a practical choice. Growing sugar and coffee was more profitable than trying to compete with foreign factories. Sugar and coffee had been the base of the colonial economy. Demand for them was still high.

Later in the 1800s, Brazil added rubber to this list. It used its abundant land and large agricultural workforce to supply raw materials to industrialized nations.

This made sense to planters and politicians. But it locked former Spanish and Portuguese colonies into a bad deal. They supplied raw materials at low prices. The finished products made from those materials sold for much more.

## A Growing Gap

Latin America sold large amounts of cash crops to the United States and Europe. This enriched the planter class. But their earnings never exceeded what they paid for imports. In many cases, they did not even equal it.

This gap hurt society in several ways:

- Wealthy plantation owners and urban professionals could afford factory-made products from other continents.
- Agricultural laborers could not.
- The class divide grew wider.

Money also left the region. European and U.S. banks funded many industrial projects, like mines and railroads. Steam engines and other machinery were imported from Europe. Little money was left at home for domestic projects such as building roads and telegraph lines.

Regional wars added to the damage. They destabilized South America and slowed industrialization. One major example:

- **The War of the Triple Alliance (1864–1870):** Paraguay fought against the combined forces of Uruguay, Brazil, and Argentina. By the time the war ended, it had killed much of Paraguay's population. Infectious diseases made things worse.

## The Result

Many forces worked together to block industrialization in Latin America. The region remained primarily an exporter of cash crops.

Railroads were built, but they were short lines. They linked the interior to the coast so raw materials could be shipped out. No national rail networks developed like those in the United States and Europe. Electrification reached only major cities.

# The Second Industrial Revolution and Empire

## New Materials Were Needed

The Second Industrial Revolution brought new inventions. These inventions needed new raw materials.

- **Petroleum** fueled engines.
- **Natural rubber** made valves and tires.
- **Palm oil** lubricated machinery.
- **Copper** carried heat and electricity.
- **Silver** was used in medicine and photography.
- **Lead** made pipes.

Coal had many uses too. It turned iron into steel. It produced gas to heat homes. It generated electricity for machines, streets, and buildings.

Not all industrialized nations could produce enough of these materials. They needed more than they had at home.

## New Tastes Created New Demand

Fashions also drove demand for foreign goods.

Middle-class families in Europe and the United States wanted their daughters to play piano. Piano keys were once made from **ivory**. This created a market for ivory imports.

Industrial workers needed quick energy. They drank more coffee, tea, and sugar. Demand for these items rose sharply.

Elites and aspiring middle-class people filled their homes with fine wood furniture. They used **mahogany**, **rosewood**, and **ebony**.

Cotton textiles stayed fashionable. But the United States had abolished slavery. Cloth makers could no longer rely on cheap raw cotton from enslaved laborers.

## Reaching Beyond Borders

The industrializing powers needed more materials. They also needed new markets for their goods. Their own borders were not enough.

They looked to **Africa**, **Asia**, and the **Pacific Ocean**.

But there was a problem. To make large profits, they had to buy raw materials at very low prices. Africans, Asians, and Pacific Islanders would not agree to such terms on their own.

There was a second problem. These nations would have to buy manufactured goods from the industrial powers. But many of them could already make those things themselves. They would not simply agree to import foreign products.

So business owners and politicians in industrialized nations decided they needed **control**. They wanted to rule distant countries as part of an empire. Military conquest was often the tool they used.

Once a territory was secured, markets were set up, and money was invested, the imperial powers faced a new task. They had to keep other industrial powers out. This meant tighter control over existing colonies. It also meant trying to conquer neighboring regions.

**Example:** Great Britain competed with Russia for control of Afghanistan. Why? To limit Russian access to India, Britain's most valuable colony.

## These Colonies Were Different

The new colonies were not like the old ones. In the 1500s and 1600s, European powers built "settler colonies." Large numbers of Europeans moved there and made permanent homes. The colonies had a close relationship with the home country.

That was not the plan this time.

European powers did not expect large numbers of people to relocate to Africa or Asia. They did not intend these colonies to mirror the old settler model.

The United States treated the Philippines very differently from how North American colonists had been treated by Great Britain. The industrial nations wanted to **exploit** the resources and people of their new colonies. They did not want to settle them.

## A Few Exceptions Existed

Some colonies broke this pattern.

- France took control of **Algeria** in 1830. In 1848, it became part of France itself.
- Many French and other European people moved to the coastal areas of Algeria and Tunisia. The government encouraged this migration during the 1800s.
- Many Europeans also settled in British and Dutch colonies in **southern Africa**.

But these cases were not the rule. Exploitation, not settlement, remained the norm for most new colonies.

# The Cold War: Many Fronts, Many Strategies

## Aiding New Nations

The Cold War was fought on many fronts. Both sides used many strategies.

After World War II, many countries in Latin America, Asia, and Africa gained independence from European rule. Both the United States and the Soviet Union offered these new nations aid and technical help.

The U.S. had a goal. It wanted to stop communism from spreading. The U.S. hoped that by giving economic aid, it could remove the reason for poor countries to side with the Soviet Union.

Communism appealed to many poor people. Why? It promised that a nation's wealth would be shared by all its citizens. Under the Soviet system, people received jobs, housing, education, health care, and public transportation.

The standard of living in the Soviet bloc was lower than in the West. But for people who faced hunger and homelessness every day, communism looked like a real alternative. They saw no other way to improve their lives.

## Propaganda: Words, Images, and Radio

Both sides used propaganda to support their own policies. They also tried to damage the other side's reputation. Propaganda took many forms: literature, visual imagery, and films.

In 1950, the U.S.-funded **Radio Free Europe** began broadcasting news into Eastern Bloc countries. In 1953, **Radio Liberty** started broadcasting into the Soviet Union.

The U.S. government also created the **Free Europe Committee**. This group was made up of American business executives and lawyers. The committee printed leaflets and posters. These materials praised life in democratic, capitalist countries. Workers dropped them from weather balloons over East Germany, Poland, Czechoslovakia, and Hungary.

## Soviet Propaganda

Soviet propaganda sent a different message. It stressed the USSR's desire for world peace. It praised the communist ideal of a classless society. In this society, people were treated equally regardless of race or gender.

This message resonated in Latin America, Africa, and Asia. Some African Americans also felt drawn to these promises. They faced racism and segregation at home in the United States.

In fact, opponents of the civil rights movement often attacked it by calling it "communist."

## Sports as a Battlefield

Propaganda sometimes took the form of athletic competition. Each side used its swimmers, runners, weightlifters, and gymnasts to show that its system was superior.

Sports and news broadcasts tracked medal counts closely during Olympic competitions. U.S. athletes and Soviet athletes were measured against each other.

At other times, cultural exchanges happened. Soviet ballet dancers toured the United States. American jazz musicians and symphony orchestras visited Eastern Bloc countries.

## Technology and the Space Race

Both sides highlighted their ingenuity and technological achievements.

In 1959, U.S. Vice President Richard Nixon visited Moscow for an exhibition. He proudly showed off a model kitchen to Soviet Premier Nikita Khrushchev. The kitchen featured labor-saving gadgets. Khrushchev's response was sharp. He asked whether American families also had machines to put food in their mouths and swallow it.

The two countries also competed to dominate space.

- **1957:** The Soviet Union launched *S Sputnik*, the first satellite. This was a serious blow to U.S. pride (Figure 14.7).
- **1958:** President Dwight D. Eisenhower called on Congress to create a space agency. That year, the **National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)** was established.
- **1961:** The Soviet Union sent the first astronaut into space.
- **1969:** The United States put the first humans on the surface of the moon.

## Espionage: Spies and Sabotage

Espionage was another key tool in the Cold War.

The United States carried out espionage through the **Central Intelligence Agency (CIA)**, formed in 1947. The USSR used its spy agency, the **KGB**.

These agencies did more than surveil each other's nations. They also:

- Plotted and carried out acts of sabotage
- Assassinated people deemed enemies of their country
- Fomented discontent in foreign nations
- Trained fighting forces
- Encouraged revolution and insurgency to topple foreign governments
- Installed leaders friendly to their own country

For example, the CIA trained Cuban insurgents. Their goal was to overthrow Fidel Castro's communist government on the Caribbean island in 1961.

Similarly, the KGB gave assistance to Vietnamese communists. These groups were trying to defeat the government of South Vietnam during the Vietnam War.

## Nuclear Weapons: The Most Dangerous Front

The most dangerous venue for competition was the stockpiling of massive nuclear arsenals. This was also each side's chief means of reining in the other's aggression.

- **1949:** The Soviet Union detonated an atomic bomb. This ended the U.S. monopoly on nuclear weapons.
- **1952:** The United States developed the hydrogen bomb. Some of the same atomic scientists who had worked on the Manhattan Project during World War II opposed this step. The U.S. tested the hydrogen bomb at the Pacific atoll of Eniwetok in 1952. This weapon was one thousand times more powerful than the bomb dropped on Hiroshima.

U.S. development of such a weapon meant the Soviet Union needed to do the same.

## Missiles and Mutually Assured Destruction

In the 1950s, both the United States and the USSR developed **intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs)**.

Now, missiles armed with nuclear warheads could be launched from within a country's own territory or from satellite nations. An air force that could intercept bomb-bearing planes was no longer enough to protect against a nuclear attack.

Countries in both blocs prepared for potential war. They built shelters to protect citizens in the event of nuclear war. But neither side put great faith in its ability to win such a war.

Both countries quickly came to believe that survival depended on one thing: building an immense retaliatory capacity. The idea was simple. If you could unleash devastation so great, the other side would never fire first. They would fear their own annihilation.

In the United States, this defense policy became known as **"mutually assured destruction" (MAD)**.

If nuclear stockpiles failed to deter a conflict, there was still a backup. The large military forces built up during the Cold War ensured both sides could fight a conventional war. These forces included billions of dollars' worth of battleships, submarines, and fighter jets.

# France and Its African Colonies

France did not want colonies in Africa at first. It controlled one island called Gorée. This island sits off the coast of Senegal. France also had a few trading posts deep inside the continent. In the 1850s, France moved further into the interior of Senegal. After that, it did very little for many years.

This changed at the end of the nineteenth century. The European powers met at the Congress of Berlin in 1878. They needed to decide what would happen to the Ottoman Empire's lands in North Africa. The Ottoman Empire had been defeated. France was given Tunisia.

## Why France Got Tunisia

Tunisia had borrowed a lot of money from European powers. It used this money for development and to modernize its army. In 1869, Tunisia declared bankruptcy. Britain, France, and Italy set up a commission. This group managed Tunisia's finances. Its job was to make sure the debt got repaid.

At the Congress of Berlin, each power had its own goals:

- **Italy** wanted Tunisia. Many Italian citizens now lived there.
- **Britain** did not want Italy in control of both sides of the Strait of Sicily. That would block British access to the eastern Mediterranean. Britain also wanted France to back its claim to Cyprus.
- **Germany** wanted France focused on North Africa. Germany hoped to grow its own influence in continental Europe.

The result: France got Tunisia. Italy got the city of Tripoli, in Libya.

## The Protectorate Over Tunisia

Britain and Germany were happy with this deal. But the Tunisians refused to accept it. In 1881, a Tunisian attack hit the French colony of Algeria. France used this as an excuse to invade Tunisia. France set up a protectorate over the country. Under this system:

- The Tunisian government stayed in place.
- Its leader was Muhammad III as-Sadiq.
- He managed domestic affairs at home.
- France controlled defense and foreign relations.

## A Rush for West Africa

France then moved quickly to grab more land. Belgium wanted nearby regions in Central Africa. France did not want to lose ground. From 1880 to 1900, much of West Africa fell under French control. An Italian-born French naval officer named Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza traveled the region. He negotiated with local rulers. He signed treaties on behalf of France.

Many areas that are now nations (or parts of nations) became French possessions:

- Côte d'Ivoire
- Benin
- Niger
- Mali
- Mauritania
- Cameroon
- Central African Republic
- Republic of the Congo
- Democratic Republic of the Congo
- Gabon
- Burkina Faso
- Chad

These colonies served two main purposes. First, they provided markets for French manufactured goods. Second, they produced large amounts of palm oil. France used this oil to lubricate industrial machinery.

France also took control of two other areas:

- **French Somaliland** (now Djibouti), in East Africa
- **Madagascar**, an island off the East African coast

## Peaceful Deals and Brutal Conquest

The French takeover was not always violent. Sometimes it was peaceful. For example, Brazza signed a treaty with King Illoh Makoko. He was the Bateke ruler of what is now the Republic of the Congo and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

Other times, the conquest was brutal. Captain Paul Voulet built a reputation for cruelty. He marched his troops through French Sudan (modern-day Niger). His destination was Lake Chad. Along the way, Voulet's soldiers looted villages that were already under French control. They raped and killed the people who lived there.

# France and Its African Colonies


France did not want colonies in Africa at first.

It controlled one island called **Gorée**. This island sits off the coast of **Senegal**.

France also had a few trading posts deep inside the continent.


In the **1850s**, France moved further into the interior of Senegal.

After that, it did very little for many years.



---


This changed at the end of the nineteenth century.


The European powers met at the **Congress of Berlin** in **1878**.

They needed to decide what would happen to the **Ottoman Empire's** lands in north Africa. The Ottoman Empire had been defeated.

France was given **Tunisia**.



## Why France Got Tunisia


Tunisia had borrowed a lot of money from European powers.

It used this money for development. It also used it to modernize its army.

In **1869**, Tunisia declared bankruptcy.

Britain, France, and Italy set up a commission to manage Tunisia's finances. Its job was to make sure the debt got repaid.


At the Congress of Berlin, each power had its own goals:


**Italy** wanted Tunisia. Many Italian citizens now lived there.


**Britain** did not want Italy in control of both sides of the **Strait of Sicily**. That would block British access to the **Eastern Mediterranean**. Britain also wanted France to back its claim to **Cyprus**.


**Germany** wanted France focused on north Africa. Germany hoped to grow its own influence in continental Europe.


The result:

- France got Tunisia.
- Italy got the city of **Tripoli**, in **Libya**.



## The Protectorate Over Tunisia


Britain and Germany were happy with this deal.

But the Tunisians refused to accept it.

In **1881**, a Tunisian attack hit the French colony of **Algeria**.

France used this as an excuse to invade Tunisia. It set up a protectorate over the country.


Under this system:

- The Tunisian government stayed in place.
- Its leader was **Muhammad III as-Sadiq**. He managed domestic affairs at home.
- France controlled defense and foreign relations.



## A Rush for West Africa


France then moved quickly to grab more land.

**Belgium** wanted nearby regions in central Africa. France did not want to lose ground.

From **1880 to 1900**, much of west Africa fell under French control.

An Italian-born French naval officer named **Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza** traveled the region. He negotiated with local rulers. He signed treaties on behalf of France.


Many areas that are now nations (or parts of nations) became French possessions:

- Côte d'Ivoire
- Benin
- Niger
- Mali
- Mauritania
- Cameroon
- Central African Republic
- Republic of the Congo
- Democratic Republic of the Congo
- Gabon
- Burkina Faso
- Chad


These colonies served two main purposes.

**First**, they provided markets for French manufactured goods.

**Second**, they produced large amounts of palm oil. France used this oil to lubricate industrial machinery.


France also took control of two other areas:

- **French Somaliland** (now Djibouti), in east Africa
- **Madagascar**, an island off the east African coast



## Peaceful Deals and Brutal Conquest


The French takeover was not always violent. Sometimes it was peaceful.

For example, Brazza signed a treaty with **King Iloh Makoko**. He was the Bateke ruler of what is now the Republic of the Congo and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.


Other times, the conquest was brutal.

**Captain Paul Voulet** built a reputation for cruelty. He marched his troops through **French Sudan** (modern-day Niger). His destination was **Lake Chad**.

Along the way, Voulet's soldiers looted villages that were already under French control. They raped and killed the people who lived there.

# Germany's Late Start in the Colonial Scramble

Germany joined the race for colonies later than other nations. Several reasons explain why.

**Before 1871:** Germany was not one country. It was a group of German-speaking states and kingdoms. These sat in northern and central Europe. None were rich enough to build colonies. None were strong enough either.

**After unification (1871):** Germany became one nation. But it still had a problem. It lacked an ocean-going navy. Without that navy, it could not trade with distant lands. It also could not defend any colonies it might claim.

**Bismarck's early view:** The first chancellor was Otto von Bismarck. He served from 1871 to 1890. At first, he had no interest in an overseas empire. He saw empire building as a foolish venture. In his view, it cost more than it returned.

**A change of mind:** By the 1880s, Bismarck changed his position. Two forces may have pushed him:

- German merchants wanted trade and investment opportunities abroad.
- The public demanded colonies to raise Germany's prestige.

**Germany's African claims:** In Africa, Germany took land that France and England had not yet claimed. These regions were scattered across the continent.

In the **west**, Germany claimed:

- **Togoland** (today Togo and part of Ghana)
- **German Cameroon** (now parts of Cameroon, Chad, the Central African Republic, and Gabon)

Further south and east, it claimed:

- **German South-West Africa** (now Namibia)
- **German East Africa** (today Rwanda, Burundi, and parts of Tanzania)

# The Calm Before the Storm

## A Long Peace

The decades before World War I were mostly peaceful. People called that war "the Great War." Europe had been stable for a long time.

In 1815, European leaders created a balance of power. This came after the Napoleonic Wars. It worked well.

They formed something called **the Concert of Europe**. This was an informal agreement. Its goal: keep things as they were (maintain the status quo). The Concert handled some internal conflicts. It also absorbed new, more liberal political ideas. Neither caused major instability.

There were a few military clashes. But they were short. And small in scale.

## Prussia and Austria Go to War (1866)

Prussia was different from most nations. It had a militarized culture. Prussia still saw war as a tool to get what it wanted. France felt the same way.

In 1866, **Austria-Hungary** went to war with **Prussia**. The conflict lasted about seven weeks. Prussia won easily. Why? Prussia had invested in better military technology and weaponry. After the war, Prussia annexed several German states.

This changed everything for Austria:

- Austria was barred from taking part in German affairs.
- Prussia became the dominant German state.
- The war forced Austria into a **dual monarchy** system — an alliance with Hungary.

Austria agreed to this alliance because it needed partners after losing its role in German politics. But the arrangement was unwieldy. Austria and Hungary each kept their own national government and parliament. They had different goals. Yet they shared one empire.

## The Franco-Prussian War (1870–1871)

This war was also brief, but it caused major change.

France declared war on Prussia. Why? A dispute over who would inherit the Spanish throne. The fighting lasted only a few months. But the results were severe:

- The Prussian army besieged Paris.
- Napoléon III was captured.
- France had to pay a large **war indemnity** to Prussia.
- France also paid for the occupation forces stationed in its territory.
- France lost the territories of **Alsace and Lorraine**. (These regions changed hands several times during the first half of the twentieth century.)

For France, this was a humiliating defeat. But it opened the door to something bigger: the unification of the German Empire.

The treaty was signed in the **Hall of Mirrors** at the Palace of Versailles. This act cemented Prussia's leadership of the new empire. It also completed what the revolutions of 1848 had left undone. Germany emerged as a major power in Europe.

## Why These Wars Felt "Safe"

The fighting in these wars stayed local. The wars were short. So no country needed to mobilize its full economy or all its resources. They did not involve many nations. The fighting rarely crossed into other countries' lands.

With one exception — the Franco-Prussian War — the impact on civilian life was minimal. Few civilians died. Little property was destroyed.

In a sense, this pattern lulled Europe into a false comfort. People expected that any future war would be just as swift and small.

# The World After the War

## Europe's Broken Economy

World War I wrecked economies around the world. Four years of fighting caused massive losses. The labor force across Europe was disrupted. Government budgets were thrown into chaos.

Germany owed reparations to the other nations. Britain and France planned to use those payments to cover their own debts. But this plan built an economic house of cards. It could tumble down at any moment.

The war also hit Africa, Asia, and Latin America hard.

## Trade in Africa Before and During the War

Before the war, African nations traded a lot with Europe. Germany was the biggest partner. It handled most European trade with sub-Saharan Africa.

Then the war started. Trading with countries at war became very difficult. European goods got more expensive. Many Africans could no longer afford them.

## Colonial Exploitation After the War

After the war, Britain and France turned to their African colonies for money. They also took over Germany's former colonial possessions. Both powers focused on agriculture.

The United States did not suffer the physical destruction that other Allies faced. It came out of the war as a creditor nation. Britain and France owed it money for wartime loans.

# Pearl Harbor and U.S. Entry into the War

## The Road to Conflict

In August 1941, the United States imposed sanctions on Japan. These included an embargo on oil and gas sales. The goal was to pressure Japan to stop its aggression.

This action pushed Japan further toward a plan. Japan wanted to move south. It aimed to take natural resources from two sources:

- The crumbling European imperial regimes in the South Pacific
- The Philippines, which was a U.S. colony

Japan saw the United States as a soft enemy. Japan believed America would not make the sacrifices needed to win a war. So Japan planned a surprise assault on Pearl Harbor, Hawaii. This was a major U.S. naval base.

At the same time, last-ditch diplomatic talks were still happening between Tokyo and Washington. The U.S. wanted Japan to withdraw from China. Japan refused. Japan also felt the U.S. would not open up to further negotiations. Japanese leaders decided they had to strike while they still could.

## The Attack on Pearl Harbor

U.S. intelligence services had broken several Japanese codes. By late November 1941, warnings were sent to U.S. forces. These warnings said war with Japan was likely. The Philippines was named as the probable target.

Early in the morning of December 7, a Japanese task force struck. It eluded detection. The surprise attack devastated the U.S. fleet at Pearl Harbor. Here is what happened:

- Eight battleships were sunk or damaged
- Other smaller craft were damaged
- Approximately three hundred aircraft were destroyed or damaged
- More than two thousand people were killed
- More than one thousand others were injured

Near-simultaneous attacks hit U.S. bases in the Philippines, Guam, and Wake Island.

The following day, Congress voted unanimously to declare war on Japan. A few days later, Germany and Italy declared war against the United States. The country then entered the war in Europe as well. It fought on the side of the Allies.

China also joined the Allies after Pearl Harbor. However, China did not join the fighting in Europe.

## Building the U.S. Military

U.S. military planners made a grim estimate. They said victory in Europe and Asia might require:

- Nine million troops
- More than two hundred divisions

A massive recruitment and draft program had to be set up. The army needed to expand and prepare for combat.

Recruitment efforts eventually expanded to include:

- African Americans
- Women
- Native Americans
- Thirty-three thousand Japanese Americans

Leadership of the troops fell to Dwight D. Eisenhower. He was rapidly promoted through the ranks. He became a key aide to Chief of Staff George C. Marshall. He also became commanding general of the European theater of operations.

# The Human Cost of the War

The war was over. But the world faced a terrible bill. Millions of people were dead.

## Military and Civilian Deaths by Country

**Germany**
- 5.5 million military deaths
- Up to 3 million civilian deaths

**Japan**
- 2.1 million military deaths
- About 1 million civilian deaths

**China**
- Military deaths are hard to count exactly. They may have reached 4 million.
- 16 million civilian deaths

**United States**
- 416,000 deaths

**United Kingdom**
- 384,000 deaths

The U.S. and the U.K. were hit hard. But they lost fewer people than most other nations in the war.

## The Soviet Union: The Heaviest Toll

No single country suffered more than the Soviet Union.

- Military deaths: between 8.8 million and 10.7 million
- Civilian deaths: more than 13 million

Not all civilian deaths came from bombs or bullets. Many Soviets starved. Others died of disease. Wartime conditions caused these deaths.

## The War Ends, but the Work Begins

Germany surrendered. Japan surrendered. The fighting was over.

But the world still needed rebuilding. The victors had a vision for what it should look like next. Getting there would take a great deal of work.

# Yugoslavia After World War II

After World War II ended, European nations chose a side. Most joined the Western Bloc or the Eastern Bloc. One country did not pick either side. That country was Yugoslavia.

## How Yugoslavia Took Power

In 1942, communist partisans fought against the Axis powers. They fought for the People's Liberation Front. These fighters formed a new government. It was called the Anti-Fascist Council for the National Liberation of Yugoslavia (AVNOJ).

In 1943, Italian forces left Yugoslavia. AVNOJ took control of the land. It set up a new state called Democratic Federal Yugoslavia. The partisans' leader was Josip Broz Tito. He became prime minister.

In 1945, Yugoslavia ended its monarchy. Tito was recognized as the country's leader. A nationwide vote soon after confirmed this result.

## Joining the Communist World

Yugoslavia was a communist state from the start. In 1947, it helped found the Cominform. The full name was the Information Bureau of the Communist and Workers' Parties.

The Cominform had one main goal. It wanted to guide the new communist governments in Europe. These governments needed to work together. They needed to oppose anti-communist activity across the rest of Europe. The Soviet Union would lead this effort. It would give direction to the other countries.

## Tito and Stalin Clash

Tito and Stalin did not get along early on. Tito wanted more land for Yugoslavia. He wanted to add Bulgaria and Albania. He also wanted parts of Greece, Italy, and Austria.

Stalin said no. He called these claims unreasonable. He feared they would cause trouble with Western Europe.

Yugoslavia also helped the Greek communists in their civil war. Stalin opposed this too. He worried the West would be angry.

Tito refused to accept a lower role for Yugoslavia. This was key. Unlike other Eastern Bloc countries, Yugoslavia had freed itself from the Axis on its own. No Soviet help was needed. So Tito believed Yugoslavia deserved equal treatment. It should not be a satellite state taking orders from Moscow.

## Expulsion and Independence

In 1948, the Cominform expelled Yugoslavia. Tito then turned to the United States for help. The U.S. helped Yugoslavia survive. This mattered because Yugoslavia could no longer trade with its Eastern Bloc neighbors.

But Tito did not want to become a puppet of the United States either. During the 1950s and 1960s, Yugoslavia built economic self-sufficiency. It traded with both the Western and Eastern Blocs.

In 1960, Tito spoke before the General Assembly of the United Nations. He called on "non-bloc countries" to unite. He listed their common goals: decolonization, disarmament, bans on nuclear testing, and equal economic development.

# India's Path to Independence

India wanted to chart its own course. It refused to join the Cold War alliances. Like Indonesia, it stayed free of those entangling ties. India also helped start the Non-Aligned Movement.

## Why Britain Left

In 1947, the United Kingdom gave India its independence.

Why did Britain let go? Several reasons pushed it out:

- Anti-British protests shook India all through 1946.
- Britain was exhausted from World War II. It could no longer afford to run a colony.
- The UK still had troops in India, but most of them were Indian soldiers. No one knew where their loyalties truly lay. In fact, in 1946, Indian sailors in the British Navy mutinied across the country.
- The United States pressured Britain to let India go. The US was Britain's greatest ally and creditor. It had already given independence to the Philippines after the war.

## Partition and Violence

The news that the British were leaving sparked waves of religious violence.

The core dispute: what would an independent India look like?

Hindus in the Indian National Congress wanted one unified India. Muslims feared a Hindu majority would dominate the government against them. Many Muslims refused to accept that arrangement.

A compromise was reached. At midnight on August 15, 1947, India became independent. At the same moment, Pakistan—a region with a Muslim majority—became its own nation.

## Cold War Balancing Act

India's location made it strategically important. It bordered both the Soviet Union and China. The West took great interest in it.

The UK kept trading with India. It supplied weapons and trained Indian military officers.

India's first prime minister was Jawaharlal Nehru. He wanted to keep his distance from the United States. Here is why:

- He sympathized with socialism.
- He had visited the Soviet Union.
- He recognized the People's Republic of China (PRC).
- He opposed the US refusal to let the PRC take China's seat on the UN Security Council.
- He was suspicious of American intentions toward India, given how the US treated its own citizens of color.

Still, Nehru accepted aid from the United States in the 1950s. He also took aid from the Soviet Union. He played both sides.

## The China Problem

In 1950, India's relationship with China changed. China set up border posts in Tibet to mark its territory. Some of that land was claimed by India.

At first, both countries tried to stay friendly. In 1954, they signed a treaty affirming the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence.

Then things broke down. In 1959, an anti-Chinese uprising erupted in Tibet. The Fourteenth Dalai Lama, Tibet's leader, fled and sought protection in India. India supported him. China was angry.

In 1962, a confrontation along the disputed border with Tibet turned into war between India and China.

The US aided India during the conflict. The Soviet Union officially stayed neutral. But it kept sending funds and technology to India anyway. That choice deepened the growing split between the USSR and China.

# After Stalin: The Soviet Union and the Eastern Bloc (1953–1968)

## A New Leader

Joseph Stalin died in 1953. Georgy Malenkov briefly took his place as leader of the Soviet Union. Then Nikita Khrushchev became the new leader.

Khrushchev was a strong opponent of the Western Bloc, just like Stalin had been. At one meeting, he bragged that communism would "bury" capitalism. But he also wanted a new attitude toward the United States. He wanted to point the Soviet Union in a new direction.

## De-Stalinization

In February 1956, Khrushchev spoke at the Twentieth Congress of the Soviet Communist Party. He denounced Stalin. He accused Stalin of crimes against the Soviet people.

After that speech, Khrushchev began an aggressive process called de-Stalinization. He changed many policies from the Stalin era:

- He ended censorship of the arts.
- He released many people whom Stalin had jailed for political reasons.
- He dissolved the special tribunals that had convicted them.
- He removed Stalin's name from public buildings.
- He took down monuments to Stalin.

## Poland, 1956

In the Eastern Bloc countries, these changes signaled a political thaw.

In June 1956, workers in Poznan, Poland, rioted. They protested food shortages and poor housing. They also had other grievances. In autumn, protests spread to other Polish cities. The protests had a nationalistic character. Protesters called for the Soviet army to leave Poland. They also wanted Russian language classes removed from Polish school curricula.

In October, Władysław Gomułka became leader of the Polish Communist Party. He was now the leader of Poland. Gomułka called for governmental reforms.

Khrushchev was alarmed. He feared that reforms might pull Poland out of the Eastern Bloc. He mobilized Soviet troops in Poland and marched them toward Warsaw. At the same time, he flew to Poland in person.

Gomułka assured Khrushchev that he had no intention of ending communism. He also said Poland would keep its relationship with the Soviet Union. Khrushchev then agreed that reforms could take place.

The following changes were made:

- The collectivization of Polish agriculture was ended.
- Soviet advisers were sent home.
- Political prisoners were released.
- The Roman Catholic Church was given greater freedom.

## Hungary, 1956

The success in Poland inspired others. On October 23, 1956, students marched through the streets of Budapest, Hungary. They demanded several things:

- Removal of Stalinist symbols.
- Improvements in wages.
- Economic reforms.
- Removal of Soviet troops from Hungary.

The State Security Police opened fire on students who gathered outside the main radio station. The students wanted to read their demands on the air. Several students were killed.

An uprising began. Angry citizens fought both the police and Soviet troops. Protesters attacked the parliament building. Ernő Gerő, head of the ruling Hungarian Working People's Party and leader of the country, fled. His prime minister, András Hegedüs, fled with him.

Imre Nagy took office as prime minister. Nagy was a reformer. Unlike Gomułka, Nagy did not want to make internal reforms while staying loyal to Moscow. He wanted more.

On October 28, Nagy called for a cease-fire. He dissolved the State Security Police. He demanded that Soviet troops leave Budapest. On November 1, he announced that Hungary was no longer a member of the Warsaw Pact. He said Hungary would remain neutral in international affairs.

## The Soviet Invasion of Hungary

Three days later, Soviet forces entered Hungary. They joined troops that the USSR had been about to withdraw until Nagy's announcement.

Why did Khrushchev order the invasion? There are several possible reasons:

- He may have feared that Hungarian neutrality threatened Soviet security.
- He may have wanted to show his resolve to conservative communists and leaders of other Soviet states.
- Some argue that the Western Bloc's failure to intervene emboldened him.

The uprising ended on November 10. About 2,500 Hungarians had been killed. The communist government was reestablished under János Kádár.

Approximately twenty thousand Hungarians were arrested. Another 200,000 fled the country. Soviet troops were permanently stationed in Hungary. In 1958, Nagy was tried and executed.

The United States did not become involved in the events in Hungary. Khrushchev later mocked this decision.

## The Berlin Crisis

Despite not wanting a confrontation with the Soviets, the United States could not ignore Khrushchev's ultimatum regarding Berlin. In 1958 and again in 1961, Khrushchev demanded that Britain, France, and the United States leave West Berlin. These demands went unheeded.

The capitalist part of the old German capital was a thorn in Khrushchev's side. Its prosperity caused discontent among residents of the communist eastern districts. Also, the openness in West Berlin allowed many people from East Germany—and elsewhere in the Eastern Bloc—to escape to freedom.

## The Berlin Wall

On the evening of August 12–13, 1961, East German troops erected a barbed wire fence. It divided western Berlin from eastern Berlin. In the days that followed, cement walls went up as well. These walls stopped free passage from east to west.

## Tanks at the Wall

On October 22, a dispute erupted between the United States and the Soviet Union. The issue was the free passage of U.S. government employees between East and West Berlin.

The United States maintained that agreements reached at Potsdam (at the end of World War II) allowed members of the Allies to travel freely throughout Berlin. To test whether the Soviets would honor this agreement, the U.S. began sending cars carrying U.S. officials across the dividing line. They wanted to see if the Soviets would stop them. If they were stopped, U.S. troops—sometimes riding in tanks—accompanied them across.

On October 27, the USSR responded. It sent some of its own tanks to the entrance of East Berlin. U.S. and Soviet tanks aimed their guns at one another. A fight was narrowly averted. Kennedy and Khrushchev agreed to remove their tanks at the same time.

## Czechoslovakia, 1968

Tensions flared in Europe again in 1968. Czechoslovakia, like Poland and Hungary before it, sought to loosen its ties to the Soviet Union.

Early in the year, the country's conservative leader Antonín Novotný was replaced by Alexander Dubček. Dubček instituted economic reforms. He ended government censorship. As Czechs called for even greater reforms, the Soviet Union became alarmed—just as it had in Poland and Hungary in 1956.

The Soviets feared that changes in Czechoslovakia would spark calls for reform elsewhere in the Eastern Bloc or in the Soviet republics themselves. ## Poland, 1956

In the Eastern Bloc countries, these changes signaled a **political thaw**.

### The Riots in Poznań

- Food shortages

- Other grievances

In **October**, **Władysław Gomułka** became leader of the Polish Communist Party.

He was now the leader of Poland.

Gomułka called for governmental reforms.

He feared that reforms might pull Poland out of the Eastern Bloc.

So he acted. He mobilized Soviet troops in Poland. He marched them toward Warsaw.

At the same time, he flew to Poland in person.

Gomułka assured Khrushchev of two things:

- He had **no intention** of ending communism.
- Poland would keep its relationship with the Soviet Union.

### The Changes Made

The following changes were made:

- The collectivization of Polish agriculture was **ended**.
- Soviet advisers were **sent home**.
- Political prisoners were **released**.
- The Roman Catholic Church was given **greater freedom**.

The success in Poland inspired others.

On **October 23, 1956**, students marched through the streets of Budapest, Hungary.

- Removal of Stalinist symbols
- Improvements in wages

The state security police **opened fire**.

Their target was a group of students outside the main radio station.

An uprising began.

Protesters attacked the parliament building.

He wanted **more**.

On **October 28**, Nagy did three things:

- He called for a cease-fire.
- He dissolved the state security police.
- He demanded that Soviet troops leave Budapest.

Hungary was **no longer a member of the Warsaw Pact**.

He said Hungary would remain neutral in international affairs.

**Three days later, Soviet forces entered Hungary.**

They joined troops that the USSR had been about to withdraw. Nagy's announcement changed that plan.

- He may have wanted to show his resolve to conservative communists and leaders of other Soviet states.

Khrushchev later **mocked** this decision.

The United States did not want a confrontation with the Soviets.

But it could not ignore Khrushchev's ultimatum regarding Berlin.

On **October 22**, a dispute erupted between the United States and the Soviet Union.

- He reversed Dubček's reforms.
- He restored censorship.
