# The Jakhanke Islamic Movement in West Africa

## Why the Jakhanke Matter

A history of Islam in West Africa is incomplete without the Jakhanke. This movement began in the 12th century. It was led by a charismatic scholar named Alhajj Salim Suwareh. He helped spread Islam across present-day Mali, Guinea, Senegal, and The Gambia. These are now the most Islamized countries in West Africa.

The Jakhanke effort bore rich fruit. But first, we must ask two questions:

- Who were the Jakhanke?
- Why do they deserve attention in our study of Islam's spread in West Africa?

## Who Were the Jakhanke?

Lamin Sanneh is a highly regarded Gambian historian. He is also the leading authority on the Jakhanke. He calls them a "specialized caste" of Muslim clerics and educators.

The word "caste" signals that they belong to a larger group. That group is the Serahuli ethnic group. In other writings, this group is called Soninke. Today, people often mislabel the Jakhanke as Mandinka. This is an error.

They do speak a dialect of Mandinka. But their "Mandikanization" happened for a practical reason. When the Jakhanke moved from present-day Mali to the Senegambia region, Mandinka chiefs hosted them. Over time, they adopted the local language.

The words "clerics and educators" describe their profession. They were literate. This made them able to teach, proselytize, and do missionary work.

Today, large numbers of Jakhanke live in the Senegambia region. They do not place much value on their ethnic origins. Instead, they take pride in their role as propagators of Islam over the past 800 years.

## Why This Matters Now

This is exactly why the Jakhanke should interest us. They started a peaceful propagation of Islam in the Senegambia region.

This point is especially relevant today. In many parts of the world, violence is associated with Islam. The Jakhanke offer a different model.

Much of what we now see as the style and technique for peacefully spreading Islam in Senegambia comes from them. In short, they set the standards for missionary work.

## Their Standards: Peaceful Methods

The Jakhanke professed a peaceful path to Islam. They did not raise the sword to spread their religion. Instead, they used these methods:

- Establishing Koranic schools
- Building mosques
- Upgrading existing mosques
- Holding sessions on Koranic exegesis (interpretation)
- Preserving holy sites where yearly Islamic gatherings take place
- Working as itinerant traders who brought Islam to their clients and customers

## Their Tactics: Growth and Retreat

The Jakhanke also had clear tactics.

**They believed in numbers.** They were keen to multiply their *talibes* (disciples). Each disciple went through years of tutelage. After training, the disciple was allowed to disperse. Then that person would gather new disciples of their own. Through this massification, the Jakhanke strengthened their religion.

**They withdrew into quiet enclaves.** They pulled back from the maddening crowds. The Jakhanke needed the quietude of a monastery. They were very good at establishing theocratic entities deep in the Senegambian Savannah. In these places, they built self-sustaining communities dedicated to Islamic scholarship and renditions (recitations).

Extant examples of such religious villages include:

- Sutukuho (The Gambia)
- Sutukung (The Gambia)
- Niokhlo (Casamance)
- Suna Karantba (Casamance)

## The Founder: Alhaji Salim Suwareh

So far, we have not discussed the man at the centre of all this. That is Alhaji Salim Suwareh, the founder of the Jakhanke Islamic movement. He was central to the success of their missionary work. His story deserves our attention.

His early life is shrouded in mystery. But a few strands are revealing:

- He died around 1500.
- He reputedly made seven pilgrimages (hajj) to Mecca.
- He had relatives in Mecca and lived there before relocating to Black Africa to spread Islam.
- He settled in the Jaka region of Masina, in present-day Mali.

This is where the name comes from. "Jakhanke" means "those who hail from Jaka" in Mandinka.

After completing his seventh hajj, Suwareh returned to Africa and stayed. He led his people from Jaka Masina to Jaka Bambuku. But the animist ruler of Bambuku became hostile. Suwareh did what the Prophet of Islam did when Meccans started throwing stones at him: he fled into exile.

Suwareh led his band of talibes towards present-day Senegambia. The historian Professor Sanneh writes that since this *hijra* (flight-like movement), the Jakhanke "have been united by a close bond of solidarity based on fidelity to Suwareh characterized by bonds of solidarity."

## A Test of Principle: Rejection of Violence

The Jakhanke were deeply committed to peaceful spread. This commitment was tested in the 19th century.

A Serahuli religious hothead named Momodou Lamin Drammeh (1835–1887) chose a different path. He opted to wage war to convert Bundu (eastern Senegal) into Islam. The Jakhanke disowned him. They fled further down to present-day eastern Gambia.

Drammeh's swashbuckling style was the opposite of their orderly ways. Without bearing the sword, the Jakhanke were able to fasten the spread and reform of Islam. This stood in contrast to jihadist figures like Drammeh, Umar Taal, or Maba Jahou Bah.

There is a paradox here that may not be obvious at first but is palpable: How could the Jakhanke, whose mentor Suwareh lived in Mecca and had relatives there, disavow the uncompromising Wahabi doctrine? They chose instead to espouse the "path of accommodation."

## Conclusion: The Significance of the Jakhanke Movement

What is the significance of this movement? Simply put: the Jakhanke epitomized a peaceful, community-led spread of Islam. This made a deep impact on the societies that received it. They presented Islam as a way of peace.

Present-day bomb throwers who claim to spread this religion through violence may want to learn a lesson or two from the Jakhanke movement. It started over 500 years ago. And it worked without a single sword being raised.

This made a deep impact on the societies that received it.

They presented Islam as a way of peace.

Present-day bomb throwers who claim to spread this religion through violence may want to learn a lesson or two from the Jakhanke movement.

It started over 500 years ago.

And it worked without a single sword being raised.

# the jakhanke islamic movement in west africa

## table of contents

1. why the jakhanke matter
2. who were the jakhanke?
3. why this matters now
4. their standards: peaceful methods
5. their tactics: growth and retreat
6. the founder: alhaji salim suwareh
7. a test of principle: rejection of violence
8. conclusion: what the jakhanke movement means

---

## 1. why the jakhanke matter

a history of islam in west africa is **incomplete** without them.

the jakhanke movement began in the **12th century**.

it was led by a scholar named **alhajj salim suwareh**.

he helped spread islam across present-day mali, guinea, senegal, and the gambia.

these are now the **most muslim** countries in west africa.

the jakhanke effort bore rich fruit.

but first, we must ask two questions:

- who were the jakhanke?
- why do they deserve our attention when we study how islam spread?

---

## 2. who were the jakhanke?

**lamin sanneh** is a well-known gambian historian.

he is also the leading expert on the jakhanke.

he calls them a **"specialized group"** of muslim teachers and educators.

the word "group" tells us they belong to a larger family.

that family is the **serahuli** ethnic group.

in other books, this group is called **soninke**.

today, people often get it wrong and call the jakhanke "mandinka."

this is an error.

they do speak a dialect of mandinka.

but they picked up that language for a **practical reason**.

when the jakhanke moved from present-day mali to senegambia, mandinka chiefs welcomed them in.

over time, they learned and used the local language.

the words "teachers and educators" describe their job.

they could read and write.

this made them able to **teach**, share their faith, and do outreach work.

today, large numbers of jakhanke live in the senegambia region.

they do not place much value on where they came from as an ethnic group.

instead, they take pride in their role as **spreaders of islam** over 800 years.

---

## 3. why this matters now

this is exactly why the jakhanke should interest us.

they started a **peaceful** way of sharing islam in senegambia.

this point is especially relevant today.

in many parts of the world, violence is linked to islam.

the jakhanke offer a **different model**.

much of what we see as the style for peacefully spreading islam comes from them.

in short, they set the standards for outreach work.

---

## 4. their standards: peaceful methods

the jakhanke followed a **peaceful path** to share islam.

they did not raise a sword to spread their religion.

instead, they used these methods:

- setting up **quranic schools**
- building **mosques**
- improving existing mosques
- holding sessions on **reading and explaining the quran**
- keeping holy sites where yearly islamic gatherings take place
- working as **traders who travelled from town to town**, bringing islam to their customers

---

## 5. their tactics: growth and retreat

the jakhanke also had clear ways of growing their community.

they believed in **numbers**.

they wanted to grow the number of their **talibes** (students).

each student went through years of learning.

after training, the student was allowed to go out into the world.

then that person would gather new students of their own.

through this way of growing, the jakhanke made their faith stronger.

they also knew when to **pull back**.

they stepped away from busy, noisy crowds.

the jakhanke needed the quiet of a monastery.

they were very good at setting up small, self-governing communities deep in the senegambian savannah.

in these places, they built communities that could look after themselves, focused on **islamic learning and recitation**.

examples of such religious villages still standing today include:

- **sutukuho** (the gambia)
- **sutukung** (the gambia)
- **niokhlo** (casamance)
- **suna karantba** (casamance)

---

## 6. the founder: alhaji salim suwareh

so far, we have not talked about the man at the centre of all this.

that is **alhaji salim suwareh**, the founder of the jakhanke movement.

he was central to the success of their outreach work.

his story deserves our attention.

his early life is wrapped in mystery.

but a few details help us understand him:

- he died around **1500**.
- he reportedly made **seven pilgrimages (hajj)** to mecca.
- he had relatives in mecca and lived there before moving to black africa to spread islam.
- he settled in the **jaka region of masina**, in present-day mali.

this is where the name comes from.

**"jakhanke"** means "those who come from jaka" in mandinka.

after finishing his seventh hajj, suwareh returned to africa and stayed.

he led his people from jaka masina to **jaka bambuku**.

but the local ruler of bambuku turned against him.

suwareh did what the prophet of islam did when meccans threw stones at him: **he left in exile**.

suwareh led his group of talibes towards present-day senegambia.

the historian professor sanneh writes that since this flight, the jakhanke "have been united by a close bond of solidarity based on loyalty to suwareh."

---

## 7. a test of principle: rejection of violence

the jakhanke were deeply committed to **peaceful spread**.

this commitment was tested in the **19th century**.

a serahuli religious leader named **momodou lamin drammeh** (1835–1887) chose a different path.

he decided to wage war to convert bundu (eastern senegal) into islam by force.

the jakhanke **disowned him**.

they fled further down to present-day eastern gambia.

drammeh's bold, violent style was the opposite of their calm, orderly ways.

without raising a sword, the jakhanke were able to grow and reform islam.

this stood in contrast to war-making figures like drammeh, umar tael, or maba jahou bah.

there is a puzzle here that may not be obvious at first but is real:

how could the jakhanke, whose mentor suwareh lived in mecca and had relatives there, reject the strict wahabi doctrine?

they chose instead to follow the **"path of accommodation"** — meeting people where they were, rather than forcing change.

---

## 8. conclusion: what the jakhanke movement means

what is the significance of this movement?

simply put: the jakhanke showed a **peaceful, community-led** way of spreading islam.

this made a deep impact on the societies that received it.

they presented islam as a **way of peace**.

present-day people who throw bombs and claim to spread this religion through violence may want to learn a lesson or two from the jakhanke movement.

it started over **500 years ago**.

and it worked without a single sword being raised.

# Early European Contact with West Africa

## The Portuguese Arrive

In **1442**, Portuguese ships reached the Senegal River. This was the first time European sailors reached sub-Saharan Africa.

Before that, the Portuguese had been sailing along the coasts of Morocco and Western Sahara since **1413**. In 1413, they captured the Moroccan city of Ceuta. Ceuta is still a Spanish city today.

Between **1413 and the 1440s**, the Portuguese built several fortified settlements on the Moroccan coast. Key locations included:

- Arzila
- Mogador (now called Essaouira)
- Safi
- Tangier

The Portuguese kept a strong presence in Morocco until **1578**. In that year, King Sebastião I and much of the Portuguese nobility were killed at the Battle of Alcácer-Quibir.

## Trade Links Grow

By **1471**, West African leaders between Senegal and Ghana had established trade and diplomatic ties with Portuguese traders.

Major early sites of trade and settlement included:

- The Gambia River
- Bugendo, on the São Domingos River in Guinea-Bissau
- Sierra Leone

For the next **150 years**, West African rulers and traders met the Portuguese more than any other European nation. Smaller trading missions from England and France also occurred, but these were less frequent.

## Why Did the Portuguese Come?

The Portuguese had four main motivations:

1. **Gold.** They wanted access to the extensive gold production of Bono-Mansu and the Akan states.
2. **Competition with the Ottoman Empire.** The Ottomans captured Constantinople in 1453. This caused a crisis in Christian Europe. The Portuguese wanted to reach this gold before the Ottomans did.
3. **A route to India.** They sought a sea trade route to Indian markets around the Cape of Good Hope.
4. **The slave trade.** Over time, the trade in enslaved persons became an increasingly important goal.

## The Dutch Rise

By the **1590s**, the Dutch began to rival the Portuguese as the major European trading nation in Africa.

Dutch ships were bigger and better. The goods they traded with African political leaders were of much higher quality.

By **1650**, the Dutch had captured many key Portuguese trading stations:

- Gorée, Senegal (captured 1621)
- Elmina, Ghana (captured 1637)
- Luanda, Angola (captured 1641)

At first, the Dutch were mainly interested in textiles, animal hides for the leather industry, and ivory. By the middle of the **17th century**, they too turned to slave trading.

Dutch interest in slave trading began in the **1620s**. This followed their capture of half of the Brazilian colonies from the Portuguese. From **1630 to 1654**, the Dutch controlled northern Brazil and its sugar plantations, which used the labour of enslaved persons. Their growing colonial interests drove their interest in slave trading. The slave trade took over as the dominant form of trade in the second half of the **18th century**.

## Other Nations Follow

In the second half of the **17th century**, other European nations followed this pattern. Danish, English, French, German, and Swedish traders established factories at various points along the West African coast. The pattern of African-European trade and interaction deepened over time.

## What This Chapter Covers

This chapter focuses on the early period of African-European interaction, up to **1650**. This is before the trade in enslaved persons came to dominate all other trade. A separate chapter on the trans-Atlantic slave trade covers that topic in more detail.

text:
# Portuguese Voyages Along the West African Coast

## Reaching Senegal, Gambia, and Beyond (1442–1456)

In 1442, the Portuguese reached the Senegal River. Their voyages continued from there.

By 1448, some Portuguese sailors had gone up the Gambia River. They reached a major trading town called Kantora. Kantora sat not far east of what is today Basse Santa Su, in the far east of the country. At that time, Kantora was a key centre for trans-Saharan trade.

By the mid-1450s, two new contacts had formed:

- Trade began with the Wolof state of Kajoor on the coast.
- The Bijagós Islands, off the coast of Guinea-Bissau, entered discussions with European traders.

The first language used was probably Arabic. Many people in 15th-century Portugal spoke Arabic. Granada in Spain was still an Islamic kingdom. And Arabic was widely spoken across much of West Africa.

In 1456, one sailor wrote about the Bijagós Islands. He said this was the last place where African peoples shared a language with Portuguese sailors. This also marked the southernmost reach of Arab and Trans-Saharan trade at that time.

## Cape Verde and Ghana (c. 1456–1471)

The Cape Verde Islands were first reached, probably in 1456. Capeverdean historians still debate whether people already lived there. Archaeological evidence is inconclusive. The islands may have served as a salt depot for Saharan states.

Around 1471, the Portuguese reached the coastline of Ghana.

## Gold and the Fortress at Elmina (1481)

Ghana's coast was different from other areas. It sat close to the gold mines in the Akan forests. Soon, Akan traders began selling gold informally to the Portuguese.

The Portuguese state wanted a share of that trade. In 1481, they sent a large fleet. They negotiated with Kwamena Ansa, the ruler at Edina (now called Elmina). The goal was to build a fortress.

The talks were tense. At one point, the Portuguese tried to build their fort on the site of a holy shrine. This caused a serious stand-off. In the end, negotiations concluded. The fortress at Elmina was built. It still stands today on what became known as the Gold Coast.

Later, in the 17th century, the Dutch took over the fortress. Over time, the Dutch and English became the main European nations trading in Ghana.

## More Forts Along the Gold Coast

The Gold Coast had a great deal of commerce. Many Akan rulers wanted to expand their trading connections. The Portuguese built forts at other locations along the coast, such as Axim and Komenda. Many of these were completed by 1500.

Over time, more forts appeared. They stood almost every few miles along the Gold Coast. Some focused on the gold trade. Others, like Anishan, specialised in exporting corn. European ships had high demand for corn.

The slave trade did not become dominant on the Gold Coast until the 18th century.

## Benin and Its Trade with Portugal (1485–1700s)

Meanwhile, other rulers from West and West-Central Africa were making contact with the Portuguese.

In 1485, Oba Ozolua of Benin received Portuguese visitors. Around 1490, the Atlantic trading post of Gwatón was founded.

At first, Benin sold malaguetta peppers to the Portuguese. But in 1499, a sea route to India was established. After that, Benin's peppers became less in demand in Europe.

The Portuguese tried to set up a trade in enslaved persons from Benin to the gold suppliers at Elmina. The Oba refused.

Over the 16th century, relations between Benin and Portugal declined. In the early 17th century, the Obas renewed links with European traders. The Dutch wanted the cloth produced in Benin.

Throughout the 17th century, cloth remained Benin's main export. Ambassy cloths were traded regularly to Elmina. They also went as far afield as Brazil.

By the late 17th century, demand for Benin cloth fell. Imports of luxury cloths from India grew. By the 18th century, Benin's Obas had to turn to the trade in enslaved persons. This was needed to preserve and renew the power of Edo and the Benin state.

## Kongo, São Tomé, and Wider Connections (1485–1510s)

The Portuguese continued south after Benin. They reached the mouth of the Kongo River. There, they established relations with the manikongo at Mbanza Kongo, the capital of Kongo. His name was Nzika Nkuwu.

By 1485, the island of São Tomé had been settled. Many BaKongo peoples were taken there as enslaved persons. They worked on sugar plantations.

In 1491, Nzika Nkuwu converted to Christianity. He took the name Joao I. This created a link between Kongo and Elmina through São Tomé. The island traded with both places.

By the 1510s, traders from Benin were mentioned as present at the Kongolese port of Mpinda. A new manikongo, Afonso I (ruling 1509–46), wrote about this in a letter in Portuguese.

## A Network Takes Shape

By the 1510s, many different peoples and rulers across West Africa had established connections with the Portuguese. Some places, like Benin and Elmina, also had links further south to Kongo.

African rulers hoped to expand their trading contacts. At times, they also sought military support against rivals. In 1516, Benin fought a major battle against Nupe with Portuguese support. Civil wars in Jolof and Kongo also drew on outside connections.

# Portuguese Voyages Along the West African Coast



## 1 · Reaching Senegal, Gambia, and Beyond (1442–1456)



In **1442**, the Portuguese reached the **Senegal River**.

From there, their voyages continued.


By **1448**, some Portuguese sailors had gone up the **Gambia River**.

They reached a major trading town called **Kantara**.


**Kantara** sat not far east of what is today **Basse Santa Su**.

This was in the far east of the country.

At that time, Kantara was a key centre for **trans-Saharan trade**.


By the mid-1450s, two new contacts had formed:



- Trade began with the **Wolof State of Kajoor** on the coast.


- The **Bijagós Islands**, off the coast of Guinea-Bissau, entered discussions with European traders.



The first language used was probably **Arabic**.

Why? Many people in 15th-century Portugal spoke Arabic.

Granada in Spain was still an Islamic kingdom.

And Arabic was widely spoken across much of West Africa.


In **1456**, one sailor wrote about the Bijagós Islands.

He said this was the last place where African peoples shared a language with Portuguese sailors.

This also marked the **southernmost reach** of Arab and trans-Saharan trade at that time.



---

## 2 · Cape Verde and Ghana (c. 1456–1471)



The **Cape Verde Islands** were first reached, probably in **1456**.


Cape Verdean historians still debate whether people already lived there.

Archaeological evidence is inconclusive.

The islands may have served as a **salt depot** for Saharan states.


Around **1471**, the Portuguese reached the coastline of **Ghana**.



---

## 3 · Gold and the Fortress at Elmina (1481)



Ghana's coast was different from other areas.

It sat close to the **gold mines** in the Akan forests.

Soon, Akan traders began selling gold informally to the Portuguese.


The Portuguese state wanted a share of that trade.

In **1481**, they sent a large fleet.

They negotiated with **Kwamena Ansa**, the ruler at **Edina** (now called Elmina).

The goal was to build a fortress.


The talks were tense.

At one point, the Portuguese tried to build their fort on the site of a **holy shrine**.

This caused a serious stand-off.

In the end, negotiations concluded.


The **Fortress at Elmina** was built.

It still stands today on what became known as the **Gold Coast**.


Later, in the 17th century, the **Dutch** took over the fortress.

Over time, the Dutch and English became the main European nations trading in Ghana.



---

## 4 · More Forts Along the Gold Coast



The Gold Coast had a great deal of commerce.

Many Akan rulers wanted to expand their trading connections.


The Portuguese built forts at other locations along the coast.

These included **Axim** and **Komenda**.

Many of these were completed by **1500**.


Over time, more forts appeared.

They stood almost every few miles along the Gold Coast.



- Some focused on the **gold trade**.


- Others, like **Anishan**, specialised in exporting **corn**. European ships had high demand for corn.



The slave trade did not become dominant on the Gold Coast until the **18th century**.



---

## 5 · Benin and Its Trade with Portugal (1485–1700s)



Meanwhile, other rulers from West and West-Central Africa were making contact with the Portuguese.


In **1485**, **Oba Ozolua** of Benin received Portuguese visitors.

Around **1490**, the Atlantic trading post of **Gwatón** was founded.


At first, Benin sold **malaguetta peppers** to the Portuguese.

But in **1499**, a sea route to India was established.

After that, Benin's peppers became less in demand in Europe.


The Portuguese tried to set up a trade in enslaved persons from Benin to the gold suppliers at Elmina.

**The Oba refused.**


Over the 16th century, relations between Benin and Portugal declined.


In the early 17th century, the Obas renewed links with European traders.

The Dutch wanted the **cloth produced in Benin**.


Throughout the 17th century, cloth remained Benin's main export.

**Ambassy cloths** were traded regularly to Elmina.

They also went as far afield as **Brazil**.


By the late 17th century, demand for Benin cloth fell.

Imports of luxury cloths from India grew.


By the **18th century**, Benin's Obas had to turn to the trade in enslaved persons.

This was needed to preserve and renew the power of **Edo** and the Benin state.



---

## 6 · Kongo, São Tomé, and Wider Connections (1485–1510s)



The Portuguese continued south after Benin.

They reached the mouth of the **Kongo River**.


There, they established relations with the **Manikongo** at **Mbanza Kongo**, the capital of Kongo.

His name was **Nzika Nkuwu**.


By **1485**, the island of **São Tomé** had been settled.

Many BaKongo peoples were taken there as enslaved persons.

They worked on **sugar plantations**.


In **1491**, Nzika Nkuwu converted to Christianity.

He took the name **João I**.


This created a link between Kongo and Elmina through São Tomé.

The island traded with both places.


By the **1510s**, traders from Benin were mentioned as present at the Kongolese port of **Mpinda**.

A new Manikongo, **Afonso I** (ruling 1509–46), wrote about this in a letter in Portuguese.



---

## 7 · A Network Takes Shape



By the **1510s**, many different peoples and rulers across West Africa had established connections with the Portuguese.

Some places, like Benin and Elmina, also had links further south to Kongo.


African rulers hoped to expand their trading contacts.

At times, they also sought **military support** against rivals.



- In **1516**, Benin fought a major battle against **Nupe** with Portuguese support.


- Civil wars in **Jolof** and **Kongo** also drew on outside connections.

# How Missionaries Improved Health Services

## Traditional Medicine Before the Missionaries

Before Christian missionaries arrived, most sick people relied on traditional remedies. They used herbs, roots, and tree barks to make their cures. This practice continued well into the pre-independence period.

Modern science has confirmed that many of these concoctions do have medicinal properties. However, traditional medicine had serious shortcomings:

- Preventive medicine was almost unknown. As a result, epidemics struck often.
- Traditional doctors could not always diagnose illness accurately.
- They often blamed natural ailments on supernatural causes.
- Before treating the sick person, they would perform mystic rituals to appease an "unknown" spirit.
- They prescribed many taboos that had no real link to the illness being treated.

## The Missionaries' Response

The early missionaries set up medical centres. At first, these were at their mission posts. Over time, they spread far and wide across the region. Later, leprosariums (leprosy hospitals) and orphanages were built to add to their services.

---

## Medical Services in Nigeria

### The Roman Catholics

The Roman Catholics were among the first groups to bring organised medical care to Nigeria.

Father Jean Marie Coquard worked in and from Abeokuta for forty years. In the second half of the nineteenth century, he became well known among the Egba people as both a priest and a surgeon.

In 1892, the Church Missionary Society opened Iyi Enu Hospital in Onitsha. Today it is a leading hospital in Anambra State.

### The Methodists

In 1902, the Methodists opened a clinic at Igbo-Ora.

### Mary Slessor

Mary Slessor was a Scottish missionary and nurse. She worked in the Cross River area. Through hard work and persuasion, she succeeded in stopping the local practice of killing twins.

### J. R. Stephen

J. R. Stephen was another important missionary doctor. For many years, he headed a missionary hospital at Ilesha.

As happened in other West African countries, many more mission-sponsored hospitals were founded during the twentieth century.

---

## Medical Services in Ghana

Christian missionaries in Ghana were just as zealous as those in Nigeria when it came to pioneering medical care.

### The Roman Catholic Sisters

The Roman Catholic Sisters provided medical care in the Upper and Northern Regions of Ghana. They did this before the government began building hospitals and clinics at regional and district headquarters.

In the Western Region, the Catholic Sisters ran a hospital at Eikwe. It specialised in maternity cases. Like Slessor in Nigeria, they also succeeded in stopping the practice of killing twins at birth.

Other Roman Catholic hospitals were built across all nine regions of Ghana. These included:

- Asikuma and Foso (Central Region)
- Akyem Swedru (Eastern Region)
- Berekum (Brong-Ahafo)
- Maase (Asante Region)
- Anfoega (Volta Region)

### The Presbyterians

The Presbyterians also opened hospitals in several parts of Ghana. One notable example is the hospital at Agogo, in Asante-Akyem.

### Other Long-Standing Mission Hospitals

Two more missionary hospitals gained a long-standing reputation:

- **Wenkyi** (Brong-Ahafo Region) – run by the Methodists
- **Kwahu Atibie** (Eastern Region) – run by the Seventh Day Adventists

# How WWII Changed West Africa

World War II changed West Africa in deep ways. It made nationalism grow faster. It shook the power of imperialism. The war also hit the economy hard. Its effects were wide and long-lasting.

Below are seven major changes the war brought.

---

## 1. West Africa Became More Important to the World Market

Europe needed raw materials badly during the war. It turned to tropical Africa for supplies. These included rubber, cotton, cocoa, palm produce, and groundnuts.

West African colonies had to grow more of these cash crops. Production went up sharply.

**Nigeria as an example:**

- Exports rose from **£10,300,000 in 1931** to **£24,600,000 in 1946**.
- Imports rose from **£6,800,000** to **£19,800,000** over the same period.

---

## 2. Workers Grew Angry at Colonial Rules

The colonial government introduced new controls. These caused real hardship for workers:

- Price controls on goods
- Government control of export crop marketing
- Wage ceilings (a cap on how much workers could earn)
- Pressure to produce more, with no extra pay

On top of this, African businessmen were shut out of trade. Import and export business was now reserved **only** for European firms.

Workers felt squeezed from every side. Grievances built up fast.

---

## 3. Trade Unions Grew Rapidly

The cost of living rose. Wages did not keep pace. This gap pushed workers to organise.

In Nigeria, the number of trade unions jumped **from 5 to 70**. In 1943, the **Nigerian Trade Union Congress** was formed as a central coordinating body.

These unions worked closely with nationalist leaders. Together, they pressed for an end to colonial rule.

---

## 4. Cities Grew Fast and Became Overcrowded

The war created new jobs in cities. People moved from the countryside into towns. Many West African cities **more than doubled** their population.

- **Lagos:** 100,000 (1939) → 230,000 (1950)
- **Accra:** 70,000 (1941) → 166,000 (1948)

Towns became overcrowded. Job-seekers and workers lived in slums. Right next to them, whites lived in spacious European reservations with paved streets, lawns, and gardens.

This contrast was painful to watch. People grew receptive to nationalist messages. They became the first willing recruits for militant nationalist movements.

---

## 5. Education Expanded

The wartime economic boom brought more prosperity. More parents could now afford school fees for their children. Literacy spread. Newspaper readership went up.

Nationalists seized on this. Newspapers became a powerful tool. They used them to push for political, economic, and social change.

---

## 6. A New Class of Unemployed People Appeared

More jobs existed than before. But thousands of school-leavers still could not find work. For the first time, West African cities had a visible class of unemployed young people.

They were angry. They blamed the colonial government and European firms for their situation. Nationalist agitators found them easy to win over.

---

## 7. Returning Soldiers Were the Most Decisive Factor

This was the single biggest driver of nationalism.

Over **176,000 men** from British West Africa served in the British colonial army during the war. After the war, large numbers of survivors came home:

- About **100,000 returned to Nigeria**.

# Collecting Data for African History

A historian cannot rely on written sources alone. They also need non-documentary sources. To check for bias, prejudice, and exaggeration, the historian must use several methods. These are outlined below.

---

## 1. Personal Enquiry and Interview

One way to gather information is to interview knowledgeable people about a community's culture.

The historian interviews people who know about the past. These include:

- Eye-witnesses
- Traditional historians (such as court linguists)
- Older court officials
- Elderly members of the community

The historian can record these interviews. Later, they play back the recordings, write them out, and analyse the information given.

---

## 2. Inter-Disciplinary Approach

Another method is the **interdisciplinary approach**. This means working with scholars from other fields.

The historian cooperates with specialists such as:

- Linguists
- Archaeologists
- Botanists
- Ethnographers

Together, they gather materials to reconstruct African history. The researcher works alongside these scholars to collect important information and draw valid conclusions.

---

## 3. Reviewing Written Sources

A historian can also use the **review method**. This means examining written sources for information. These include:

- Books
- Newspapers
- Journals
- Broadcasts
- Diaries
- Manifestoes
- Private letters

The historian reviews both primary and secondary sources. They examine the content and cross-check it against other records.

Written records do have shortcomings. But a careful review helps ensure an accurate reflection of the past. This process produces unbiased history backed by evidence.

---

## 4. Questionnaire

To get the best results, a historian should use a carefully composed **questionnaire**. It must cover these areas:

- Political
- Economic
- Social
- Religious
- Technological

The questionnaire contains well-structured questions. These are given to people who know about the past. The purpose is to solicit information.

The historian then gathers and analyses the responses. This helps them draw a reasonable conclusion.

---

## 5. Personal Observation and Records

A historian can also collect data through **personal observation**. This involves:

- Visiting places of historical importance (slave sites, castles, forts)
- Personally recording events such as festivals and funerals

These observations produce important findings. They are first-hand information because the events happened before the observer's own eyes. In other words, they are eye-witness accounts.

The historian can compare these accounts with others. They can also ask questions about them. This helps to get a reliable view of what actually happened in the past.

---

## 6. Reliability of Sources for African History

### Written (Documentary) Sources

Written and unwritten sources both have shortfalls. Yet they are still adequately reliable. Why? Because the historian uses scientific methods when drawing conclusions.

Written records carry a high level of precision. They are very reliable. All documentary sources can be reviewed and cross-checked for a fair assessment of the past. This process helps remove prejudice and bias to ensure truthfulness.

By placing written records side by side with other forms of evidence, the historian can establish an objective conclusion.

### Unwritten (Non-Documentary) Sources

The reliability of unwritten sources cannot be underestimated. They also involve scientific methods in research.

**Example – Linguistics:**
The Ghanaian linguist Professor Abena Dolphyne undertook research on the Bono, Asante, and Fante people. She reached an important conclusion: the Asante language is less related to the Fante language than previously thought.

**Example – Archaeology:**
Archaeology is a main source of information for African history. It uses scientific methods such as:

- Reconnaissance (discovering sites and plotting them for digging)
- Stratification
- Radiocarbon dating
- Potassium-argon dating
- Data analysis

These methods help archaeologists reach accurate and reliable conclusions that are significant for historical writing.

### Flaws in Archaeology

Archaeology does have some problems:

- There is no conscious system of preserving archaeological knowledge. What archaeologists find may be an accidental preservation. Excavation often relies on chance, if not luck.
- Archaeological remains suffer from wear and tear, weathering, and disfigurement. This makes it difficult for historians to derive very reliable information from them.
- Radiocarbon dating is very expensive. This cost hinders effective research.

### Flaws in Oral Tradition

Oral tradition also has limitations:

- It is full of exaggeration. Narrators may shape information to suit their own interest.
- It often excludes portions that do not meet the narrator's interest.
- It may fail to give specific details due to genuine loss of memory.
- It tends to emphasise personalities and events like wars, while playing down social and economic aspects of the past.

As a result, information becomes very scanty. This is a disadvantage for scholarship and for future generations (posterity).

---

## Conclusion

Both documentary and non-documentary evidence must be used together. They complement each other in the writing of African history.

Since both types of source are the work of human beings, neither can be said to be more reliable than the other. People tend to be subjective, biased, and impressionistic. Using all sources together is the best way to approach the past.

yet they are still adequately reliable.

why?

because the historian uses **scientific methods** when drawing conclusions.

written records carry a high level of precision.

they are very reliable.

all documentary sources can be reviewed and cross-checked.

this helps remove prejudice and bias to ensure truthfulness.

the reliability of unwritten sources cannot be underestimated.

the asante language is less related to the fante language

# West Africa and the Mediterranean World

## Ancient Connections

West Africa has been connected to the Mediterranean world for a very long time. These links go back far before Islam rose in the late 600s CE.

The Greek historian **Herodotus** (c. 484–425 BCE) wrote about peoples in Africa. He did this several centuries before the Roman Empire rose. Herodotus wrote often about the peoples of the Nile Valley. He stressed that many were Black Africans. He also suggested links to people further west.

Rock art from this period and later shows wheeled chariots south of what is now the Sahara. This points to a connection with the Mediterranean world.

## The Sahara Was Once Green

The Sahara was not as harsh in ancient times as it is today. Rock art across the desert is abundant. Some pieces are up to **12,000 years old**.

Two key examples:

- **Tassili n'Ajjer**, north of Tamanrasset in the Algerian Sahara. This is one of the oldest rock art sites in the Sahara.
- The **Tibesti Massif** in Chad. It also has rock art from around this same time.

These old paintings show areas that are now desert as fertile land. They depict animals that can no longer live there, such as:

- Buffaloes
- Elephants
- Rhinoceroses
- Hippopotamuses

This era of fertility in the Sahara coincided with the **European Ice Age**. The Ice Age was not a problem in Africa. In fact, this seems to have been a time of plenty.

## Desertification and the Caravan Trade

The Sahara began desertifying more rapidly around **3000 BCE**. Still, strong links with the Mediterranean lasted for some time after that.

A clear example is **Hannibal**, a Carthaginian general. Carthage was an empire based in Libya. It was the most powerful empire in the Mediterranean until Rome rose. Around **220 BCE**, Hannibal attacked Roman forces in Europe. His army crossed the high Alps mountain range. His military supplies were carried by elephants. These were African elephants linked to the peoples and lands south of the Sahara.

Over time, desertification increased. The geographical boundaries became harder to cross. By the rise of Islam in the early 7th century CE (from c. 610 CE, with the first Caliphs), there were fewer direct connections across the desert.

However, powerful Islamic kingdoms grew in Morocco. Centres of learning rose in Cairo, Tripoli, and the Middle East. This led to the growth of the **caravan trade**.

## The Empire of Ghāna

By the 9th century CE, the empire of **Ghāna** (also called Awkar) had been founded. It was located in what is now Mauritania. The first historical references date from c. 830 CE. Its capital was **Koumbi-Saleh**. The main trading route ran through Western Sahara and ended at **Sījīlmassa**.

By the 10th century CE, Koumbi-Saleh had separate settlements for people practising African religions and people practising Islam. This shows how many North African traders were arriving.

The gold trade was already shaping commerce and society in the Mediterranean. Around **1000 CE**, West African gold was first minted for markets in Europe.

## The Almoravid Movement

By the 11th century, events in West Africa were clearly linked to those in North Africa and even Europe. A vital change came with the **Almoravid movement**.

The Almoravids appear to have grown from Berber Muslims. They migrated north from the Senegal River after the middle of the 11th century. They sought a purer form of Islam.

Their actions:

- They conquered the Kingdom of Morocco.
- They founded **Marrakech** in 1062.
- In the 1080s, they swept into **Al-Andalus** (southern Spain).
- There, they defended the Caliphate of Córdoba from Christian reconquest.

Córdoba had already split into many small states called the **Taifa states** in the 1030s. In the 12th century, the **Almohads** came from Morocco and overtook the Almoravids in 1147.

## The Fall of Ghāna

In West Africa, the most important changes happened in Ghāna. Until **1076**, Muslims and worshippers of African religions had co-existed there. In that year, the Almoravids sacked the city. Ghāna fell into decline after this. Mali would not rise until the 13th century.

Afterward, the gold trade became the centrepiece of trans-Saharan commerce. Money was the reason Arabic traders first took an interest in West Africa. They called it **"the golden country."**

The influence of this trade reached Europe. For example, the Spanish word for a gold coin, **maravedí**, comes from the Almoravid *murabitūn* dinar. This term appeared in the 15th century.

## A Lasting Legacy

The gold trade helped build powerful empires such as:

- Mali
- Bono-Mansu
- Songhay

It also drove the expansion of urban centres like **Kano**. It raised up powerful trading classes, such as the **Wangara**.

Arabic grew in influence through the spread of Islam. It became a script used for administration.

By the 15th century, when the Atlantic trade was about to begin, the trans-Saharan trade had been flourishing for at least **five centuries**. It had already shaped the rise, fall, and consolidation of many West African states and societies.

# The Kingdom of Mali

The most famous kingdom linked to the **trans-Saharan trade** was **Mali**.

It was founded by **Sunjata Keita** in the 13th century. He defeated a blacksmith king named **Sumanguru Kante**.

However, the ruler who reached world fame was **Emperor Mansa Musa**.

---

## Who Was Mansa Musa?

Mansa Kankan Musa Keita was the son of **Mansa Aboubacarr II**, called "the Navigator."

In the 1300s, Aboubacarr sent an expedition across the Atlantic Ocean. It left from the River Gambia to find new lands.

His son, Mansa Musa, ruled Mali from **1312 to 1337**.

His reign lasted barely a quarter of a century. Yet people still call the entire 1300s the **"Century of Mansa Musa."** His legacy was that powerful.

---

## The Pilgrimage to Mecca (1324–1325)

Mansa Musa's lasting fame came from his journey to **Mecca**. It mattered more than any war he fought, won, or lost.

He did not want to go at first. He was still a nominal Muslim.

Then something terrible happened. He accidentally killed his mother.

To purify himself and atone for this capital crime, he decided to perform the **Hajj** (the Islamic pilgrimage).

He brought his entire court with him:

- Doctors
- Princes
- Griots (traditional storytellers)
- An army of **8,000 bodyguards**

He left the Capital of Mali. He crossed the Sahara through **Walata** (in present-day Mauritania), then through **Libya**, and entered **Cairo**. From Cairo, he reached the Holy City of Mecca.

---

## What Changed After the Pilgrimage?

The journey had three big effects: economic, religious, and political.

### Economic Impact

Mansa Musa gave away so much gold on his way to Mecca that people still call him **the richest human being ever to live on Earth**.

He also strengthened trade links between Mali and the Middle East, especially Cairo.

From 1325 onward, caravans of over **10,000 camels** crossed the Sahara into Mali at **Gao** and **Timbuktu**.

### Religious Impact

Mansa Musa and his huge group returned as renewed Muslims. They wanted to strengthen Islam and spread it far and wide.

Most Malian people were still animist at that time. The returning pilgrims soon converted many of them.

Mali also opened its doors to more **Arab scholars**. They were drawn by the immense wealth Mansa Musa had shown the world.

These Arab builders constructed grand mosques and courts for Mansa Musa.

He also brought back great scholars. Together, they helped build the famous libraries in:

- Gao
- Jenne
- Timbuktu

The Hajj became one of the **greatest public relations events** in world history.

### Political Impact

Mali became well known across the globe. Mansa Musa earned international respect. His pilgrimage put Mali firmly on the map.

Before his death in 1337, he had expanded Mali into a sprawling empire. It held over **400 cities**. The empire stretched from the **Atlantic coast** in the west to the **forest zones** in the south.

All the known states of that time became part of Mansa Musa's Mali:

- Songhay
- Ghana
- Galam
- Tekrur

---

## A Final Thought

Mansa Musa gave Mali its glory. And Mali, in turn, gave Mansa Musa his glory.

# The Trans-Saharan Trade and the Transformation of West Africa (10th–15th Century)

## A Big Shift

The trans-Saharan trade grew from the 10th to the 15th century. This growth changed all of West Africa. In the 15th century, major changes spread across the region. They moved from west to east and from north to south.

These were political, economic, and social transformations. They drove globalisation. Europe played a role in this process. But West Africa was not simply reacting to Europe. The direction of cause ran the other way.

## Changes in Nigeria

Several key events happened in Nigeria during this period:

- **Borno.** The gold trade from Bono-Mansu grew. This pushed the capital to move south. It left the old centre at Kanem. By around 1470, the new capital was Gazargamo (Ngazargamu) in Borno.

- **Kano.** A new system of governance was established. It is called the Sarauta system.

- **Ijebu (Yorubaland).** Earthworks called "Eredos" surround this town. They are 10 metres deep. The archaeologist Gérard Chouin recently dated them to between 1370 and 1420.

## Changes in Mali, Burkina Faso, and the Gold Coast

Similar transformations were happening elsewhere:

- **Mali.** The Dogon people probably moved to the Bandiagara escarpment in the 15th century.

- **Burkina Faso (present day).** The Mossi kingdom rose during this period. Its power was linked to taxing the gold trade as it moved onward. Al-Sa'dī records the Mossi attacking the town of Mâssina at this time.

- **Bono-Mansu.** This state also rose to prominence in the 15th century.

- **The Gold Coast.** The key gold-trading centre of Bighu became very important later, in the 17th and 18th centuries. Al-Ouazzan mentions it (as "Bito") in the 1520s. This suggests it rose to prominence in these decades too.

## Changes in Senegambia

At the end of the 15th century, a major military leader named Koli Tenguela rose to power. He was Fula. His rise probably linked to an attempt to control the gold trade from the kingdom of Wuuli. Wuuli sat on the north bank of the Gambia River.

Tenguela led an army south. They crossed the Gambia River. They reached the Fuuta Jaalo mountains in present-day Guinea-Conakry. There, he established a new polity. This, in turn, led to the founding of Fuuta Tooro on the Senegal River.

## The Bigger Picture

All across West Africa, political change was underway. From Borno in the north-east to Fuuta Tooro in the west, new states were forming. These changes happened well before trade with Europe began.

West African mining technology advanced. Economic structures transformed. Political systems reorganised. Together, these shifts created a framework. European powers later entered this framework as they began sailing along the West African coast in the 15th century.

## Kano: A Case Study

The most striking example came in northern Nigeria. Kano grew very fast in the 15th century. It sent military expeditions south. It became a regional hub. It linked trading networks from southern Nigeria to present-day Mali and beyond. The *Kano Chronicle* records some of these changes.

During the reign of Sarkin Dauda (c. 1421–38), Kano's links with the province of Nupe are described. Zaria was the major power between Kano and Nupe. It had conquered a large area of land.

The *Kano Chronicle* says:

> "At this time, Zaria, under Queen Amina, conquered all the towns as far as Kwararafa and Nupe. Every town paid tribute to her. The Sarkin Nupe sent forty eunuchs and ten thousand kolas to her… in time the whole of the products of the west were brought to Hausaland [of which Kano was the capital]."

## Conclusion: A Global Century

European power began expanding along the West African coast in the 15th century. At the same moment, the trans-Saharan trade reached its peak. The 15th century was not only a time of European expansion. It was also a time of global expansion. Networks grew. Trade expanded. Production increased. More complex states emerged. This happened in West Africa and beyond.

# The Ghana Empire

Ghana was one of the most famous empires in West Africa. It was also one of the earliest.

It existed from the 5th century to the 13th century. Its land is now part of modern Mali and Mauritania. Trade across the Sahara Desert shaped its history.

The capital city was Kumbi Saleh, in present-day Mauritania. Do not confuse this empire with modern Ghana. Modern Ghana has its capital at Accra. The country took its name from this older empire.

The main people of the Ghana Empire were the Serahuli. They are also called Soninke. They belonged to the Mande-speaking group.

## Trade Made Ghana Powerful

Ghana grew rich because of its role in Trans-Saharan trade. Its location was key.

British historian Kevin Shillington said it clearly:

> "Ghana's position with regard to the trade made it grow powerful and its rulers became rich. It seems likely that trade was a major factor in the growth of Ghana from the very beginning."

Ghana sat halfway between two key goods:

- **Salt** came from the desert to the north.
- **Gold** came from Bambuk to the east.

Ghana acted as the middleman. This role brought great wealth.

The camel changed everything. Camels carried heavy loads across the sand. Trade between Ghana and desert peoples, such as the Berbers, grew fast.

## What Arab Visitors Saw

Ghana's fame spread because Arabic traders wrote about it. They recorded what they saw in detail.

In the 11th century, an Arab geographer named al-Bakari visited Kumbi Saleh. He described the great wealth he found there. He also noted how well the empire was run.

He reported that Kumbi Saleh had two separate areas:

- A **foreigners' quarter** where Arab traders lived.
- The **main ward** where the king and his people lived.

Al-Bakari was amazed by what he saw. He wrote about:

- The king dressed in gold.
- An army of 200,000 men.
- Both Islam and animism being practised openly in Kumbi Saleh.

These Arab writers mostly met kings, nobles, and traders. They cared most about gold. So they wrote little about ordinary people. Still, their writings show that common folk fished and farmed along the River Senegal to survive.

## The Fall of Ghana

Ghana rose through trade. It also fell because of trade.

The Almoravids began waging war against other Berber tribes. Trade routes became unsafe. Trade dropped.

Dry weather hit hard too. Drought made it difficult to feed the people and the large army. The state weakened.

By the 12th century, vassal states like Mali began to rebel. They wanted freedom from Ghana's control.

# The Songhay Empire

Songhay lasted from the 11th century to the 16th century. It also rose because of Trans-Saharan trade.

By the 14th century, Muslim traders were settled in Gao. Gao was the main trade town of Songhay. It became the hub for trade across the central and eastern Sahara.

Farmers and fishermen in Songhay fed the traders well. This kept caravans moving.

## How Songhay Made Money

Songhay collected most of its revenue from taxes on trade caravans.

One great emperor was Muhamed Ture, also called Askia Muhamed. He did two important things:

- He introduced Islam into Songhay.
- He expanded the empire's reach.

Like Mansa Musa of Mali, he made a pilgrimage to Mecca. There, he showed how rich and powerful his kingdom was.

The Trans-Saharan trade made Songhay rich and prosperous.

# The Ghana Empire


Ghana was one of the most famous empires in West Africa.

It was also one of the earliest.


It existed from the **5th century to the 13th century**.

Its land is now part of modern **Mali** and **Mauritania**.

Trade across the **Sahara Desert** shaped its history.



---


## The Capital City


The capital was **Kumbi Saleh**, in present-day Mauritania.


> ⚠️ Do not confuse this empire with modern Ghana.
>
> Modern Ghana has its capital at **Accra**.
>
> The country took its name from this older empire.



---


## The People


The main people of the Ghana Empire were the **Serahuli**.

They are also called **Soninke**.

They belonged to the **Mande-speaking** group.



---


## Trade Made Ghana Powerful


Ghana grew rich because of its role in trans-Saharan trade.

Its location was key.


British historian **Kevin Shillington** said it clearly:


> "Ghana's position with regard to the trade made it grow powerful and its rulers became rich. It seems likely that trade was a major factor in the growth of Ghana from the very beginning."



---


### Two Key Goods


Ghana sat halfway between two sources:


- **Salt** came from the desert to the north.
- **Gold** came from **Bambuk** to the east.


Ghana acted as the middleman.

This role brought great wealth.



---


### The Camel Changed Everything


Camels carried heavy loads across the sand.

Trade between Ghana and desert peoples, such as the **Berbers**, grew fast.



---


## What Arab Visitors Saw


Ghana's fame spread because Arabic traders wrote about it.

They recorded what they saw in detail.


In the **11th century**, an Arab geographer named **al-Bakari** visited Kumbi Saleh.

He described the great wealth he found there.

He also noted how well the empire was run.



---


### Two Areas of Kumbi Saleh


Al-Bakari reported that the city had two separate areas:


- A **foreigners' quarter** where Arab traders lived.
- The **main ward** where the king and his people lived.



---


### What Al-Bakari Was Amazed By


He wrote about three things:


1. The king dressed in gold.
2. An army of **200,000 men**.
3. Both **Islam** and **animism** being practised openly in Kumbi Saleh.



---


### A Note on Sources


These Arab writers mostly met kings, nobles, and traders.

They cared most about gold.

So they wrote little about ordinary people.


Still, their writings show that common folk fished and farmed along the **River Senegal** to survive.



---


## The Fall of Ghana


Ghana rose through trade.

It also fell because of trade.



---


### War and Drought


The **Almoravids** began waging war against other Berber tribes.

Trade routes became unsafe.

Trade dropped.


Dry weather hit hard too.

Drought made it difficult to feed the people and the large army.

The state weakened.



---


### Rebellion


By the **12th century**, vassal states like **Mali** began to rebel.

They wanted freedom from Ghana's control.



---


# The Songhay Empire


Songhay lasted from the **11th century to the 16th century**.

It also rose because of trans-Saharan trade.


By the **14th century**, Muslim traders were settled in **Gao**.

Gao was the main trade town of Songhay.

It became the hub for trade across the central and eastern Sahara.



---


### Food Kept Caravans Moving


Farmers and fishermen in Songhay fed the traders well.

This kept caravans moving.



---


## How Songhay Made Money


Songhay collected most of its revenue from taxes on trade caravans.



---


### Askia Muhamed


One great emperor was **Muhamed Ture**, also called **Askia Muhamed**.

He did two important things:


- He introduced **Islam** into Songhay.
- He expanded the empire's reach.


Like **Mansa Musa** of Mali, he made a pilgrimage to **Mecca**.

There, he showed how rich and powerful his kingdom was.



---


### In Summary


The trans-Saharan trade made Songhay rich and prosperous.

# The Jihad of Dan Fodio: Why It Happened

## A Religious Mission

For Dan Fodio, the main goal of the jihad was to purify Islam. This happened in territories that were already Muslim at the start of the 19th century. He believed Muslim leaders had only practiced an impure form of Islam up to that point. This belief gave his struggle its legitimacy.

## A Social Revolution?

Some historians saw the Sokoto jihad as a revolution. Why? Because the Hausa kingdoms had deep socio-economic inequalities in the early 1800s. Dan Fodio favoured equality. He also fought openly against corruption. In this way, he became a champion of ordinary people.

In 1804, he launched his fight against the king and aristocracy of Gobir.

That said, we should not ignore the social side of the jihad. But Dan Fodio himself pointed to mainly religious reasons. He stated these in his book *Kitab al-Farq*.

## Letters to Borno

Correspondence from the 1800s helps us understand his motives. After trying to invade a kingdom that had existed since the 9th century, Dan Fodio wrote to Mohammed el-Kanemi, the leader of Borno. He tried to convince him of the religious and legal merits of his struggle.

For Dan Fodio, the jihad was mainly a way for pure Muslims to reform lax ones. It was not *only* that, but it was the core idea.

## An Ethnic Conflict?

In the 1970s, some historians argued for an ethnic reading. They said Dan Fodio was a descendant of Fulanis who had settled in Hausa regions since the 15th century. On this view, he pitted Islam against the Hausas.

But this is hard to accept. Most leaders of the Sokoto jihad were indeed Fulani. Yet the Fulani were numerically inferior. It is difficult to believe they thought they could overthrow the Hausa kings on ethnic grounds alone. Dan Fodio himself wrote *against* ethnic discrimination in his treatise *Bayan Wayan Wujub al-Hijra*.

## Not a New Idea

Scholars have also shown that the jihad was not entirely new in West Africa. Debates about Islam's role in society had already taken place before Dan Fodio. These debates covered:

- Food bans
- Marriage laws
- What clothes women should wear

It was this last point that drew the attention of Shaikh Jibril b. 'Umar, one of Usman dan Fodio's own teachers.

Other jihads had already happened in West Africa before Dan Fodio's:

- **Bundu** – late 17th century
- **Futa Jallon** – 1725
- **Futa Toro** – 1776

In short, some Muslim scholars had already become reformers and conquerors before Usman dan Fodio arrived.

## What Made Him Different?

The religious questioning behind the jihad was therefore not completely original. What *was* unique was his lasting political victory over a vast territory. That is what ensured his long-term success.

text:
# The Sokoto Caliphate (1804–1810 and Beyond)

## A New Kind of State

The first six years of the jihad ran from 1804 to 1810. These years built the political and religious base for a new state. This state was never an empire. It was a collection of territories. All of them answered to one leader: the caliph in Sokoto.

The Caliphate of Sokoto was highly decentralised. The caliph ruled, but power was spread out. This was a new idea in the Hausa regions. It gave dan Fodio and his successors both moral and political authority.

Fulani scholars joined the jihad as companions of the caliph. The caliph placed them as emirs over each territorial subdivision. Each emir answered directly to the caliph.

Because the state was so large, it split into two zones:

- **Western emirates** – under the direct authority of Sokoto
- **Eastern emirates** – more or less autonomous

## Keeping Power Through War

dan Fodio's successors had to fight military campaigns. They needed these wars to assert their authority. As a result, jihad became a near-constant feature until the mid-nineteenth century.

Mohammed Bello was dan Fodio's son and direct successor. He took the title of sultan. He led many campaigns. He compared them to the conquest of the Arabian Peninsula by the first Muslims in the seventh century.

Bello followed three main policies:

- Appointing family members as heads of frontier towns
- Settling Fulani nomadic populations into villages
- Building fortified villages to monitor borders

The caliphate needed security at its outer borders. It also needed security in the buffer zones between emirates. Soldiers were recruited during the dry season. With these troops, Sokoto could crush any rebellion. They could also stop Tuareg incursions from the north.

## Where the Caliph's Power Came From

The caliph's authority rested on three things:

1. Controlling his borders
2. Redistributing spoils from military campaigns to allies and family
3. Redistributing taxes to allies and family

The new state replaced the old Hausa leader taxes with Islamic taxes, such as the zakat. In theory, all revenues were subject to Islamic law.

In practice, each emirate set its own taxes. For example, Kano and Zaria had a property tax. Sokoto did not. This showed that central control was limited. Two things held it back:

- The old pre-jihad structures of the Hausa cities
- The difficulty of reaching large parts of the rural population

## Law, Schools, and Bureaucracy

The caliphate stayed true to the original goal of the jihad. It sought to establish Islamic law in the courts across the whole territory.

This created a need for educated men. That need encouraged schools to appear in urban centres. The first years were hard. There was a shortage of qualified personnel.

A defining feature of the Caliphate of Sokoto was its literate administrative staff. Each emirate had trained men working in government. Some were born free. Others were born into slavery. Together, they formed a functioning bureaucracy.

## Slavery and the Economy

The caliphate faced a serious shortage of labour. This drove many expeditions to capture slaves. The state used them for two purposes: selling them or putting them to work in plantations and other production sites.

Slave labour powered key industries:

- **Salt mines** – in the north
- **Iron, cotton, indigo, and leather production** – in the central regions

The wealth of the state rested on a servile economy. Wars and raids fuelled it.

North African merchants traded heavily in slaves. In Kano during the 1820s, the ratio was stark: for every one freeman, there were thirty slaves.

## Islam Spreads Through the Region

Islam first reached the Hausa regions in the fourteenth century. Travellers and traders brought it from neighbouring Borno and from lands north of the Sahara. The jihad then spread it much further.

Pre-Islamic religions – often called "traditional" religions – did not disappear. They persisted alongside Islam. But Islamic culture came to permeate the whole region. Books written by dan Fodio's family helped. So did books sold through Saharan trade routes.

The Hausa regions grew more integrated with the wider Muslim world. Three channels drove this integration:

- The pilgrimage to Mecca
- Trade
- The spread of Sufi brotherhoods

This integration may have existed before the jihad. But the jihad greatly accelerated the process.

text:
# Al Hajj Umar Tal (1797–1864)

Alhaji Salim Suwareh did not raise the sword.
Al Hajj Umar Tal did.
He was just as successful as the Jakhanke missionaries.

Before we look at his full life, let us start with his wars.
These jihads took place in present-day Mali and Guinea Conakry.
They lasted from 1848 to 1864.


## The First Campaigns (1848–1854)

His first target was the gold states of Bambuk and Bure.
Animist Malinke people ruled and lived there.

In just six years, he conquered them.
He forcibly converted the Malinke of Bandjogou, Bougary, and Farabana.
All three are in present-day Guinea Conakry.

He raised the flag of the Tijaniya sect of Islam.
He pitched his tent at Jalafara.
This became his first capital.


## The Expansion into Mali

His success pushed him further south.
He attacked the Bambaras of Kaarta and Segou.
He also attacked the animist Fulani of Macina.
All are in present-day Mali.

By 1854, Tal had built a huge Muslim state.
It included Kaarta, Segou, Macina, and Khasso.

The Bambara were the only well-organized fighting force in this part of the Sahel.
Tal brought them under his Tijaniya sect.

The Malian historian Sekene Mody Cissokho wrote:
"Al Hajj Umar brought Islam to the Western Sudan."
This is a fitting tribute to a brilliant scholar, jihadist, and empire builder.


## His Early Life and Training

His success showed early on.

In 1820, he was 23 years old.
He finished his studies that year.
He was awarded the title *alfa*, meaning scholar.

Also in 1820, he made a pilgrimage to Mecca.
He stayed in Arabia for 13 years.
There, he was ordained as the Kalifa of the Tijaniya sect in West Africa.
This meant emissary or representative.

Now he had full recognition and approval.
He could lead jihads across the Sahel.

On his way back, he passed through Kanem Borno and Sokoto.
Jihads there had just been completed.
He likely studied how they were prepared.
He used those lessons for his own campaigns in the Sahel.


## His True Aim

Cissokho tells us Umar's goal was not to destroy existing states.
His aim was conversion.
He wanted rulers and people to leave animism for Tijaniya Islam.
Or to move from Qadriya to Tijaniya.

But his quick success was not due to the sword alone.
Umar's version of Tijaniya helped the poor.
It lifted people up socially.

For example, he freed slaves in conquered lands.
He helped the poor and down-trodden meet their basic needs.


## His End and Legacy

In 1864, Umar met his end at Dinguiray.
A bloody battle with the French killed him.

Until that day, he remained a popular figure.
Jihadist turned empire builder.

His son Amadou Seku took over after him.
But Amadou struggled to hold together the vast Imamate his father had built.

# Early European Contact with West Africa

## The Portuguese Arrive

In **1442**, Portuguese ships reached the Senegal River. This was the first time European sailors reached sub-Saharan Africa.

Before that, the Portuguese had been sailing along the coasts of Morocco and Western Sahara since **1413**. In 1413, they captured the Moroccan city of Ceuta. Ceuta is still a Spanish city today.

Between **1413 and the 1440s**, the Portuguese built several fortified settlements on the Moroccan coast. Key locations included:

- Arzila
- Mogador (now called Essaouira)
- Safi
- Tangier

The Portuguese kept a strong presence in Morocco until **1578**. In that year, King Sebastião I and much of the Portuguese nobility were killed at the Battle of Alcácer-Quibir.

## Trade Links Grow

By **1471**, West African leaders between Senegal and Ghana had established trade and diplomatic ties with Portuguese traders.

Major early sites of trade and settlement included:

- The Gambia River
- Bugendo, on the São Domingos River in Guinea-Bissau
- Sierra Leone

For the next **150 years**, West African rulers and traders met the Portuguese more than any other European nation. Smaller trading missions from England and France also occurred, but these were less frequent.

## Why Did the Portuguese Come?

The Portuguese had four main motivations:

1. **Gold.** They wanted access to the extensive gold production of Bono-Mansu and the Akan states.
2. **Competition with the Ottoman Empire.** The Ottomans captured Constantinople in 1453. This caused a crisis in Christian Europe. The Portuguese wanted to reach this gold before the Ottomans did.
3. **A route to India.** They sought a sea trade route to Indian markets around the Cape of Good Hope.
4. **The slave trade.** Over time, the trade in enslaved persons became an increasingly important goal.

## The Dutch Rise

By the **1590s**, the Dutch began to rival the Portuguese as the major European trading nation in Africa.

Dutch ships were bigger and better. The goods they traded with African political leaders were of much higher quality.

By **1650**, the Dutch had captured many key Portuguese trading stations:

- Gorée, Senegal (captured 1621)
- Elmina, Ghana (captured 1637)
- Luanda, Angola (captured 1641)

At first, the Dutch were mainly interested in textiles, animal hides for the leather industry, and ivory. By the middle of the **17th century**, they too turned to slave trading.

Dutch interest in slave trading began in the **1620s**. This followed their capture of half of the Brazilian colonies from the Portuguese. From **1630 to 1654**, the Dutch controlled northern Brazil and its sugar plantations, which used the labour of enslaved persons. Their growing colonial interests drove their interest in slave trading. The slave trade took over as the dominant form of trade in the second half of the **18th century**.

## More Nations Join In

In the second half of the **17th century**, other European nations followed this pattern. Danish, English, French, German, and Swedish traders established factories at various points along the West African coast. The pattern of African-European trade and interaction deepened over time.

## What This Chapter Covers

This chapter focuses on the early period of African-European interaction, up to **1650**. This is before the trade in enslaved persons came to dominate all other trade. A separate chapter on the trans-Atlantic slave trade covers that topic in more detail.

# Early European Contact with West Africa


## The Portuguese Arrive

In **1442**, Portuguese ships reached the **Senegal River**.

This was the first time Europeans reached **Sub-Saharan Africa**.

Before that, they had been sailing along **Morocco's coast** since **1413**.

In **1413**, they captured the Moroccan city of **Ceuta**.

Ceuta is still a Spanish city today.


Between **1413** and the **1440s**, the Portuguese built several fortified settlements on the Moroccan coast.

Key locations included:

- Arzila
- Mogador (now called Essaouira)
- Safi
- Tangier


The Portuguese kept a strong presence in Morocco until **1578**.

In that year, **King Sebastião I** and much of the Portuguese nobility were killed at the **Battle of Alcácer-Quibir**.


## Trade Links Grow

By **1471**, West African leaders between **Senegal** and **Ghana** had established trade and diplomatic ties with Portuguese traders.

Major early sites of trade and settlement included:

- The Gambia River
- Bugendo, on the São Domingos River in Guinea-Bissau
- Sierra Leone


For the next **150 years**, West African rulers and traders met the Portuguese more than any other European nation.

Smaller trading missions from **England** and **France** also occurred.

These were less frequent.


## Why Did the Portuguese Come?

The Portuguese had four main motivations:


**Gold.**
They wanted access to the extensive gold production of **Bono-Mansu** and the **Akan states**.


**Competition with the Ottoman Empire.**
The Ottomans captured **Constantinople** in **1453**. This caused a crisis in Christian Europe. The Portuguese wanted to reach this gold before the Ottomans did.


**A route to India.**
They sought a sea trade route to Indian markets around the **Cape of Good Hope**.


**The slave trade.**
Over time, the trade in enslaved persons became an increasingly important goal.


## The Dutch Rise

By the **1590s**, the Dutch began to rival the Portuguese as the major European trading nation in Africa.

Dutch ships were bigger and better.

The goods they traded with African political leaders were of much higher quality.


By **1650**, the Dutch had captured many key Portuguese trading stations:

- Gorée, Senegal (captured 1621)
- Elmina, Ghana (captured 1637)
- Luanda, Angola (captured 1641)


At first, the Dutch were mainly interested in textiles.

They also wanted animal hides for the leather industry and ivory.

By the middle of the **17th century**, they too turned to slave trading.


Dutch interest in slave trading began in the **1620s**.

This followed their capture of half of the Brazilian colonies from the Portuguese.

From **1630** to **1654**, the Dutch controlled northern Brazil and its sugar plantations.

These plantations used the labour of enslaved persons.

Their growing colonial interests drove their interest in slave trading.

The slave trade took over as the dominant form of trade in the second half of the **18th century**.


## More Nations Join In

In the second half of the **17th century**, other European nations followed this pattern.

Danish, English, French, German, and Swedish traders established factories at various points along the West African coast.

The pattern of African-European trade and interaction deepened over time.


## What This Chapter Covers

This chapter focuses on the early period of African-European interaction, up to **1650**.

This is before the trade in enslaved persons came to dominate all other trade.

A separate chapter on the trans-Atlantic slave trade covers that topic in more detail.
