# Portuguese Voyages and Trade in West Africa

## Sailing Further South

The Portuguese reached the Senegal River in 1442. Their voyages continued after that date.

By 1448, some Portuguese sailors had gone up the Gambia River. They reached a major trading town called Kantora. Kantora sat not far east of what is now Basse Santa Su, in the far east of the country. At that time, Kantora was a key centre for trans-Saharan trade.

By the mid-1450s, the Portuguese were trading with the Wolof state of Kajoor on the coast. The Bijagós Islands, off the coast of Guinea-Bissau, also began talks with European traders.

Arabic was probably the first language used between them. Many people in 15th-century Portugal spoke Arabic. Granada in Spain was still an Islamic kingdom at that time. Arabic was also widely spoken across much of West Africa.

In 1456, one sailor wrote about the Bijagós Islands. He said this was the last place where African peoples shared a language with Portuguese sailors. This likely marked the southern edge of Arab and trans-Saharan trade at that time.

The Cape Verde Islands were first reached probably in 1456. Capeverdean historians still debate whether people already lived there. Archaeological evidence is inconclusive. The islands may have served as a salt depot for Saharan states.

Around 1471, the Portuguese reached the coastline of Ghana.

## Gold and Forts on the Gold Coast

The coast of Ghana was different from other areas they had visited. It sat close to the gold mines in the Akan forests. Akan traders soon sold gold to the Portuguese informally.

The Portuguese state wanted a share of this trade. In 1481, they sent a large fleet. They negotiated with Kwamena Ansa, the ruler at Edina (now called Elmina). The goal was to build a fortress there.

The negotiations were tense. At one point, the Portuguese tried to build their fort on the site of a holy shrine. This caused a serious stand-off. In the end, the deal was made. The fortress at Elmina was built. It still stands today on what became known as the Gold Coast.

Later, in the 17th century, the Dutch took over the fortress. Over time, the Dutch and English became the main European nations trading in Ghana.

## More Forts Along the Coast

There was a lot of commerce on the Gold Coast. Many Akan rulers wanted to grow their trading connections. The Portuguese built forts at other spots along the coast. Axim and Komenda are two examples. Most of these were finished by 1500.

In time, there would be many more forts. They appeared almost every few miles along the coast. Some forts specialised in the gold trade. Others focused on different goods. Anishan, for example, exported corn. European ships wanted that corn badly.

The slave trade did not become dominant on the Gold Coast until the 18th century.

## Benin and the Portuguese

Other rulers in West and West-Central Africa also made contact with the Portuguese. In 1485, Oba Ozolua of Benin received Portuguese visitors. Around 1490, the Atlantic trading post of Gwatón was founded.

At first, Benin sold malaguetta peppers to the Portuguese. Then, in 1499, a sea route to India was established. After that, Benin's peppers were less wanted in Europe.

The Portuguese tried to set up a trade in enslaved persons from Benin. They wanted to send them to the gold suppliers at Elmina. The Oba refused.

Over the 16th century, relations between Benin and Portugal declined. In the early 17th century, the Obas renewed links with European traders. The Dutch had a strong demand for cloth made in Benin.

Throughout the 17th century, cloth stayed as Benin's main export. Ambassy cloths were traded regularly to Elmina. They also went as far away as Brazil.

By the late 17th century, demand for Benin cloth fell. Luxury cloths from India flooded into Europe. This changed things. By the 18th century, the Obas of Benin had to turn to the trade in enslaved persons. They did this to preserve and renew the power of Edo and the Benin state.

## The Kongo Kingdom

The Portuguese kept sailing south after Benin. They reached the mouth of the Kongo River. There they established relations with the manikongo at Mbanza Kongo, the capital of Kongo. His name was Nzika Nkuwu.

By 1485, the island of São Tomé had been settled by Europeans. Many BaKongo people were taken there as enslaved persons. They worked on sugar plantations.

In 1491, Nzika Nkuwu converted to Christianity. He took the name Joao I. This created new links between Kongo and Elmina. Both traded through São Tomé.

By the 1510s, traders from Benin were present at the Kongolese port of Mpinda. The new manikongo, Afonso I (ruling 1509–46), mentioned them in a letter written in Portuguese.

## A Web of Connections

By the 1510s, many different peoples of West Africa had made connections with the Portuguese. Their rulers were involved too. Some places, like Benin and Elmina, also had links further south to Kongo.

African rulers hoped to expand their trading contacts. At times, they also wanted military help against rivals. This happened in several cases:

- In 1516, Benin fought a major battle against Nupe with Portuguese support.
- Civil wars broke out in Jolof and in Kongo, where outside connections played a role.

# Diplomacy and Royal Exchanges

Princes from Benin, Jolof, and Kongo often went to Portugal to study. Their royal elders also sent them as ambassadors to the Portuguese court. This pattern lasted well into the 17th century.

By then, Kongo was sending ambassadors in three directions:

- To the Dutch colonial court in Brazil
- To the Vatican (the home of the Catholic Church)
- To Portugal itself

In the 1650s, Allada sent ambassadors to the Spanish court.

The pattern continued even later. Between 1755 and the 1810s, Dahomey sent ambassadors five times to the Portuguese in Brazil and Portugal. In fact, when Brazil declared independence from Portugal in 1811, Dahomey was the first state to recognise it.

---

## The Portuguese Side

The Portuguese also treated these relationships as diplomacy. Under King João II (r. 1481–95), Portugal sent ambassadors to many royal courts in Africa. They went to Benin, Kongo, and the court of the Mandimansa, the emperor of Mali. One envoy was sent as far as Timbuktu. However, it is not certain that he arrived.

Letters from Portuguese kings addressed West African rulers as fellow monarchs. In both Africa and Portugal, kingship was seen as a divine gift. This created a shared understanding between the two sides.

---

## Portraits of Ambassadors

Fortunately, some portraits of these ambassadors survive. The most important were painted in Brazil by a Dutch artist (probably Jasper Beckx). They show Dom Miguel de Castro.

Miguel de Castro was the ambassador of the manikongo (king) Garcia II Ncana a Luquini nzenze atumba. His king sent him as an envoy to the Dutch court in Brazil, probably in 1643.

## Why Were Ambassadors Sent?

The aims of these embassies were varied. They fall into three broad categories:

### 1. The Quest for a Military Alliance

**Example one – Jolof (1488):**

In 1488, the Jolof prince Bumi Jeléen came to Portugal. He claimed he was the rightful king of Jolof. His brothers and rivals had unseated him. He came to Portugal asking for help.

João II received him at court. The king sent a military fleet to support Bumi Jeléen on his return journey to the Senegal River.

However, when they reached West Africa, the leader of the fleet treacherously murdered Bumi Jeléen. This man was Pero Vaz de Cunha. He claimed he suspected Bumi Jeléen of betraying them.

This was an ignominious episode. João II put many of the leaders of this plot to death. The followers and relatives of Bumi Jeléen moved to the Cape Verde islands, which by then were under Portuguese control.

**Example two – Kongo (1640s):**

In the 1640s, the Kingdom of Kongo allied with the Dutch against the Portuguese. The Dutch seized Luanda in 1641. Then Kongo armies fought against Portuguese troops stationed at their forts in the interior of Angola. These forts were called Ambaca and Massangano.

Dom Miguel de Castro was sent by the manikongo to discuss military strategy. The goal was to throw the Portuguese out for good from West-Central Africa. However, this alliance was finally defeated in 1648.

Some African peoples had a genuine interest in Christianity. This motivated some embassies.

Princes from Benin studied in Portuguese missions. Princes from Kongo did the same. Over time, interest in Christianity waned in Benin. But in Kongo it did not fade. Ambassadors were sent to the Vatican again and again. They asked for more priests and missionaries. This continued long into the 17th century.

Trade was often a key motivation for sending ambassadors. Access to Atlantic trade was an important way to expand supplies of money.

Just as today there is the Cedi, Dalasi, Leone, and Naira, in the past many types of money were in use across West Africa. These included cowries, iron bars, and cloth strips. More specifically:

1. **Gold** – especially on the Niger Bend and in the Akan kingdoms of the Gold Coast
2. **Cowries** – in Benin, Oyò, on the Niger Bend, and later in Hueda and Dahomey

The two ambassadors travelled first to Salvador, in Brazil. There they spent large sums on fine silk and damask clothing and hats. All of it was paid for by the Portuguese crown.

They then moved on to Lisbon late in the year. When they arrived, they visited the theatre and the opera every night.

---

## In Summary

The diplomatic element of African-European relations shows that these interactions took place at a grand political scale, not just at a local level. West African rulers' interests were those of many leaders anywhere: commercial success, military strength, and religious belief.

Yet while the Portuguese crown also despatched many embassies in the early period, by the 1530s the European presence was becoming increasingly "informal." Small-scale traders took over from royal diplomacy.

# European Trading Communities in West Africa

## Two Main Types of Community

There were two main types of European trading community in West Africa:

1. **Informal communities.** Europeans settled in local areas. They married women from the area. Together they formed African families. These families often became important in local trade networks.

2. **Formal communities.** These grew up around fortified trading posts along the coast. The Portuguese called these posts *factories*. This word comes from the Portuguese word *feitoria*. Factories were especially found:
   - Along the Gold Coast
   - In Hueda
   - In the rivers around Gambia and Bissau

The rivers included the Gambia, Casamance, São Domingos, Corubal, Nunez, and Pongo.

## The Fortified Factories

Most fortified factories were modelled on **Elmina**. Elmina was the first, oldest, and biggest of these trading posts. It showed how important the gold trade was from the start. Elmina was built in the 1480s.

However, apart from Elmina and a few smaller forts on the Gold Coast, the informal model was more common in the 1500s.

## The Informal Model of Trade

Male Portuguese traders came to several areas:

- Senegambia
- The rivers of Guinea-Bissau
- Sierra Leone
- Benin

Here they married local women. They often acted as trading intermediaries with local rulers. This worked well because the men, their wives, and their children could speak both African and European languages.

## A Famous Trader: Ganagoga

One trader became quite famous in Senegambia in the 16th century. His original name was **João Ferreira**. He was known as **"Ganagoga"**.

He married the daughter of the ruler of Fùùta Tòòro, which is on the Senegal River.

His name "Ganagoga" meant *"he who speaks all the languages"* in the Biafada language of Guinea-Bissau. This shows how important that ability was.

## Marriages into Ruling Families

Relations with daughters of ruling families were not unusual for these traders.

In another case, in the early 17th century, a Dutch Jewish trader got into trouble. He had an affair with the daughter of the **Buur of Kajoor** in Senegal.

## Religious Roles and "Tangomãos"

Some historians think that these early traders also took on religious roles.

In the 1500s, the Portuguese called their own people who settled in Africa **"tangomãos"**. This word came from the name of a shrine in Sierra Leone called **tunguma**.

A writer in 1506 recorded an important detail. One of the earliest Portuguese men to settle in Sierra Leone (in the 1480s) officiated at this shrine. He did so at the request of the **Temni peoples** there.

It is worth noting that Sierra Leone's human communities changed a lot during the 16th century. A wave of Mande-influenced warriors called the **Manes** arrived. They defeated the warriors of existing communities. By 1600, they had intermarried with those communities.

So "tangomão" meant a European person who did two things:

- Settled in West Africa
- Adopted West African beliefs and practices

## Women Ran the Trade

In many of these communities, it was the **African women** married to the traders who ran the trading networks.

Their male European spouses were often very ill. They suffered from malaria and other diseases. Their bodies had no resistance to these illnesses. The men looked awful. They spent much of their time in bed. Most died young.

The female traders spoke African languages far better than their husbands did. They could form trading networks and human connections with their home communities. They ran the day-to-day business while their male spouses fought weakly against disease.

Some historians think this strong role for women traders had a lasting effect. It may have influenced the powerful place that women took in independence movements against colonial rule in the 20th century. This was especially true in **Guinea-Bissau** and parts of **Nigeria**.

## Two Powerful Women in Cacheu

as noted above, informal settlements were the majority in the **16th century.**

but towards the end of that century and into the early **17th century,** fortified european trading posts became common.

this was especially true on the gold coast and in hueda.

in casamance and guinea-bissau, forts were built at:

- **cacheu** (1589)
- **ziguinchor** (1645)
- **bissau** (1687)

the 17th century also saw the fort at **james island** (1651), at the estuary of the gambia river.

along the gold coast, the dutch presence led to more castles being built.

the most famous were:

- **cape corso** (cape coast) – built in 1610, expanded in 1652
- **secondi** (1642)
- **axim** and **elmina** (mentioned earlier)

---

## 12. the slave trade changed everything

the huge expansion of the atlantic slave trade in the late **17th century** drove the growth of this fortified model.

european factories at **offra** (1660, the port for allada) and at hueda were fortified.

by the middle of the **18th century,** these communities of european settlers had become more important than the informal ones described above.

by then, members of the informal communities had largely settled down and fully integrated into their host african communities.

---

## 13. military protection, but still dependent on africans

although these communities were protected militarily, they relied very heavily on **african intermediaries** in their trade.

the military captains of these forts often attended royal ceremonies of the local african state.

this happened frequently in **dahomey,** for example.

they also sent gifts for the funeral rites of any deceased person of importance.

in practice, this meant they had to accept and take part in african religious practices linked to those funerals.

---

## 14. how fortified communities differed from informal ones

the communities that grew up around fortified trading posts were quite different from the informal ones described earlier.

the military aspect was vital.

european traders rented the land for their posts.

but they were as much **occupiers** as tenants.

they had armed militias.

they often allied with one local ruler or another.

this could create problems between them.

it is important to remember that by the **18th century,** guns were one of the largest imports from the atlantic trade to africa.

this was a big change from earlier centuries, when copper, iron, and cloth had also been important goods.

these communities were accustomed to slavery.

they brought with them racial animus that became especially bad in europe from around **1650** onwards.

as a result, they were used to having **"castle slaves."**

this idea was imported from europe, via the experience of new world plantation societies.

it influenced practices of service and dependence in local communities.

---

## 15. continuity and change

many european officials in these forts had families with african women.

their children grew up around the forts.

these children often became traders.

their dual heritage gave them access to both worlds: the world of their african parents and the world of their european parents.

some of these families became important figures in local politics.

in this sense, there was a continuity from the more informal communities discussed earlier.

however, the military presence and the growth of slavery meant that, in many important respects, these communities had become very different by the **18th century.**

# European Trade in Africa: The Early Period

## Why Europeans Came

Europeans came to Africa mainly for trade. This was the almost exclusive reason they arrived. Most hoped for a short stay. They wanted to become rich quickly.

Some people saw more than material wealth. They stayed longer. They formed families. Those families became part of their host communities. Even so, the commercial side always mattered.

## What African Rulers Wanted

Trade gave African rulers many opportunities. In the first two centuries, they especially demanded currency materials.

Cloth was one of the largest imports. It came from India and Europe. In the early 1700s, some Dutch ship cargoes were almost entirely cloth. These ships carried it to Senegambia and the Gold Coast.

Cloth stayed important through the 18th and 19th centuries. The French imported a blue indigo-dyed cloth called *pièce de guinée*. It was made near Pondichéry in India. They brought it to Senegambia. People used it as currency on the Upper Senegal River for a long time.

Cloth served as money in Senegambia. It also worked as currency in parts of Angola and the Gold Coast.

Copper was another major import. Benin and the Gold Coast received large amounts. Iron bars were also significant, especially in the Gold Coast and Senegambia. African traders required a brand mark on each iron bar. The mark had to show which European company supplied it. For example, the OWIC (Dutch West Indian Company) or the RAC (English Royal African Company). Without the correct mark, African traders gave the bars less value.

Cowries were imported from the Maldives to Benin. This trade started as early as 1505.

## Other Imports and Their Use

This period also saw imports of jewels. Manufactured goods like mirrors and basins arrived too. But most cargo value came from goods that could be turned into currency.

Evidence shows that imported metals had specific dimensions for trade. Copper rings, called manillas, were standardised. Iron bars had a set length, especially in Senegambia. People used these as mediums of exchange.

After trade, smiths melted the metals down. They made agricultural tools. They made weapons. They made artistic works. In Benin, this meant the famous Benin bronzes. Bronze production grew sharply in the 16th century. Copper imports increased at that time. The bronzes had been important before, but their production expanded greatly then.

## A Shift in the Late 17th Century

In the second half of the 17th century, a major shift happened. Currency imports declined. They were replaced by luxury goods for personal use. Alcohol and tobacco topped the list, especially from Brazil. Guns and gunpowder also became key imports.

The Nigerian historian Joseph Inikori links this change to a slowing in African economic growth. The drop in currency imports showed a market that had stopped growing. That market no longer needed as much money for exchange.

## A More Balanced Trade (Before the Late 1600s)

Until the second half of the 17th century, trade between Africa and Europe was fairly balanced. African rulers wanted more supplies of currency. Europeans did not focus only on the slave trade. That would come later. They also wanted to import gold and ivory.

Many places exported cloth. These included Allada, Benin, Cape Verde, Loango, and the rivers of Cameroon and Gabon. Some of this cloth was sold very far away. In the 17th century, it reached Brazil, Curaçao, and the United States. Curaçao is a Caribbean island near the coast of Venezuela. It belonged to the Dutch at that time.

Oyò cloth was traded to Yorubà communities in Brazil throughout the 18th century and into the 19th. In Salvador, Brazil, marketwomen of Yorubà ancestry worked as "cloth sellers" (*vendedoras de panos*) well into the 19th century.

In 1630, the Dutch invaded Portuguese colonies in Brazil. The Portuguese colonists formed an army. It included many Africans from the Gold Coast and Angola. The Gold Coast group demanded specific cloths as part of their pay and clothing. The Dutch sent those cloths specially from their fortress at Elmina.

## African Goods Beyond Cloth

The West African textile industry was not the only one that found overseas markets in the 16th and 17th centuries. Basketwork made by Gold Coast communities was highly prized in Holland in the early 17th century.

Ivory carvings made by the Sape peoples of Sierra Leone were found across Europe. People turned them into everyday items like salt cellars and candle holders. These objects were part of the export trade from that region of West Africa. In the 20th-century colonial era, some European art historians assumed these ivories came from Benin. The American art historian Peter Mark has now established that they actually came from Sierra Leone.

## Equal Partners at First

In sum, Europeans who settled in Africa did so as part of a commercial enterprise. Their trading presence in West Africa began between more or less equal partners. Diplomatic embassies show this clearly. Each side saw the other as kings and rulers by divine power.

Each side also imported money from the other. Europeans imported gold. Africans imported copper, cowries, cloth, and iron.

An Atlantic slave trade existed at this time. But it was not yet as important as it later became. In West Africa, the slave trade stayed quite minor until the 1640s. It had expanded a lot in Angola after 1580, with a trade to Brazil and the rest of Latin America. But that is West-Central Africa, not West Africa proper. In West Africa itself, only Senegambia saw a meaningful slave trade before the 1640s. After that, it began to grow in Allada and Calabar.

## The Later 17th Century: A New Pattern

The later 17th century brought change. European settlement and trade in West Africa followed a different pattern from then on. By this time, the slave trade was dominating. Europeans settled in fortified trading positions. They no longer lived informally among their African hosts. The economic terms of trade became less equal overall. That imbalance remained through the 18th century.

chapter_key: VI: Environmental Change, Competition and Changes in the European Presence
text:
# Changes in the First Half of the 17th Century

The first half of the 1700s saw many changes. These changes were vital in West Africa. They were also part of a bigger shift around the world. Wars and revolutions broke out in China, Europe, and Africa at the same time.

Two main causes drove these transformations:

- **Environmental pressures** from the "mini ice age" (which peaked in the 1640s)
- **Political competition** from the rise of the capitalist world system

---

## The Mini Ice Age

The world's climate changed a lot. This shift is called the **"mini ice age."**

From the 1570s onwards, global temperatures dropped sharply. This caused serious problems in many places.

In Africa:

- Droughts hit **Angola** (from around 1600)
- Droughts hit **Senegambia** (from around 1640)
- Floods struck the **Yorubà-speaking areas** of Nigeria and Benin (early 17th century)
- Heavy snow fell in **Morocco**

In the 1650s, the King of Allada sent ambassadors to Spain. He said one reason was to try to stop the terrible storms that had been hitting Allada.

Other parts of the world suffered too. Freezing temperatures ruined wheat and other crops. Food prices went up. The coldest temperatures came around **1640**. This is also when the biggest revolutions began.

In **China**, a civil war started. It ended with the fall of the Ming dynasty.

In **Europe**:

- Portugal declared independence from Spain in 1640
- A civil war in Portugal lasted until 1668
- A civil war began in England in 1641. The King was deposed and executed
- Civil conflict broke out in France

---

## What Caused the Cooling?

European historians used to blame changes in the sun's patterns.

A team of archaeologists based in **Colombia** now offers a new explanation.

In the 16th century, Europe conquered the Americas. This caused a massive population collapse among indigenous Americans. Recent estimates suggest that **90% of Native Americans died** from disease and war. That may have been 10–15% of the entire world's population.

When so many people died, two things happened:

- Forests grew back over old settlements and farmland
- There was less deforestation and fewer fires

The new forest growth absorbed carbon dioxide. Fewer fires meant less carbon dioxide was released. This is similar to how we understand global warming today: a balance between carbon emissions and carbon capture.

According to the Colombian archaeologists, this shift in carbon levels caused the drop in temperatures.

---

## Political Competition and Trade

Political competition grew as trade expanded. States that could control trade gained power.

In West Africa, building trading relationships with European partners became very important. States that did so prospered. But there was a cost.

In larger kingdoms like **Jolof** and **Kongo**, the coastal provinces grew stronger:

- **Kajoor** (in Jolof) broke away from central control by the 1550s
- **Nsoyo** (in Kongo) broke away in the early 17th century

Rival rulers wanted to open their own trading stations. They fought each other for the best access to international trade. This created conflict. It also increased demand for European goods. The result was a huge number of fortified trading posts built along:

- The **Gold Coast**
- The coasts of **Hueda** and **Allada**

These were built in the second half of the 17th century.

---

## Competition Among Europeans

European nations also competed for access to African trade. They often struggled against each other for the best positions.

However, this competition never led to direct military confrontations between European powers in Africa during this period. Wars between European nations were fought in Europe itself.

In Africa, European traders worked within a shared structure of trade. They cooperated even as they competed.

By the second half of the 17th century, trading companies from **Denmark, the Netherlands, England, France, and Germany** all wanted a foothold in West Africa. Each brought its best and most fashionable goods. The companies also negotiated with one another to swap items and build the best possible "assortment" for African buyers.

---

## What This Meant for African Rulers

The competition among European traders gave African rulers more power at the negotiating table. They could play one trader against another to get a better price.

But there was a catch. If a ruler did not meet the traders' demands, those traders would simply move on. They would go elsewhere in search of captives, ivory, and gold.

# Changes in the First Half of the 17th Century


The first half of the 1700s saw many changes.


These changes were vital in West Africa.


They were also part of a bigger shift around the world.


Wars and revolutions broke out at the same time.


China, Europe, and Africa all felt them.


---


## Two Main Causes


Two forces drove these transformations:


1. Environmental pressures from the "mini ice age" (which peaked in the 1640s)


2. Political competition from the rise of the capitalist world system


---


## The Mini Ice Age


The world's climate changed a lot.


This shift is called the **mini ice age**.


From the 1570s onwards, global temperatures dropped sharply.


This caused serious problems in many places.


### In Africa:


- Droughts hit **Angola** (from around 1600)


- Droughts hit **Senegambia** (from around 1640)


- Floods struck the **Yorubà-speaking areas** of Nigeria and Benin (early 17th century)


- Heavy snow fell in **Morocco**


In the 1650s, the king of Allada sent ambassadors to Spain.


He said one reason was to try to stop the terrible storms.


Those storms had been hitting Allada for years.


### In Other Parts of the World:


Freezing temperatures ruined wheat and other crops.


Food prices went up.


The coldest temperatures came around **1640**.


This is also when the biggest revolutions began.


In **China**, a civil war started.


It ended with the fall of the Ming dynasty.


In **Europe**:


- Portugal declared independence from Spain in 1640


- A civil war in Portugal lasted until 1668


- A civil war began in England in 1641. The king was deposed and executed.


- Civil conflict broke out in France


---


## What Caused the Cooling?


European historians used to blame changes in the sun's patterns.


A team of archaeologists based in **Colombia** now offers a new explanation.


In the 16th century, Europe conquered the Americas.


This caused a massive population collapse among indigenous Americans.


Recent estimates suggest that **90% of native Americans died**.


They died from disease and war.


That may have been 10–15% of the entire world's population.


### What Happened Next:


When so many people died, two things happened:


- Forests grew back over old settlements and farmland


- There was less deforestation and fewer fires


The new forest growth absorbed carbon dioxide.


Fewer fires meant less carbon dioxide was released.


This is similar to how we understand global warming today.


It is a balance between carbon emissions and carbon capture.


According to the Colombian archaeologists, this shift in carbon levels caused the drop in temperatures.


---


## Political Competition and Trade


Political competition grew as trade expanded.


States that could control trade gained power.


In West Africa, building trading relationships with European partners became very important.


States that did so prospered.


But there was a cost.


### Coastal Provinces Grew Stronger:


In larger kingdoms like **Jolof** and **Kongo**, the coastal provinces grew stronger:


- **Kajoor** (in Jolof) broke away from central control by the 1550s


- **Nsoyo** (in Kongo) broke away in the early 17th century


Rival rulers wanted to open their own trading stations.


They fought each other for the best access to international trade.


This created conflict.


It also increased demand for European goods.


The result was a huge number of fortified trading posts built along:


- The **Gold Coast**


- The coasts of **Hueda** and **Allada**


These were built in the second half of the 17th century.


---


## Competition Among Europeans


European nations also competed for access to African trade.


They often struggled against each other for the best positions.


However, this competition never led to direct military confrontations between European powers in Africa during this period.


Wars between European nations were fought in Europe itself.


In Africa, European traders worked within a shared structure of trade.


They cooperated even as they competed.


By the second half of the 17th century, trading companies from **Denmark**, **the Netherlands**, **England**, **France**, and **Germany** all wanted a foothold in West Africa.


Each brought its best and most fashionable goods.


The companies also negotiated with one another to swap items.


They built the best possible "assortment" for African buyers.


---


## What This Meant for African Rulers


The competition among European traders gave African rulers more power at the negotiating table.


They could play one trader against another to get a better price.


But there was a catch.


If a ruler did not meet the traders' demands, those traders would simply move on.


They would go elsewhere in search of captives, ivory, and gold.


So a **mutual dependence** grew between African rulers and European traders.


Each side needed the other.


At the same time, the environment was becoming more fragile.


In Africa and around the world, food shortages became common.


Resource problems also became common.


These problems often led to conflict.

# Reparation

Reparation is a form of payment. It is meant to make up for past harm. A group that was suppressed can receive this payment from the society that wronged them.

Most societies in the world have faced subjugation. More powerful groups or classes imposed control over them. Examples include:

- Colonialism
- The Jewish Holocaust during World War II
- The Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade (TAST)

After a suppressed group gains freedom, they often seek reparation. This payment can take two forms. It can be "in kind" (goods or services). Or it can be materialistic (money or property).

The most well-known and controversial case is reparation for slavery in Africa. The argument goes like this: descendants of Africans who were enslaved during the TAST deserve a compensatory payment.

# The Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade

The TAST moved millions of Africans to the New World. In this trade, humans were treated as goods. They were bought and sold like gold or ivory.

European merchants carried Africans across the Atlantic Ocean. This began after the discovery of the New World. The goal was to supply labour for plantations.

This trade caused deep harm in two places:

- **In Africa:** local societies were devastated.
- **In the diaspora:** enslaved people and their descendants suffered greatly.

Slaves were obtained through several means:

- Warfare
- Kidnapping
- Sale from markets
- Other sources

The suffering was severe at every stage:

1. The Middle Passage (the ocean crossing)
2. Life on the plantation system
3. Psychological trauma even after emancipation

These injustices affected slaves and their descendants in the Americas. Because of this, African-Americans and members of the Caribbean diaspora are increasingly calling for reparation.

# Christian Missions in Africa: A New Era

## Why Europe Turned to Africa

The missionary movement expanded into Africa for several reasons.

One key reason was a growing belief that Christians had a duty to help regenerate African peoples. The anti-slavery movement also played a vital role. Humanitarian conscience stirred European interest in the continent. Together, these forces gave new energy to mission work.

This "opening up" of Africa brought four major changes:

- **Commerce** – called "legitimate commerce," meaning trade that did not involve slaves
- **Christianity**
- **Civilization** (as Europeans defined it)
- **Colonization**

The idea of Christian responsibility for the regeneration of African peoples ran through all of these.

## The Costs and Early Challenges

Mission work came at a heavy cost. Many missionaries died young. The unfriendly tropical climate was often the cause.

In West Africa, another challenge appeared. Missionaries tried to move beyond the coast to reach people inland with the gospel. At the same time, Islam was expanding southward. This posed a real threat to Christian evangelizing efforts.

At first, the missionaries had little success. Many local people received the message with indifference. However, Christianity did win some early ground in coastal areas. These were territories filled with mulattos and other European trading communities.

## Early European Contact (Late 15th Century)

The first Europeans reached the West African coasts at the end of the fifteenth century. For several years, they focused on the slave trade. They paid little attention to evangelization or Christianizing the people of West Africa.

By the turn of the nineteenth century, that changed. Churches in Christian Europe began systematic efforts:

- **Anglicans, Methodists, and Baptists** were active in Sierra Leone
- **Presbyterians** worked alongside them in Nigeria
- **Methodists** also set up missions in Ghana, Gambia, and Dahomey

In the nineteenth century as well, Afro-Brazilians returned to Benin and Nigeria. They brought Catholicism with them.

## A New Era Begins (1787–1799)

Two events marked a new era:

- In **1787**, Black Christians from Nova Scotia settled in Sierra Leone.
- In **1799**, J. T. van der Kemp arrived at Cape Town. This began the missionary advance inland from that point.

New missionary societies also started work across many parts of Africa. These included:

- The LMS (London Missionary Society)
- The CMS (Church Missionary Society)
- The Holy Ghost Fathers
- The White Fathers

## Early Successes (1804–1811 and Beyond)

The CMS began working in freed slave villages in Sierra Leone in **1804**. The Methodists followed in **1811**.

Early successes included:

- Freetown and the surrounding villages
- The Liberian coast, where Afro-Americans and freed slaves were converted
- French trading posts at Grand Bassam (Ivory Coast), Assinie, and Libreville (Gabon)

## The Interior Remained Untouched… For Now

Apart from the extreme south and the Horn of Africa, Europeans had barely touched the interior before the last quarter of the nineteenth century.

At the end of the eighteenth century, the Evangelical Revival began bringing a large influx of missionaries to Africa. Their labours would produce the first fruits of an enduring Christian presence in Sub-Saharan Africa.

## Catholic Efforts in the Interior (1867–1892)

In the later nineteenth century, the vast African interior became the principal focus of Catholic priests. From **1867** until his death in **November 1892**, Cardinal Lavigerie planned the planting of churches across Africa south of the Sahara.

## When Did Modern Mission History Begin?

It is important to note: the modern history of Christian missions in Africa started in the **late eighteenth century**. However, Catholics had been present much earlier. They were there in the first centuries of the Christian era, especially during the early Portuguese voyages.

Because of this earlier presence, the rise of Christianizing missions in the late nineteenth century has been described as a **reprise** – a return or renewal rather than a brand-new start.

## Key Organizations and Dates

The late eighteenth century saw the rise of Christian groups in Europe that turned to the evangelization of Africa. Here are some key dates:

- **2 October 1792** – The Baptist Missionary Society was formed
- **1795** – The interdenominational London Missionary Society was established
- **1804** – The British and Foreign Bible Society was founded. Its task was to promote the translation and printing of the Holy Bible

At first, most missionary journeys were carried out by English-speaking Protestants. Later, in the **1820s and 1830s**, they were joined by continental Protestantism from Germany, Switzerland, and France. Related organizations also sprang up in Scandinavia, Holland, and the USA.

## What West Africa Owed to the Missionaries

West Africa owes much to Christian missionaries. They brought:

- A new religious faith that changed the beliefs and daily life of millions
- The foundation of Western-style education

The Portuguese were the first to introduce Christianity into West Africa. But after they left the West Coast in the mid-seventeenth century, the religion survived only in Upper Guinea. There, a bishop was maintained on the Cape Verde Islands. He also served part of the mainland.

It was not until the **nineteenth century** that the new religion was truly established across West Africa.

## What This Chapter Covers

In this chapter, we will examine how Christianity and Western-style education influenced West African values, attitudes, and life-styles.

In the nineteenth century as well, Afro-Brazilians returned to Benin and Nigeria. They brought Catholicism with them.


## A New Era Begins (1787–1799)

Two events marked a new era:

- In **1787**, Black Christians from Nova Scotia settled in Sierra Leone
- In **1799**, J. T. van der Kemp arrived at Cape Town

This began the missionary advance inland from that point.

New missionary societies also started work across many parts of Africa. These included:

- The LMS (London Missionary Society)
- The CMS (Church Missionary Society)
- The Holy Ghost Fathers
- The White Fathers


## Early Successes (1804–1811 and Beyond)

The CMS began working in freed slave villages in Sierra Leone in **1804**. The Methodists followed in **1811**.

Early successes included:

- Freetown and the surrounding villages
- The Liberian coast, where Afro-Americans and freed slaves were converted
- French trading posts at Grand Bassam (Ivory Coast), Assinie, and Libreville (Gabon)


## The Interior Remained Untouched… For Now

Apart from the extreme south and the Horn of Africa, Europeans had barely touched the interior before the last quarter of the nineteenth century.

At the end of the eighteenth century, the evangelical revival began bringing a large influx of missionaries to Africa. Their labours would produce the first fruits of an enduring Christian presence in sub-Saharan Africa.


## Catholic Efforts in the Interior (1867–1892)

In the later nineteenth century, the vast African interior became the principal focus of Catholic priests.

From **1867** until his death in **November 1892**, Cardinal Lavigerie planned the planting of churches across Africa south of the Sahara.


## When Did Modern Mission History Begin?

It is important to note this: the modern history of Christian missions in Africa started in the **late eighteenth century**.

However, Catholics had been present much earlier. They were there in the first centuries of the Christian era, especially during the early Portuguese voyages.

Because of this earlier presence, the rise of Christianizing missions in the late nineteenth century has been described as a **reprise** – a return or renewal rather than a brand-new start.


## Key Organizations and Dates

The late eighteenth century saw the rise of Christian groups in Europe that turned to the evangelization of Africa. Here are some key dates:

- **2 October 1792** – The Baptist Missionary Society was formed
- **1795** – The Interdenominational London Missionary Society was established
- **1804** – The British and Foreign Bible Society was founded

Its task was to promote the translation and printing of the Holy Bible.

At first, most missionary journeys were carried out by English-speaking Protestants. Later, in the **1820s and 1830s**, they were joined by continental Protestantism from Germany, Switzerland, and France. Related organizations also sprang up in Scandinavia, Holland, and the USA.


## What West Africa Owed to the Missionaries

West Africa owes much to Christian missionaries. They brought:

- A new religious faith that changed the beliefs and daily life of millions
- The foundation of Western-style education

The Portuguese were the first to introduce Christianity into West Africa. But after they left the west coast in the mid-seventeenth century, the religion survived only in Upper Guinea. There, a bishop was maintained on the Cape Verde Islands. He also served part of the mainland.

It was not until the **nineteenth century** that the new religion was truly established across West Africa.


## What This Chapter Covers

In this chapter, we will examine how Christianity and Western-style education influenced West African values, attitudes, and life-styles.

# Evangelical Missionary Movements

In the second half of the 18th century, a strong wave of evangelical faith spread across the United Kingdom, Europe, and the New World. This movement inspired men and women to start new religious societies. The members of these societies went to Africa and other lands. They had three main goals:

- Spread the message of the Gospel
- Provide social services to local people
- Help end slavery and the slave trade

These movements saw their work as a form of reparation. They believed Europe owed this to Africa. For centuries, Europeans had exploited African peoples. The Trans Atlantic slave trade had caused deep harm to African society. These missionaries viewed their efforts as part of making amends for that history.


## Protestant Evangelical Societies

Several early Protestant evangelical societies were founded in Great Britain:

- The Baptist Missionary Society
- The Church Missionary Society for the Propagation of the Gospel
- The Wesleyan Missionary Society
- The Presbyterian Missionary Society of the Church of Scotland (this is what it became known as)

Similar groups formed in other European countries. For example:

- The Basel Missionary Society, founded in Switzerland
- The Breman Mission, formed in Germany

In the Americas, evangelical societies also emerged:

- The Baptist Missionary Board
- The Nova Scotian Methodists

The Nova Scotian Methodists worked among the Maroons. These were people who had settled mainly in Liberia.


## Roman Catholic Missionary Societies

While Protestant evangelical movements grew in West Africa, the Roman Catholic Church was also active in Europe. The Vatican supported these efforts through its Propagation of Faith office. The Cardinal Secretary of this office later became Pope Gregory XVI.

With this support, several Roman Catholic missionary societies were founded:

- The Congregation of the Holy Ghost (commonly called the "Holy Ghost Fathers")
- The Society of African Missions (SMA)
- The Society of Missionaries of Africa (popularly known as the "White Fathers" because they wore white, Muslim-like clothing)
- The Society of the Divine Word (SVD, from its Latin name)

These societies laid the foundations of the Roman Catholic Church in West Africa. This presence lasted through to the independence period. At that time, African clergy replaced the white pastors.

text:
# The Coming of Christianity to Nigeria

## Early Catholic Missions

In the days of Portuguese contact with Nigeria, Catholic priests set up missionary stations in Benin and nearby areas. Portuguese missionaries worked from the island of São Tomé. Later, Spanish missionaries worked in Benin.

However, Christianity was not firmly established in Nigeria until the nineteenth century.

## The Yoruba Recaptives

The real start came among the Yoruba recaptives. These people had embraced Christianity while in Sierra Leone. The British Royal Naval Squadron had freed them from slave trading ships. They returned home between 1839 and 1845.

Pastors of the Church Missionary Society (C.M.S.) visited these new Christian communities. They came first from Badagry, then later from Sierra Leone. They worked in Abeokuta and other towns.

One of the first missionaries was Rev. Henry Townsend. He went from Sierra Leone to Badagry in 1842. In his company was Rev. Ajayi Crowther.

## C.M.S. Churches Grow

The pioneer missionaries saw success. C.M.S. churches were firmly established in several important towns:

- Abeokuta (1846)
- Lagos (1851)
- Ibadan (1853)
- Oyo (1856)

Next, branches of the C.M.S. church were founded in south-eastern Nigeria. The chief centres were Bonny and Brass.

Bishop Ajayi Crowther did important work in these parts of southern Nigeria. He was assisted by the Igbo recaptive Rev. J. C. Taylor. Their effects can still be seen today.

## Other Missionary Groups

Other missionaries also opened stations in the country.

**The Baptists.** Under the American evangelist Thomas Bowen, Baptist missionaries started work from Ogbomosho in 1855.

**The Church of Scotland (Presbyterian).** The Rev. Hope Waddell led this group. He started pioneering work in Calabar in 1846. He was later joined by the Rev. Hugh Goldie and William Anderson.

**Mary Slessor.** She arrived in Nigeria in 1876. For many years, she worked hard as a missionary nurse. Her memory is revered in Nigeria. She succeeded in stopping the killing of twins in the areas where she served.

## The Roman Catholic Church

The story would be incomplete without Father Berghero. He was an Italian Roman Catholic priest. He operated from Whydah, in what is today the People's Republic of Benin (formerly Dahomey).

In 1860, Father Berghero visited Abeokuta and Lagos. Freed Catholic slaves from Brazil welcomed him warmly. A permanent station was set up in Lagos in 1868. Soon, others followed at Lokoja, Abeokuta, and Ibadan.

Within ten years of Father Berghero's visit, the Roman Catholic Church in Nigeria was well established. It no longer needed to be administered from Dahomey.

By 1885, the church had spread further inland. This was thanks to Father Joseph Lutz. He started work around Onitsha in 1886. He spread the gospel in many parts of present-day Imo and Anambra States. Another important Catholic missionary in this area was the Irishman Bishop Shanahan.

## Missionaries Enter Hausaland

Lokoja had a small C.M.S. station as early as 1858. But it was not until 1889 that missionaries entered Hausaland. This region was predominantly Muslim.

For many years, their converts were limited to two groups:

- People of southern Nigerian extraction who lived in the north
- The large non-Muslim population of the north

# Europe in the 14th Century

Europe was in a bad way. The Plague spread between **1346** and **1353**. It killed an estimated **30 to 50%** of the European population.

Some archaeologists believe the Plague also hit West African populations. This idea is still debated. The archaeologist **Gérard Chouin** has been its strongest supporter.

---

# A Labour Crisis in Portugal

The population collapse caused many problems for nations like Portugal. The workforce had more than halved. Much farming land was abandoned. Forests and wild plants took over the fields.

African labourers helped fill this gap. In **1471**, the Portuguese parliament (the **Cortes**) met at Évora. Their records show that African workers were vital for clearing wasteland in Portugal. This points to a serious labour shortage after the Plague. It also shows the role of African labour in fixing it.

Many nobles had lost their serfs (their farm workers). Civil wars broke out in Portugal in the **1380s**. Bread was scarce because wheat was short. The Portuguese currency, called the **escudo**, suffered very high inflation.

These problems pushed Portugal to look outward:

- **Morocco** was a fertile country that grew wheat.
- Sailing along the West African coast might give access to **gold supplies**. This could help protect the escudo.

---

# Growth in West Africa

The situation in West Africa was very different. In the 15th century, many states there were expanding and growing:

- **Mossi** was established in what is now Burkina Faso.
- **Kano** became a major power.
- **Songhay** rose to take over from the Mali Empire.

Much of this growth came with increased gold production in the **Akan states of Ghana**. So much gold was produced that traders at Kano could not find enough goods to exchange for it. Many left empty-handed. This account comes from an early 16th-century Muslim traveller from southern Spain, known as **Leo Africanus**.

---

# How Portugal Learned About Africa

Portugal learned about this growth through several channels.

Around **1375**, a Majorcan Jew named **Abraham Cresques** drew the **Catalan Atlas**. This map showed the power of Mali and its gold production in detail. It also showed strong trade links between Spain and West Africa across the Sahara. These routes were often used by Jewish traders.

These traders spread news about West Africa in Spain and Portugal. Jewish communities lived in Saharan settlements such as **Tuat**. After riots against Spanish Jews in **1391**, more of them settled in Morocco. There, they worked in the carpet and textile trade with the Mali Empire.

---

# Why Portugal Sailed

Portuguese leaders knew something about conditions in Africa. They were keen to connect with West African gold producers. (Portugal itself had a large Jewish population.)

They also hoped to find **Prester John**. This was a Christian king they believed lived somewhere in Africa. They wanted a Christian alliance against the growing Islamic **Ottoman Empire**. They also wanted to divert some of the gold supply toward Europe. Prester John probably referred to the Christian King of Ethiopia, but no one knew this at the time.

---

# The Result

All of these factors shaped the Portuguese voyages to West Africa. In **1442**, they arrived at the **Senegal River**.

# The Church in Medieval Europe

## One Institution Ruled All

After Rome fell, one institution remained organized: the Christian Church. It was united in its beliefs. But it was also split into two branches. One branch was western. The other was eastern. This split was not official at first.

In 1054, the split became real. This event is called the **Great Schism**.

## Two Branches, Two Centers

The **eastern branch** set up its center in Constantinople. It was led by the Patriarch of Constantinople. This title was roughly equal to the pope's role in the west. The eastern Church used **Greek** for its services.

The **western branch** stayed in Rome. It was led by the **pope**. It became known as the **Roman Catholic Church**. It kept using **Latin**.

## A Strict Hierarchy

After the split, each branch kept a strict chain of authority. In the western Church, it looked like this:

- The **pope** in Rome sat at the top.
- He oversaw a large bureaucracy led by **cardinals**. They were called "princes of the church."
- Below them came **archbishops**.
- Then **bishops**.
- At the bottom were **priests**.

During this time, the Roman Church became the most powerful international organization in western Europe.

## Life Revolved Around the Church

Farm life depended on the seasons. Village and family life depended on the Church. The two ideas fit together.

The Church held special ceremonies called **sacraments**. These marked every stage of a person's life:

- Birth
- Growing into adulthood
- Marriage
- Burial

These events brought people back to church again and again.

## Replacing Old Beliefs

As Christianity spread across Europe, it replaced older beliefs. Pagan views went away. Animistic views went away. The Church explained supernatural events in its own way. It explained the forces of nature in its own way.

The new story was this:

A **benevolent God** lived in heaven. He created the universe. He existed beyond nature and beyond what people could see or know. He controlled all events on earth.

He also waged war against a force of darkness. That force was called the **Devil**, or **Satan**. Satan operated here on earth. In the end, God would defeat him. But until then, Satan still had power. He could trick humans. He could lead them to do evil. He could make them sin.

## Every Event Had a Spiritual Meaning

Nothing happened by chance. Everything carried a spiritual message.

- If a person got sick, it might mean they had sinned.
- If crops failed, it might mean the villagers had not said their prayers.

People who felt guilty became **penitents**. They went to the priest and confessed their sins. The priest then did two things:

1. He **absolved** them (forgave their sins).
2. He assigned **penance** (a task or act of self-punishment) so they could atone for what they had done. This was meant to save them from eternal damnation.

Because of this role, the parish priest held enormous power over his parishioners' lives.

## The Pope's Power

The pope made final decisions on all matters of **theology**. He interpreted God's will and shared it with the people. But his authority did not stop there. He also had power over **temporal** (everyday, political) matters.

The Church could **excommunicate** a person. This meant cutting them off from the faith. It meant sending their soul to hell forever. Even kings and queens feared this power. They dared not challenge the Church openly.

## The Seat of All Knowledge

The Church also held all learning in medieval Europe.

**Latin**, the language of the Church, served as a unifying force. Europe was made up of many isolated regions. Each region had its own dialect. People could not always understand one another. Latin bridged that gap. In the early Middle Ages, nations as we know them today did not yet exist.

Most serfs could not read or write. They were illiterate. So they depended on their literate priests. The priests read the Bible for them. The priests interpreted it for them. The Bible was understood to be the word of God. Without those priests, the serfs had no access to that word at all.

# Jerusalem and the Crusades

## A Holy City

Jerusalem is a holy city. Three faiths claim it: Judaism, Christianity, and Islam.

King Solomon built the Temple there in the tenth century BCE. In 33 CE, the Romans crucified Jesus on that same ground. Christians believe he rose into heaven from here. They also believe he promised to return. Muslims believe Muhammad traveled to heaven from this place in 621. He went to receive instructions about prayer.

Claims on this land go very deep. Emotions run high among all three faiths. Yet evidence shows the three religions lived in harmony for centuries.

## The Crusades Begin

In 1095, European Christians made a decision. They would retake Jerusalem from Muslim rulers. They also wanted to conquer what they called the Holy Lands. This area stretched from modern-day Turkey in the north. It ran along the Mediterranean coast down to the Sinai Peninsula. Muslims held all of it.

The Crusades had begun.

## Why Knights Fought

Religious zeal drove many knights. Four Crusades took place over the years. But other motives mattered too:

- Adventure
- The chance to win land and a title
- The Church's promise of full forgiveness of sins

Most Crusaders were French knights. In June 1099, they retook Jerusalem. What followed was horrific slaughter.

A French writer went with them. He wrote this eyewitness account:

> "On the top of Solomon's Temple, to which they had climbed in fleeing, many were shot to death with arrows and cast down headlong from the roof. Within this Temple, about ten thousand were beheaded. If you had been there, your feet would have been stained up to the ankles with the blood of the slain. What more shall I tell? Not one of them was allowed to live. They did not spare the women and children."

A Muslim eyewitness gave a different detail. The conquerors stripped the temple of its wealth. They also looted private homes.

## Saladin Takes Back Jerusalem

In 1187, Muslim forces took back the city. Their leader was the legendary Saladin.

Europe reacted fast. King Richard I of England went by the name "the Lionheart." He joined others to launch another campaign.

The fight for the Holy Lands did not end quickly. In 1291, the Crusaders lost their Mediterranean stronghold at Acre. Acre is in present-day Israel. A few years later, the last Christians left the area.

## Lasting Effects: The Negative Side

The Crusades had lasting effects. Some were good. Many were not.

On the negative side, wide-scale persecution of Jews began. Christians grouped Jews with "infidel" Muslims. They labeled them "the killers of Christ." In the centuries that followed, kings acted against Jewish people. Some expelled them from their kingdoms. Others forced them to pay heavy tributes just for the right to stay.

Hatred between Muslims and Christians also grew. Intolerance spread.

## Lasting Effects: The Positive Side

On the positive side, maritime trade between East and West expanded greatly.

Crusaders experienced new things. They felt silk. They tasted spices. They used porcelain. Desire for these goods created new markets for merchants.

Venice benefited most. This Adriatic port city prospered enormously from trade with Islamic merchants. From the tenth century on, merchant ships carried valuable goods between western European ports and the East. These routes were collectively called the Silk Road.

In the days of Marco Polo, Venetian sailors traveled to ports on the Black Sea. They set up their own colonies along the Mediterranean Coast.

But the old Silk Road had serious problems:

- It was costly
- It was slow
- It was unprofitable

Muslim middlemen collected taxes every time goods changed hands. Robbers waited in ambush for treasure-laden caravans.

A new route was needed. Sailors wanted a direct water path to the East. This would cut out the land portion of the trip entirely. They also wanted a route to the Spice Islands. These islands are in modern-day Indonesia. Muslim rulers kept their location secret.

Venice had longtime rivals. The merchants of Genoa and Florence also looked west, searching for new paths.

# The Long History of Slavery

Slavery is very old. It has existed for thousands of years.

The ancient Greek philosopher Aristotle made a claim. He said some peoples were *homunculi*. This word means "humanlike but not really people." For example, he thought this applied to anyone who did not speak Greek.

Both the Bible and the Koran contain passages about enslaved people. These texts address how enslaved people should be treated.

Vikings raided lands from Ireland all the way to Russia. They brought back enslaved people of many different nationalities.

During the Middle Ages, traders worked in the interior of Africa. They moved enslaved people along well-established routes. They sold them along the Mediterranean coast.

Slavers also brought enslaved Europeans to the Caribbean. Many of these people were children. They were orphaned or homeless. They were captured in the cities of Ireland.

---

## When Did Slavery Become Based on Race?

This is a key question. The answer appears to lie in the New World.

European colonists introduced new crops. These included sugar and coffee. Both required grueling, labor-intensive work.

The colonists needed more workers. They could not fill this need from prisoners. They also could not rely on indentured servants. So they turned to African laborers.

The Portuguese wanted a trade route to India. But they did something else too. They built forts along the West African coast. The purpose was to export people to Europe.

Historians believe that by the year 1500, Black enslaved people made up 10 percent of the population in Lisbon and Seville.

The Catholic Church frowned on enslaving Christians. Because of this, European slave traders expanded their reach further down the coast of Africa. They looked for non-Christian peoples to enslave.

---

## Racially Based Slavery in the New World

Europeans settled in Brazil, the Caribbean, and North America. There, they built a system of slavery based on race.

The need for a massive labor force was greater here than in western Europe. The land was well suited to growing sugar, coffee, rice, and later cotton.

To meet the ever-growing demand for these crops, large plantations were created.

These plantations needed a specific kind of labor supply. It had to be:

- **Permanent** – workers who would stay
- **Plentiful** – enough people to work at scale
- **Identifiable** – easy to recognize and track
- **Skilled** – able to do the hard physical work

Africans fit this need for several reasons. They were already familiar with farming. They also knew animal husbandry well. They had a distinct, identifying skin color. And they could be supplied through the existing African slave trade networks.

This process set the stage for New World slavery to expand into North America.

# Portugal and the Age of Exploration

## Prince Henry and Early Voyages

In the 1400s, Portugal's Prince Henry the Navigator led his country's exploration of Africa and the Atlantic Ocean.

With his support, Portuguese sailors found an eastward route to Africa. They set up a foothold there. This foothold became the base for Portugal's trade empire in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

## Building an Atlantic Empire

Portuguese mariners colonized several island groups:

- The Canary Islands
- Cape Verde
- The Azores Islands
- The island of Madeira

Merchants used these islands as stopping points. From there, they launched longer voyages.

From these strategic spots, Portugal spread its empire in three directions:

- Down the western coast of Africa to the Congo
- Along the western coast of India
- To Brazil on the eastern coast of South America

Portugal also set up trading posts in China and Japan.

## A Small Empire with Big Reach

The Portuguese did not rule over a huge landmass. But they held key islands and coastal ports. This gave them near-total control of sea trade routes. By the 1400s, Portugal ran a global network of trading posts.

## Sugar, Slavery, and the Atlantic World

Portuguese traders traveled to western Africa. There, they encountered the African slave trade. This trade was already active among African states.

The Portuguese saw a use for enslaved labor. They wanted to grow sugar on their Atlantic islands. Sugar was very profitable. So the Portuguese began exporting enslaved Africans, along with ivory and gold.

Sugar drove the Atlantic slave trade forward. The Portuguese islands quickly filled with sugar plantations.

The Portuguese also sold enslaved people to other European nations. This gave those nations a labor force they needed.

In the years that followed, European exploration spread. Slavery spread with it. Over time, much of the Atlantic World became one vast sugar-plantation system. In this system, Africans worked to produce sugar for European buyers.

# Columbus's Letter: A Window Into Spanish Goals

## How the Story Was Built

The most famous Spanish explorers told a story. That story said Europeans were superior. It also said Native Americans were savage.

But where did that story come from?

It came from the conquistadors themselves. They wrote documents called *pruebas de méritos*. This means "proofs of merit." Their goal was simple: win royal favor back in Spain. They exaggerated. They embellished. They shaped facts to flatter their kings and queens.

What follows is a passage from one such document. It comes from Columbus's letter, written in 1493, addressed to Luis de Santángel. This letter shows how wild reports from explorers created lasting myths about the Spanish conquest and the New World.

---

## What Columbus Wrote (1493)

### The Land

"This island is very large. Like all the others, it stretches far and wide.

It has many ports along the coast. They are better than any in Christendom. There are also many fine, large rivers that flow steadily.

The land rises high. It has mountains and peaks. These are much higher than those on the centre isle [Cuba]. The mountains are beautiful. They come in a thousand different shapes. You can climb them. They are covered with trees of endless kinds. The trees grow so tall they seem to touch the sky. I was told they never lose their leaves."

### What Grows There

"There is honey. There are many kinds of birds. There is a great variety of fruit.

Inland, there are numerous mines of metal. There are also innumerable people living there."

### Hispaniola as a Whole

"Hispaniola is a marvel. Its hills and mountains are fine. Its plains and open country are rich. The land is fertile for planting crops. It is good for grazing animals. It is well suited for building towns and villages.

The seaports are incredibly fine. The rivers are magnificent. Most of them carry gold in their beds.

The trees, fruits, and grasses here differ widely from those on Juana [Cuba]. There are many spices. There are vast mines of gold and other metals on this island."

### The People

"They have no iron. They have no steel. They have no weapons. And they do not seem fit for them.

They are well-made men. They stand tall. But they appear extraordinarily timid.

Their only arms are sticks of cane, cut while still in seed. A sharpened stick is fixed to the end. Even these, they are afraid to use.

Often I sent two or three men ashore to a town to talk with them. The natives came out in great numbers. But the moment they saw our men arrive, they fled. They did not wait even a second. And yet I had protected them from all injury."

---

## Questions for You

**1.** What does this letter reveal about what Spain wanted in the New World?

Look at what Columbus highlights: gold, spices, fertile land, ports, metals. Now look at how he describes the people who already lived there. What pattern do you see?

**2.** Imagine you are a European reader in 1493. You have never seen this place. You read this letter for the first time. How might it shape what you believe about the New World and its people?

Think about:
- What words make the land sound like a treasure to be claimed?
- What words make the native people sound weak or childlike?
- Why would those choices matter to a king deciding whether to fund more voyages?

# The Impact of European Exploration

European explorers changed the world in two places at once: the Americas and Europe.

Their discoveries started a big exchange of ideas. New World goods helped pay for it. This exchange linked European nations together. It also reached the lands that Europeans conquered.

## Spain's Golden Age

Spain received gold and silver from the Americas. These riches fueled a golden age called the *Siglo de Oro*. During this time, Spanish art and literature flourished.

Two things poured into Spain:

- Riches came in from the colonies.
- New ideas came in from other countries and new lands.

The Hapsburg dynasty ruled many territories. These included Austria, the Netherlands, Naples, Sicily, and Spain. The Hapsburgs encouraged and paid for artists of all kinds. They funded painters, sculptors, musicians, architects, and writers. This support created a bloom of Spanish Renaissance culture.

## Don Quixote

One famous work from this period is *The Ingenious Gentleman Don Quixote of La Mancha*. Miguel de Cervantes wrote it. It came out in two volumes: 1605 and 1618.

The book tells a colorful story. The main character is an hidalgo, which means a gentleman. He reads many tales of chivalry and knighthood. He reads so much that he can no longer tell reality from fiction.

His faithful sidekick is Sancho Panza. Together, they leave reality behind. Don Quixote sets out to revive chivalry. He does battle with what he sees as the enemies of Spain.

# The Spanish Come to New Mexico

## A New Empire Looks North

Farther west, Spain wanted more land.

The Spanish in Mexico looked north. They saw the land of the Pueblo Natives. They wanted it for their empire.

King Philip II gave orders. Juan de Oñate explored the American southwest for Spain. This happened in the late 1590s.

The Spanish hoped to find gold and silver. They thought New Mexico would be rich. But the land produced little of value to them.

## Santa Fe Is Founded

In 1610, Spanish settlers moved into the area. They settled at a place called Santa Fe.

Santa Fe had a very long original name: *La Villa Real de la Santa Fe de San Francisco de Asís*. This means "Royal City of the Holy Faith of St. Francis of Assisi."

Many Pueblo villages were near this spot.

Santa Fe became the capital of the Kingdom of New Mexico. That kingdom was part of a larger Spanish territory called the Viceroyalty of New Spain. The headquarters for that territory sat in Mexico City.

## Missionaries and Conflict

Franciscan missionaries came to the area. They worked to convert the Pueblo people to Catholicism. This was their way of "conquering" souls, just as they had done in other Spanish colonies.

At first, the Pueblo accepted some parts of Catholicism. These parts fit with their own long-standing beliefs about the world.

But then things changed.

Spanish priests told the natives to drop all old ways. They wanted total change. The priests also focused on the young people. They drew children away from their parents. This deeply insulted the Pueblo.

Other troubles piled up:

- A long drought hit the land.
- Apache and Navajo groups attacked more often in the 1670s.
- The Pueblo came to believe these hardships were linked to the Spanish presence.

All of this pushed the Pueblo toward action. They wanted the Spanish gone. They wanted their own religion back.

## Popé Calls for Change

# English Colonies in North America

## Who Promoted Colonization?

Many people promoted English colonization of North America. Most of them never crossed the Atlantic Ocean. They wrote about the wealth the English would find there.

These boosters had two main goals. First, they wanted to make money. They hoped to import raw resources or sell English goods in new markets. Second, they wanted to spread Protestantism.

The migrants who actually made the journey had different goals.

## The Chesapeake Colonies: Virginia and Maryland

In Chesapeake Bay, English migrants founded two colonies. These were Virginia and Maryland. Both colonies had a clear commercial focus.

Early Virginians at Jamestown hoped to find gold. They did not. Settlers in both colonies quickly learned one thing. Growing tobacco was the only sure way to make money.

Thousands of young Englishmen came to these colonies. Most were unmarried, unemployed, and impatient. A few Englishwomen also came. All of them pinned their hopes for a better life on the tobacco fields.

## New England: A Different Story

A very different group of English men and women went to New England. The climate there was cold. The soil was rocky. What drove these settlers was religion, not profit.

Many Puritans crossing the Atlantic brought their families. They brought their children. Often, they followed their ministers in a migration "beyond the seas."

They envisioned something specific. They wanted to build a new English Israel. In this place, reformed Protestantism would grow and thrive. It would serve as a model for the rest of the Christian world. It would also act as a counter to what they saw as the Catholic menace.

While Virginia and Maryland expanded their tobacco fields, New England built towns around the church. Each congregation decided what was best for itself. The Congregational Church is the result of this Puritan enterprise in America.

Many historians believe something important happened here. The fault lines that later separated the North and South in the United States began with the profound differences between the Chesapeake colonies and New England.

## Why the Differences Began: Problems in England

The source of those differences lay in England itself. In the early 1600s, the English state church grew more demanding. This was the Church of England, established in the 1530s. It demanded conformity. That meant compliance with its practices.

Puritans pushed for greater reforms. They did not want to simply comply.

By the 1620s, things got worse. The Church of England began to see leading Puritan ministers as outlaws. It saw their followers as a national security threat. Why? Because they opposed the church's power.

As the noose of conformity tightened around them, many Puritans made a decision. They would remove themselves to New England. By 1640, New England had a population of twenty-five thousand people.

Meanwhile, loyal members of the Church of England went the other way. These were the people who ridiculed and mocked Puritans at home and in New England. They flocked to Virginia for economic opportunity.

## Civil War and Its Aftermath

The troubles in England escalated in the 1640s. A civil war broke out. On one side stood the Royalists. These were supporters of King Charles I and the Church of England. On the other side stood the Parliamentarians. These were Puritan reformers and their supporters in Parliament.

In 1649, the Parliamentarians gained the upper hand. They made an unprecedented move. They executed Charles I.

In the 1650s, England became a republic. This was a state without a king.

English colonists in America closely followed these events. Many Puritans left New England and returned home. They wanted to take part in the struggle against the king and the national church.

Other English men and women watched from the Chesapeake colonies and elsewhere in the English Atlantic World. They looked on in horror. The Parliamentarians, led by Puritan insurgents, appeared to unleash mayhem in England.

The turmoil in England had a lasting effect. It made the administration of the colonies difficult. Imperial oversight of both the Chesapeake and New England colonies became hard to maintain. Over time, the two regions developed divergent cultures.

# From Servitude to Slavery: The Chesapeake and the West Indies

## How Slavery Took Hold

The shift from indentured servitude to slavery happened first in the West Indies. It did not happen in the mainland colonies at first.

**Barbados.** English colonists settled this small island in the 1620s. At first, they grew tobacco as their main export crop. In the 1640s, they switched to sugarcane. They began to rely more and more on African enslaved people for labor.

**Jamaica.** In 1655, England took control of Jamaica from Spain. The English quickly turned it into a sugar-producing island. It ran on forced labor. It served England's growing empire.

**The Chesapeake colonies.** Slavery came here more slowly. But by the end of the seventeenth century, both Virginia and Maryland had adopted chattel slavery. Under this system, the law defined Africans as property, not people. Enslaved people grew tobacco on large plantations. Chesapeake colonists also enslaved Native people.

---

## The First Africans in Virginia (1619)

The first Africans arrived in Virginia in 1619. At that time, slavery did not exist in England. It had not yet become a fixed institution in colonial America either.

Many of these early Africans worked as servants. Like their White counterparts, they could buy land and own it. Some converted to Christianity. A few became free landowners. They even had White servants working for them.

The status of Africans in the Chesapeake changed over time. In the last decades of the seventeenth century, they shifted from being treated as servants to being treated as enslaved people.

---

## Bacon's Rebellion (1675–1676)

### What it was

Bacon's Rebellion was an uprising in Virginia. Both White and Black people took part. They believed the Virginia government blocked their access to land and wealth. They also felt the government did too little to remove Native Americans from the frontier. This rebellion sped up the shift toward African slavery in the Chesapeake colonies.

### Who led it
